Note: The option’s wording is imprecise. Index projections primarily project enriched data into one or more search indexes; projections into a secondary knowledge store are a separate feature.

Option B. To project vector fields onto a map.

Index projections are unrelated to geographic maps. Vector fields represent embeddings used for vector similarity search.

Option C. To index only metadata.

Index projections can include enriched content, document chunks, parent identifiers, metadata, and vector fields. They are not restricted to metadata.

Option D. To delete old documents.

Index projections do not delete outdated documents. Their purpose is to control how enriched data is projected into search indexes, not to manage document deletion.

question_html: In the context of enterprise knowledge retrieval, what is a “freshness” issue?

options.text: The index contains stale, outdated documents that no longer reflect current truth
The model only generates new words
The embedding model is too new
The chunk size is too small

explanation_html: If the knowledge base is not updated regularly, retrieved information might be obsolete, leading to incorrect answers. A good RAG system requires a process to refresh and re-index documents as they change.

question_html: If a vector search index uses Product Quantization (PQ), what trade-off is being made?

options.text: Reduced memory footprint and faster search at the cost of some recall loss
No change in memory, but slower indexing

explanation_html: PQ compresses high-dimensional vectors into short codes, reducing memory usage and speeding up distance computations. However, it is a lossy compression and can slightly degrade search accuracy compared to full-precision vectors.

question_html: In a RAG system, when using a cross-encoder reranker, which operation is most computationally heavy?

options.text: Processing each query-document pair simultaneously through the transformer

explanation_html: A cross-encoder concatenates the query and document and passes them together through a transformer, which is expensive. For thousands of candidates, this can become a bottleneck, so it’s usually applied only to top-k results from a faster retriever.

question_html: What is the role of a “fusion” step (e.g., Reciprocal Rank Fusion) in a multi-retrieval setup?

options.text: To merge and re-rank results from different retrieval sources (e.g., BM25 + vector) into a single ranked list

explanation_html: RRF combines rankings from multiple retrieval methods by aggregating reciprocal ranks, providing a simple yet effective way to produce a unified result set when using hybrid search strategies.

question_html: Which technique can automatically adjust chunk boundaries based on semantic coherence, rather than fixed character count?

options.text: Semantic chunking using embedding-based similarity thresholds

explanation_html: Semantic chunking computes embeddings for successive sentences and groups them until similarity drops below a threshold, creating chunks that are topically coherent. This can improve retrieval relevance over arbitrary fixed-size splits.

question_html: Why is it beneficial to store document-level metadata (like title, URL, last modified) alongside chunks in a vector store?

options.text: To enable filtered searches and provide source attribution in the generated answer
To replace the need for embeddings
To make the vector store read-only

explanation_html: Metadata filtering allows queries to target specific subsets (e.g., documents from a certain date range). Source attribution gives end users the ability to verify the generated answer against the original document, improving trust.

question_html: Which factor most directly influences the dimension of a dense embedding vector?

options.text: The length of the input text
The output size configured in the embedding model (e.g., 768, 1536)
The number of documents in the index

explanation_html: Embedding models produce fixed-size vectors regardless of input length (within token limits). The dimensionality is a model architecture parameter, such as 768 for many BERT-base variants or 1536 for Ada.

question_html: In Azure AI Search, how can you ensure that vector search only retrieves documents in a specific language?

options.text: It’s impossible without a custom filter
Add a metadata field for language and use a filter expression in the query
Set the embedding model to multilingual

explanation_html: By indexing a language metadata field and applying a $filter during the vector query, you can restrict results to documents of a certain language. The filter is evaluated against the metadata, not the vector similarity.

question_html: What is one advantage of using an asynchronous indexing pipeline for RAG?

options.text: It decouples document updates from real-time query traffic, allowing large-scale ingestion without affecting query latency
It eliminates the need for a reranker

explanation_html: Asynchronous indexing processes documents in the background, so the search service remains responsive for queries. This is critical for enterprise scenarios where documents are continuously added or updated.

question_html: Which approach can improve the robustness of a RAG system against irrelevant retrieved passages?

options.text: Include all retrieved passages, even noise
Instruct the model to only use information from passages that are clearly relevant and to ignore contradictory or off-topic text
Remove all retrieval and rely on the model’s internal knowledge
Set the chunk size to 1 token

explanation_html: Good prompt engineering for RAG includes explicit instructions to filter out noise. The model is told to base its answer solely on the provided excerpts that are actually relevant and to disregard distractor passages, reducing hallucination risk.

question_html: What is the main purpose of a “seed” or “initial” query when setting up a RAG pipeline for a chatbot?

options.text: It serves as the user’s first input that triggers retrieval, often augmented with conversation history for better context

explanation_html: In conversational RAG, the current user message (and possibly rephrased history) forms the query for retrieval. The “seed” question is just the first turn; subsequent queries are enriched with dialogue context to improve retrieval relevance.

question_html: Which of the following is a common method to evaluate the “faithfulness” of a RAG-generated answer?

options.text: Check if the answer is grammatically correct
Verify whether each factual claim in the answer can be attributed to the retrieved context
Measure the token count of the answer
Compute the BLEU score against a reference answer

explanation_html: Faithfulness (or groundedness) evaluation checks if the output is consistent with the provided source passages, not if it’s fluent. Factual consistency metrics (e.g., entailment-based) or human review are often used.

question_html: In vector search, what is the “curse of dimensionality” referring to?

options.text: As dimensionality increases, distance metrics become less discriminative, and index performance may degrade
The model can only embed one sentence
Embeddings can only be stored in RAM

explanation_html: High-dimensional spaces can cause distance values to become similar across points, making it harder to distinguish nearest neighbors. This affects both accuracy and the efficiency of certain indexing structures.

question_html: Which approach helps integrate streaming updates (new documents) into a live RAG system without full reindexing?

options.text: Incremental indexing and upsert operations in the vector store
Deleting the entire index and rebuilding nightly

explanation_html: Modern vector databases and search services support upserts and incremental indexing, allowing new or updated documents to be added to the index on the fly, with minimal impact on query availability.

question_html: What role does “embedding normalization” play before indexing?

options.text: It scales vectors to unit length, which can improve the stability of cosine similarity and allow using inner product as a proxy
It adds noise for differential privacy
It translates text to another language

explanation_html: Normalizing embeddings to L2 norm = 1 means cosine similarity is equivalent to dot product, which can simplify scoring and improve efficiency in some vector search engines.

question_html: What is the primary purpose of document parsing before chunking in a RAG pipeline?

options.text: To extract clean, structured text from various file formats (PDF, DOCX, HTML)

explanation_html: Document parsing extracts raw text and sometimes structure (like tables) from heterogeneous formats. Clean, well-structured text is essential for meaningful chunking and accurate embedding generation.

question_html: What is “Azure AI Search document cracking”?

options.text: The process of breaking encryption on documents
The ability of indexers to read and extract content from diverse file formats like PDF, DOCX, JSON, and images

explanation_html: Document cracking is the built-in functionality of Azure AI Search indexers to parse and extract text and metadata from various data sources, making the content available for indexing and enrichment.

question_html: When using a RAG system for code documentation, why might you want to chunk by function definition rather than by fixed size?

options.text: To keep semantically related code together, preserving documentation context and ensuring accurate retrieval
To reduce the number of vectors
Because fixed-size chunks are always better

explanation_html: Code has natural semantic boundaries (e.g., functions, classes). Chunking by these boundaries keeps logical units intact, which improves the relevance of retrieved documentation snippets for developer questions.

question_html: Which metric measures the proportion of relevant items that are successfully retrieved?

options.text: All of the above can be adapted for retrieval evaluation

explanation_html: In information retrieval, Recall measures coverage of relevant items, Precision measures how many retrieved items are relevant, and F1 is their harmonic mean. All are used depending on evaluation needs.

question_html: How does adding a “knowledge cutoff awareness” instruction to the prompt help a RAG system?

options.text: It makes the model hallucinate more
It tells the model to rely on the retrieved context for recent information, acknowledging that its parametric knowledge may be outdated
It forces the model to answer only with pre-2023 facts

explanation_html: When the system provides up-to-date documents, instructing the model that the supplied context contains the latest information can reduce conflicts between its internal (potentially outdated) knowledge and fresh retrieval.

question_html: In a RAG pipeline, what is the purpose of a “query classifier” component?

options.text: To route the query to different retrieval strategies or knowledge bases based on intent (e.g., HR docs vs. technical manuals)

explanation_html: A query classifier can determine which index or retriever to use. For example, a question about vacation policy should search HR documents, while a coding question should search the engineering knowledge base, improving precision.

question_html: What is the “embedding drift” problem that might necessitate re-indexing?

options.text: The embedding model changes or is fine-tuned, so new embeddings are no longer compatible with the old vector index
The tokenizer runs out of memory

explanation_html: If the embedding model is updated (new checkpoint or fine-tuned on domain data), the vector space shifts. All documents must be re-embedded and re-indexed to maintain consistency between query and document embeddings.

question_html: When configuring an ANN search, what does the “efSearch” parameter control in HNSW?

options.text: The maximum number of connections per node
The size of the dynamic candidate list during search; higher values improve recall but increase latency

explanation_html: efSearch is an HNSW query-time parameter that determines how extensively the graph is traversed. A larger value explores more nodes, increasing the chance of finding true nearest neighbors at the cost of speed.

question_html: What is the main reason for using a separate “ingestion pipeline” for document processing in an enterprise RAG setup?

options.text: To handle tasks like parsing, chunking, enrichment, embedding, and indexing in a scalable, repeatable manner
To limit the number of documents

explanation_html: An ingestion pipeline automates the end-to-end process of turning raw documents into searchable vectors, often with monitoring, error handling, and scheduling, which is critical for maintaining a current and reliable knowledge base.

question_html: Which of the following best describes “context enrichment” in a retrieval pipeline?

options.text: Adding unrelated jokes to the prompt
Including additional structured data (like metadata, glossaries, or entity relationships) alongside the retrieved chunk to improve answer quality

explanation_html: Context enrichment supplements the raw text chunk with helpful information such as the document title, section heading, or definitions, giving the generator a better understanding of the source and improving answer fidelity.

question_html: In a RAG evaluation framework, what does “answer correctness” typically assess?

options.text: How well the generated answer aligns with the ground truth or the expected factual content, often using semantic similarity or factual overlap
The number of tokens in the response

explanation_html: Answer correctness measures the accuracy of the final response against a reference or against the source documents. It may consider both semantic equivalence and exact factual match, and is a key metric for end-to-end RAG quality.

question_html: Why might a retrieval system use a “multi-stage ranking” architecture?

options.text: To apply different ranking criteria for each user
To balance speed and precision: a fast retriever (e.g., vector search) produces candidates, and a slow but precise reranker re-scores top results
To rank documents by file size
To create multiple copies of the index

explanation_html: Multi-stage ranking decouples efficiency and effectiveness. The first stage (often ANN) retrieves a large set quickly; a second stage (like a cross-encoder) applies a more computationally expensive model on a smaller set, improving final relevance.

question_html: When using Azure AI Search, how does the “vector” field type differ from “Edm.String”?

options.text: Vector fields store arrays of floating-point numbers and can be searched using vector similarity algorithms; string fields support keyword and full-text search
String fields are slower for BM25

explanation_html: In Azure AI Search, a field of type Collection(Edm.Single) is designated as a vector field. It supports vector search profiles and ANN algorithms. String fields can be full-text searchable, filterable, etc., but not used for vector queries.

question_html: What is a common technique to reduce the token consumption cost of a RAG system?

options.text: Summarize retrieved chunks before including them in the prompt, if they are very long
Increase the number of retrieved documents

explanation_html: Summarization or compressing retrieved context reduces prompt size, lowering per-request cost and latency. It also helps the model focus on salient information, though care must be taken to preserve critical details.

question_html: How can a RAG system handle multi-turn conversations to improve retrieval relevance?

options.text: Use a query rewriting step that takes the current question and the conversation history to produce a contextualized, standalone query
Retrieve only based on the last word
Disable retrieval after the first turn

explanation_html: In multi-turn dialogues, a question like “What about its pricing?” is ambiguous alone. A query rewriter (often an LLM call) reformulates it into “What is the pricing of product X?” using conversation history, enabling accurate retrieval.

question_html: Which Azure AI Search index configuration is necessary to enable integrated vectorization?

options.text: A vector search profile with an algorithm configuration and a vectorizer pointing to an embedding model

explanation_html: The index needs a vector search profile that specifies the algorithm (e.g., HNSW) and a vectorizer resource that references the Azure OpenAI embedding deployment. This enables automatic embedding generation during indexing and query.

question_html: Which of the following is an example of a “contextual retrieval” technique that prepends document-level context to each chunk?

options.text: Adding the document title and a short summary to the beginning of every chunk before embedding and retrieval
Using only the first sentence of a chunk

explanation_html: Contextual retrieval enriches each chunk with its originating context (e.g., document title, section header) so that the embedding captures a broader sense of the chunk’s meaning. This can significantly improve retrieval relevance, especially when chunks are ambiguous alone.

question_html: What is a common technique to protect personally identifiable information (PII) in a RAG system?

options.text: Sending PII to the language model without masking
Applying a PII detection and redaction step in the ingestion pipeline, and optionally masking in prompts, to prevent sensitive data from being exposed

explanation_html: Detecting and redacting PII (names, emails, SSNs, etc.) before indexing and during prompt construction ensures that the model never sees or outputs sensitive data, helping comply with privacy regulations like GDPR.

question_html: In Azure AI Search, what is the purpose of the “knowledge store projections” feature?

options.text: To persist enriched document data in Azure Storage for analysis, reporting, or as a cache for other applications, separate from the search index

explanation_html: Projections shape enriched data into tables, objects, or file paths and store them in Azure tables/blobs/files. This enables use cases like dash boarding or feeding another RAG system without re-processing the entire pipeline.

question_html: Which condition would prompt the use of a “multi-query retrieval” pattern?

options.text: The user query is a single, simple factoid
A complex question can be decomposed into several sub-questions that are each answered by different parts of the knowledge base
There is only one document in the index
The system has no embedding model

explanation_html: Multi-query retrieval generates multiple search queries from the original question (e.g., using an LLM to decompose it), retrieves chunks for each, and then unifies them into a comprehensive context for the final answer. This is effective for comparative or multi-faceted questions.

question_html: What is the main reason to use a “sparse-dense hybrid index” instead of a pure dense vector index?

options.text: To eliminate the need for any search
To cover both exact term matches (like part numbers) and semantic meaning in a single retrieval operation
To reduce the total number of documents

explanation_html: A hybrid index stores both sparse (lexical) and dense (semantic) representations. This allows the search to handle rare terms or codes that vector search might miss, while still capturing the meaning of natural language phrases.

question_html: When deploying a RAG application, why might you choose an “asynchronous response” pattern?

options.text: To handle long-running multi-step retrieval and generation without blocking the client, returning results via webhooks or polling

explanation_html: For complex queries that require agentic chains or heavy re-ranking, an async pattern returns an immediate acknowledgment and processes the request in the background. This prevents timeouts and improves user experience for latency-tolerant scenarios.

question_html: Which of the following is a benefit of storing “chunk offset” information?

options.text: It allows retrieval of neighboring chunks (previous/next) to expand the context window around a matched chunk
It removes the need for a language model

explanation_html: Knowing a chunk’s position in the original document enables fetching adjacent chunks without re-embedding them all together. This “context window expansion” can provide additional background to the generator, improving answer completeness.

question_html: What is the primary function of a “retrieval router” in an agentic RAG framework?

options.text: To decide which retriever, index, or tool (e.g., vector search, SQL query, web search) to use based on the query’s intent

explanation_html: A router classifies the query and selects the appropriate retrieval path. For instance, a query about sales numbers might route to a structured data SQL tool, while a policy question goes to a vector index, optimizing accuracy.

question_html: In the context of grounded generation, what is a “citation” typically used for?

options.text: To provide traceable references to the specific chunks or documents that support each part of the generated answer

explanation_html: Citations ground the output by linking claims to their sources, allowing users to verify information and increasing trust. The model can be prompted to format citations inline or as footnotes.

question_html: How can the “lost in the middle” problem be addressed during the retrieval step itself?

options.text: By always placing relevant chunks in the middle of the prompt
By reordering retrieved chunks so that the highest-relevance ones are positioned at the beginning and end of the context window

explanation_html: Since LLMs tend to ignore mid-context information, reordering the context to place top chunks at the extremes (start and end) makes it more likely the model will attend to the most critical evidence.

question_html: What is the purpose of the “semantic cache” pattern in RAG?

options.text: To cache the response to a query by using a similarity threshold on the query embedding, so that similar future queries return the cached answer directly without full retrieval-generation

explanation_html: A semantic cache computes the embedding of a new query and compares it to stored embeddings of past queries. If a match is found within a threshold, the cached response (with citations) is served, reducing latency and cost.

question_html: Which of these is an effective method to detect and filter “boilerplate” content from chunks?

options.text: Use a pre-trained classifier or rule-based heuristics (e.g., high link density, repetitive text) to identify boilerplate and discard those chunks before indexing

explanation_html: Boilerplate (navigation menus, copyright notices) contributes noise. Filtering it out improves the signal-to-noise ratio of the vector index, leading to more relevant retrieval and less distraction for the generator.

question_html: In a RAG pipeline, when would you apply “document summarization” as a preprocessing step?

options.text: To create a concise summary that can be used as a high-level overview chunk or to generate a document abstract for faster top-level retrieval

explanation_html: Summarization can produce a dense representation of a long document. This summary chunk can serve as a “retrieval entry point”; if it matches, the system can then drill down into detailed chunks, enabling a multi-level retrieval strategy.

question_html: What does “embedding space alignment” refer to when combining a pre-trained retriever with a fine-tuned generator?

options.text: Making sure both use the same programming language
Ensuring that the semantic space of the retriever’s embeddings is compatible with the generator’s understanding, often achieved through joint training or adapter layers
Aligning text to the right margin

explanation_html: If the retriever is frozen and the generator is fine-tuned on RAG tasks, the generator may learn to interpret the retriever’s output format. Alignment techniques help the two components work in concert, improving end-to-end performance.

question_html: Why is it important to control the “maximum token length” of a chunk during embedding?

options.text: Embedding models have a finite input token limit; exceeding it results in truncation, which can drop crucial information and misrepresent the chunk
Longer chunks always produce better vectors
It changes the embedding model’s architecture

explanation_html: Most embedding models have a maximum context window (e.g., 512 or 8192 tokens). Chunks longer than that are cut off, losing the tail end. Respecting the limit ensures the full chunk is embedded accurately.

question_html: In a RAG system, what is the risk of using only a single-source retrieval (e.g., one SharePoint site) without diversity measures?

options.text: The answers may reflect a narrow viewpoint and miss critical information from other parts of the organization, leading to incomplete or biased responses

explanation_html: Enterprise knowledge is often distributed. Relying on a single source may omit important context or contradictory data. Multi-source retrieval with proper merging/diversity ensures a more comprehensive and balanced answer.

question_html: How can you reduce the environmental impact of a large-scale RAG system?

options.text: Use ever-larger models for all tasks
Apply model distillation, efficient vector indexes, and cache embeddings to minimize redundant computation

explanation_html: Smaller distilled models and efficient indexes require less energy per query. Caching prevents repeated expensive embedding calls. These techniques lower the carbon footprint without significantly sacrificing quality.

question_html: What is a “function calling” or “tool use” extension to RAG?

options.text: The model can decide to call external APIs (e.g., a calculator, database query) based on the user request, and incorporate the result into its grounded response

explanation_html: Augmenting RAG with tool use allows the system to fetch structured data, perform computations, or trigger actions when retrieved text is insufficient. This creates a more capable agent that still grounds actions in external sources.

question_html: In Azure AI Search, how do “index projections” differ from “knowledge store projections”?

options.text: Knowledge store projections persist enriched data outside the search index; index projections are deprecated
Index projections are only for vectors
Knowledge store is only for images

A) The knowledge store is a synonym for the search index B) A knowledge store persists enriched data in Azure Storage for analysis, while the search index is optimized for high-speed retrieval queries C) The knowledge store only stores vectors D) The search index cannot be queried Correct Answer: B Explanation: The search index is designed for low-latency queries and relevance scoring. The knowledge store outputs enriched documents in structured formats (tables, blobs) to a storage account, enabling downstream processing like Power BI reporting.

question_html: When performing hybrid search with Azure AI Search, what does the “hybridSearch.maxTextRecallSize” parameter control?

options.text: The number of BM25 results considered for fusion
The total number of documents returned

explanation_html: This parameter limits how many BM25 results are fetched and fed into the Reciprocal Rank Fusion step. It helps balance performance and recall by controlling the pool size from the keyword search side.

question_html: What is the main advantage of using a “model-agnostic” RAG framework?

options.text: It locks you into one embedding provider
It allows swapping embedding models, vector stores, and LLMs with minimal code changes, making the system flexible and future-proof
It eliminates the need for retrieval

explanation_html: A modular design with abstraction layers enables teams to test different components (e.g., switching from Ada to a new embedding model) without rewriting the entire pipeline, which is crucial in the fast-evolving AI landscape.

question_html: In a RAG system, how can you ensure that the model does not use its internal knowledge when it contradicts the retrieved context?

options.text: Use a system message that instructs the model to answer only based on the provided context and say “Insufficient information” if needed
Always include incorrect information in the prompt

explanation_html: A strong system instruction (“Answer using ONLY the sources provided. If the answer cannot be found, say so.”) reduces the model’s tendency to fall back on parametric memory. This is a fundamental grounding technique.

question_html: What is the role of a “document parser” that outputs Markdown format in a RAG ingestion pipeline?

options.text: To convert different file formats into a uniform, structured text representation that preserves headings, lists, and tables, which aids chunking

explanation_html: Markdown provides a common structured format with explicit hierarchy (headers, emphasis). Parsing to Markdown normalizes documents from PDF, HTML, DOCX, etc., making subsequent chunking and context enrichment more reliable.

question_html: Which metric is most appropriate for evaluating a RAG system’s ability to include only true facts?
explanation_html: Factual precision measures the percentage of generated statements that are supported by the ground truth or retrieved sources. It directly reflects the system’s reliability in producing accurate content.

question_html: What is the effect of setting a low “similarity threshold” when using a semantic cache?

options.text: More queries are served from the cache, potentially improving latency but increasing the risk of returning a cached answer that doesn’t fully match the user’s intent

explanation_html: A lower threshold means a broader match, so similar but not identical queries may hit the cache, saving time. However, if the threshold is too low, the cached response might be inappropriate for the specific nuance of the new query.

question_html: In the context of Azure AI Search, what is the function of a “custom skill”?

options.text: It replaces the need for an indexer
It allows developers to plug in their own Python or Web API code to perform arbitrary document enrichment, such as calling a domain-specific model for classification
It is a built-in skill for translation

explanation_html: Custom skills extend the enrichment pipeline beyond built-in skills. They can call any HTTP endpoint, enabling integration of in-house NLP models, business logic, or external services for metadata extraction or embedding generation.

question_html: Why is it beneficial to log “query and retrieval pairs” in a RAG system?

options.text: To build a feedback dataset for fine-tuning retrievers or evaluating retrieval quality offline

explanation_html: Logging allows analysis of retrieval gaps, identification of frequent failure patterns, and creation of labeled data for training better embedding models or re-rankers, driving continuous improvement.

question_html: What is a “multi-vector embedding” strategy like “SPLADE” for sparse representations?

options.text: A learned sparse model that produces term-weight vectors, capturing lexical importance with neural expansion, enabling sparse-dense hybrid search

explanation_html: SPLADE learns sparse weightings that expand queries and documents with relevant terms, providing better lexical matching than traditional BM25 while still being compatible with inverted indexes. It can be used alongside dense vectors.

question_html: When a RAG system uses “chain-of-note” prompting, what is its goal?

options.text: To generate intermediate reading notes from retrieved documents before writing the final answer, improving comprehensiveness and attribution

explanation_html: Chain-of-note instructs the model to first create structured notes summarizing relevant passages. This explicit reasoning step helps ensure that the final answer incorporates and correctly cites the most important information.

question_html: What is a “debug session” in Azure AI Search used for during RAG pipeline development?

options.text: To interactively examine and refine enrichment pipelines, including skillset outputs and chunking, without full reindexing
To monitor query latency in production

explanation_html: Debug sessions allow developers to upload a sample document, run it through the skillset step-by-step, inspect the enriched output, and adjust skills or mappings. This iterative approach speeds up the construction of a high-quality ingestion pipeline.

question_html: In the context of RAG, what is a “document graph” approach for retrieval?

options.text: Building a graph where nodes are chunks and edges represent relationships (e.g., hyperlinks, semantic similarity), enabling multi-hop reasoning

explanation_html: A document graph can support traversing related chunks beyond simple similarity. This allows answering questions that require connecting information from multiple interconnected passages, improving complex Q&A.

question_html: When deploying a RAG system in production, why is monitoring “retrieval latency” important?

options.text: Users expect sub-second response times; high latency degrades experience and may indicate index or embedding service issues
It only matters for batch processing

explanation_html: Real-time applications need fast retrieval. Monitoring p50/p95 latency and setting alerts helps maintain SLA and detect performance regressions, such as an overloaded embedding endpoint or index fragmentation.

question_html: What does “reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)” do when combining search results?

options.text: It sums the reciprocal of the rank position from each result list to create a fused score, irrespective of the absolute score values
It only uses the highest score

explanation_html: RRF computes 1/(k + rank) for each result in each list, then sums these values for each document. This normalizes rankings from different retrieval systems and often works better than score-based merging when score distributions differ.

question_html: Which statement about vector search with filtering is true?

options.text: Pre-filtering applies metadata constraints before ANN search, reducing the candidate set but may miss results if the filter is very restrictive

explanation_html: Pre-filtering narrows the search space, which can be efficient but risks excluding relevant vectors if the filter is overly strict. Post-filtering retrieves vectors first, then filters, ensuring no missed results due to filter but may yield fewer than k after filtering.

question_html: What is the main advantage of a “re-rank then generate” pattern?

options.text: It eliminates the need for generation
By reordering retrieved passages with a more accurate model before they are passed to the generator, the most relevant information is prioritized, improving answer quality

explanation_html: Ensuring the prompt begins with the most relevant chunks helps the LLM focus on the best evidence, potentially reducing the chance of being distracted by less useful text placed prominently.

question_html: In a RAG system, how can you handle a question that requires information from multiple documents?

options.text: Aggregate chunks from multiple retrieval calls or use a multi-query expansion, then synthesize
Ignore all but the first document
Ask the user to split the question
Use a maximum chunk size of 100 tokens

explanation_html: Complex questions may need information spanning several sources. The system can decompose the query into sub-queries, retrieve for each, combine the results, and then generate a comprehensive answer.

question_html: What is a “text splitter” that respects markdown structure?

options.text: A splitter that cuts text only at sentence boundaries using a list of punctuation
A splitter that recognizes markdown headers (##, #) and splits sections, then recursively splits if needed, preserving document hierarchy
A splitter that only uses spaces
A splitter that converts markdown to PDF

explanation_html: Markdown-aware splitters use headers as strong boundary hints, then use other separators. This keeps sections together and maintains the logical structure of technical documentation, which aids retrieval.

question_html: Why is it important to securely manage API keys for the embedding and language model services in a RAG pipeline?

options.text: Unauthorized access could lead to data exfiltration, model misuse, and billing abuse; proper secrets management is essential

explanation_html: Keys grant access to paid cloud services and possibly to sensitive data if logging is enabled. Secure storage (e.g., Azure Key Vault, environment variables) and least-privilege principles protect the system.

question_html: Which practice is recommended when building a RAG system that must comply with data residency regulations?

options.text: Choose region-specific deployments for vector stores, embedding models, and language models that keep data within required geographical boundaries
Store all data in a single global region
Use only open-source models to bypass regulations

explanation_html: Many jurisdictions require data to remain in-country. Cloud services allow selecting specific regions for storage and processing, ensuring that documents and queries are handled in compliant locations.

question_html: What is a key advantage of using the “self-RAG” pattern over a standard RAG pipeline?

options.text: It always retrieves exactly one document
The model can decide on-the-fly whether retrieval is needed and can critique its own output for groundedness
It never uses an embedding model
It only works with SQL databases

explanation_html: Self-RAG extends standard RAG by training the LLM to generate special reflection tokens that control when to retrieve and when to validate the generated response against the retrieved passages. This dynamic control can improve factual accuracy and reduce unnecessary retrievals.

question_html: Which Azure AI Search built-in skill is commonly used to split large documents into smaller chunks before embedding?
explanation_html: The TextSplitSkill is designed to break text into chunks of a specified token length, optionally with overlap. This output can then be passed to the embedding skill for vector indexing, forming the foundation of a RAG ingestion pipeline.

question_html: When evaluating a RAG system, what does the “context precision” metric measure?

options.text: How fast the context was retrieved
The proportion of retrieved chunks that are relevant to the query, considering their rank position
The number of words in the context
How similar the context is to the training data

explanation_html: Context precision assesses whether relevant items appear high in the retrieved results. It is a rank-aware metric that penalizes irrelevant chunks and rewards placing relevant chunks near the top, which is crucial for the generator’s focus.

question_html: Why might you choose a scalar quantization (SQ) compression for your vector embeddings?

options.text: To reduce memory usage by mapping 32-bit floats to 8-bit integers, enabling faster search with a slight recall trade-off

explanation_html: Scalar quantization compresses each float dimension into a smaller integer type (e.g., int8), drastically reducing the memory footprint and speeding up distance computations. It is a lossy technique, so recall might drop slightly, but it’s effective for large-scale indexes.

question_html: In a RAG pipeline, what is the purpose of a “prompt compression” step before generation?

options.text: To condense long retrieved passages into a shorter form while preserving key facts, reducing token usage
To add more tokens to the prompt

explanation_html: Prompt compression uses summarization models or LLM-based distillation to shrink the context window usage, allowing more passages to fit within the token limit. This helps manage costs and latency while maintaining essential information.

question_html: What is the main function of an “embedding fine-tuning” step using domain-specific data?

options.text: To improve retrieval relevance by aligning embedding space with the domain’s semantics and terminology
To reduce the number of documents

explanation_html: Fine-tuning on domain text (e.g., medical, legal) can create embeddings that better capture specialized vocabulary and relationships, leading to more accurate retrieval in that domain.

question_html: Which of the following best describes “adaptive retrieval” in an agentic RAG system?

options.text: Always fetching the same top-k documents for every query
Dynamically choosing the retrieval strategy, number of iterations, or knowledge sources based on the query complexity and intermediate results

explanation_html: Adaptive retrieval lets the system decide if a simple single-hop retrieval is enough or if it needs to decompose the query, perform multiple retrievals, or even query external APIs, leading to more efficient and accurate answers for complex tasks.

question_html: How does a “vectorizer” in Azure AI Search’s integrated vectorization relate to RAG?

options.text: It automatically generates embeddings for text fields during indexing and queries using a specified embedding model, simplifying pipeline management

explanation_html: Integrated vectorization removes the need for an external custom embedding step by calling Azure OpenAI or other embedding models directly from the indexer and query time. This streamlines RAG integration and keeps the embedding logic server-side.

question_html: What is the main goal of the “Corrective RAG” (CRAG) approach?

options.text: To correct grammar in the retrieved passages
To evaluate the relevance of retrieved documents and, if needed, perform additional web searches to correct or supplement the context before generation
To always retrieve from a local database
To reduce the number of chunks to one

explanation_html: CRAG introduces a retrieval evaluator that grades the quality of the initial retrieval. If the retrieved passages are insufficient, it triggers an external search (e.g., web) to fetch better information, correcting the context supplied to the generator.

question_html: In a production RAG system, why would you implement an “embeddings API circuit breaker”?

options.text: To prevent cascading failures by stopping requests to the embedding service when it is experiencing high latency or errors, and falling back to cached vectors or an alternative model

explanation_html: Resilience patterns like circuit breakers detect when a downstream dependency (e.g., embedding model endpoint) is unhealthy. Instead of queueing and timing out, the system can serve stale cache or degrade gracefully, maintaining overall availability.

question_html: Which chunking strategy is most suitable for preserving the context of tabular data in PDFs?

options.text: A table-aware parser that extracts tables as separate structured chunks with surrounding text

explanation_html: Tables contain relational information that loses meaning if split mid-table. A table-aware extraction preserves the structure (e.g., as Markdown tables or JSON) so that the embedding and generator can correctly interpret the data relationships.

question_html: What is the function of an “embedding model distillation” in the context of retrieval?

options.text: To train a student model that produces similar embeddings to a larger teacher model but with lower latency and a smaller footprint
To split the embedding vector into multiple parts

explanation_html: Distillation can create a compact embedding model that approximates the quality of a high-capacity model. This is valuable for edge deployment or cost-sensitive scenarios where the full model would be too slow or expensive.

question_html: In a RAG evaluation set, why are “adversarial questions” included?

options.text: To probe whether the system can be tricked into generating harmful, off-topic, or hallucinated answers when given misleading or malicious queries

explanation_html: Adversarial test cases include attempts to jailbreak or confuse the system. Evaluating against them ensures the RAG guardrails and grounding hold up under attack, which is critical for security and trustworthiness.

question_html: Which Azure AI Search feature allows you to define a custom scoring profile that boosts results based on numeric metadata (e.g., recency)?
explanation_html: Scoring profiles let you define boost functions (magnitude, freshness, tag) and weighting to influence the relevance score of documents. For example, you can boost documents with a “lastModified” date within the last 30 days, which is useful for time-sensitive RAG.

question_html: What is the main benefit of using a “late interaction” model like ColBERT for retrieval?

options.text: It retains token-level interaction between query and document while still allowing precomputation of document token embeddings, giving high accuracy with efficient search
It does not use any neural network

explanation_html: ColBERT computes embeddings for each token in the document and query. At search time, a cheap summation of max-similarity interactions yields a relevance score. Document token embeddings can be precomputed and stored, combining expressiveness with scalability.

question_html: How does “query augmentation” using a synonym map in Azure AI Search improve retrieval?

options.text: It expands the query to include synonyms, so that documents using different terminology for the same concept can still be matched
It reduces the number of search results

explanation_html: Synonym maps are used at query time to add equivalent terms (e.g., “car” when searching for “automobile”). This improves lexical recall without the need for semantic vector search, and can complement vector search in a hybrid setup.

question_html: In a RAG system handling real-time data, what is the purpose of “streaming ingestion”?

options.text: To batch documents once a week
To continuously process and index incoming documents with minimal delay, making new knowledge searchable almost immediately
To pause indexing during peak hours

explanation_html: For use cases like news or incident response, streaming ingestion ensures that the vector index reflects the latest information. Azure AI Search indexers can be event-driven, and vector databases often support near-real-time updates.

question_html: Which practice can help prevent a RAG model from basing its answer on an outdated cached version of a document?

options.text: Implement an automated reindexing pipeline triggered by content changes and use short TTLs for caches
Use only the initial index snapshot

explanation_html: Content update triggers can push changes to the index, and cache invalidation ensures that retrieval always fetches the latest data. This keeps the answers grounded in current knowledge, which is vital in dynamic enterprise environments.

question_html: What role does the “reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) parameter k” play?

options.text: It sets the number of documents to retrieve
It is a constant that prevents very high ranks from dominating; a typical value is 60, balancing the influence of rank positions

explanation_html: The formula is 1/(k + rank). The parameter k controls how rapidly the reciprocal score decays with rank. A larger k makes the curve flatter, reducing the difference between top ranks. It is configurable in Azure AI Search’s hybrid search.

question_html: How does the “model-as-judge” approach evaluate a RAG answer’s groundedness?

options.text: By checking the length of the answer
By using a separate LLM call that is prompted to determine whether each statement in the answer is supported by the provided context
By looking at the number of citations

explanation_html: A strong LLM (or fine-tuned evaluator) can be given the context, the question, and the answer, and asked to judge if the answer is fully grounded. This method scales better than human evaluation and can capture nuanced faithfulness.

question_html: How does “Azure AI Search private endpoints” enhance RAG system security?

options.text: By exposing the service to the internet
By ensuring that traffic between your virtual network and the search service stays on the Microsoft backbone, not the public internet, reducing exposure

explanation_html: Private endpoints assign a private IP from your VNet to the search service, securing data in transit and complying with strict network security policies. This is vital for handling sensitive enterprise documents.

question_html: How does “contrastive learning” help train better retrieval embeddings?

options.text: It trains using only positive pairs
It pulls embeddings of related query-document pairs closer together and pushes unrelated ones apart, making the vector space more discriminative

explanation_html: Contrastive learning uses triplets or pairs with positive (relevant) and negative (irrelevant) examples. The loss function maximizes similarity for positives and minimizes it for negatives, directly optimizing for retrieval tasks.

question_html: What is the role of “data source credentials” in Azure AI Search indexers?

options.text: To provide secure access to the source content (e.g., blob containers, SharePoint, Cosmos DB) for crawling and ingestion

explanation_html: The data source object includes connection strings or managed identity references, allowing the indexer to securely read documents. This is fundamental for setting up an automated RAG ingestion pipeline.

question_html: Which metric is best suited to evaluate the diversity of retrieval results?

options.text: Self-similarity or average pairwise dissimilarity among retrieved chunks

explanation_html: To measure diversity, you can compute the average cosine similarity between pairs of retrieved chunks; a lower value indicates greater diversity. This ensures the generator receives a broad range of information.

question_html: In a RAG system with guardrails, what is a “prompt shield” supposed to prevent?

options.text: Direct and indirect prompt injection attacks that attempt to override system instructions or exfiltrate data

explanation_html: Prompt shields detect and block malicious user inputs designed to manipulate the model’s behavior. This is a critical security component, especially when dealing with untrusted user data.

question_html: Why might you choose to generate multiple answers from the same retrieved context and then select the best one using an evaluator?

options.text: To improve the likelihood of a correct and well-grounded response by sampling and then applying a self-consistency or grounding check
To always return the first answer

explanation_html: Self-consistency generates several candidate answers and picks the one that is most consistent or best supported by the context. This can overcome sampling randomness and improve factual accuracy.

question_html: What is a “text-embedding-3-small” style model characteristic?

options.text: It is a smaller, faster embedding model that still produces high-quality dense vectors, often using Matryoshka representation learning to allow flexible dimension reduction
It cannot be used for retrieval

explanation_html: Newer embedding models support Matryoshka embeddings, where you can truncate the vector to a smaller dimension without losing much quality. This allows trading off accuracy for speed and storage within a single model.

question_html: How does “caching the top-k retrieval results” for popular queries help?

options.text: It speeds up only rare queries
It reduces load on the vector database and embedding generation for frequent queries, improving throughput and latency

explanation_html: A simple cache storing the top-k chunks for exact match queries can serve repeated requests instantly, offloading the ANN index. This is effective for head queries in many enterprise chatbot scenarios.

question_html: In the context of Azure AI Search, what are “complex types” useful for?

options.text: To model nested structures like a document with multiple authors (each with name and bio) within the same index item, enriching the metadata

explanation_html: Complex types allow sub-objects and collections within a document, enabling rich metadata representation. This metadata can be used for fine-grained filtering or context enrichment in a RAG prompt.

question_html: What is the main reason for using a “mock embedding model” during integration testing?

options.text: To test with real API costs
To avoid dependencies on external services and obtain deterministic results, making tests fast and reliable

explanation_html: In CI/CD pipelines, replacing the embedding service with a mock that returns fixed vectors ensures tests are deterministic and not flaky due to network issues or rate limits, while still exercising the retrieval logic.

question_html: Which retrieval challenge does “query2doc” (generating a pseudo-document) aim to address?

options.text: Lexical gap between query terms and document vocabulary, by expanding the query with a rich pseudo-document before retrieval

explanation_html: Query2doc asks an LLM to write a relevant document for the query, then concatenates it to the query or uses its terms for keyword search. This enriches the query with terms likely to match relevant documents.

question_html: What is the effect of setting a high “m” parameter (max connections) in HNSW construction?

options.text: It increases graph connectivity, improving recall but consuming more memory and build time

explanation_html: The M parameter controls the number of bi-directional links created per node. Higher M leads to a more navigable graph with better search accuracy, at the cost of larger index size and slower indexing.

question_html: In a RAG system, why would you use a “structured output” format like JSON for the generated answer?

options.text: To make the answer harder to parse
To enable downstream processing, including separating the answer text from citations and confidence scores in a predictable schema
To increase token usage with no benefit
To avoid using a language model

explanation_html: Returning a JSON object with fields for “answer”, “sources”, and “confidence” allows the consuming application to clearly present information and handle citations programmatically.

question_html: Which of the following is a key indicator that your chunking strategy is failing?

options.text: Generated answers frequently miss important details that are present in the document but were split across chunks

explanation_html: If an answer is incomplete because the relevant information straddles a hard chunk boundary, the chunk is effectively lost. This suggests the chunk size or overlap needs adjustment.

question_html: What is the purpose of “multi-layer reasoning” in RAG prompted systems?

options.text: To break down the question into a step-by-step plan, retrieve information for each step, and synthesize a final answer, often using a tool-augmented language model

explanation_html: Multi-layer reasoning involves planning, tool use (retrieval, calculator), and synthesis. It’s a core component of agentic RAG, capable of handling complex, multi-step problems by iteratively calling the retriever.

question_html: What is a “fused hybrid search” in the context of a single request?

options.text: A search that uses only one algorithm
A single query that simultaneously performs keyword and vector search, then merges the results using RRF, returning a unified result set
A search that ignores vector results

explanation_html: Azure AI Search supports a single hybrid query that includes both a text search and a vector query. The service internally runs both, fuses the ranked results, and returns the merged list, simplifying client logic.

question_html: What is the main benefit of “scalar quantization” over “product quantization” for vector compression?

options.text: It is simpler and faster to encode/decode, with lower computational overhead, while product quantization provides better compression ratios but is more complex

explanation_html: SQ simply maps floats to ints per dimension, making it lightweight. PQ compresses vectors into short codes using clustering in sub-vector spaces, achieving better compression but requiring more complex search algorithms.

question_html: In a RAG system, what is a “contradiction detector”?

options.text: A tool that finds all similar documents
A component that compares the generated answer against the retrieved context to flag statements that contradict the sources, enabling automatic correction
A tool to increase answer length

explanation_html: Contradiction detection uses NLI or an LLM prompt to check if any claim in the answer is negated by the context. If found, the system can regenerate that part or alert the user to the discrepancy.

question_html: Why might you use “just-in-time (JIT) chunking” rather than pre-chunking all documents?

options.text: To apply dynamic, query-dependent chunking at retrieval time, potentially creating more relevant context windows for each specific query

explanation_html: JIT chunking delays splitting until a query is received, using the query as a signal to determine optimal chunk boundaries (e.g., using sliding windows around query terms). This can improve context relevance but increases query-time computation.

question_html: What is the role of a “document watermark” in the retrieval pipeline?

options.text: To track the last processed timestamp of a document, enabling efficient incremental ingestion by only processing changes since the watermark

explanation_html: A high-watermark (e.g., a datetime field) indicates which documents have been updated. The ingestion pipeline can query “since last watermark” to only process new or modified items, making index updates efficient.

question_html: In the context of Azure AI Search, what does the “retrievable” attribute on a field control?

options.text: Whether the field can be used in filters
Whether the field’s content can be returned in search results; if false, it can still be searched but not returned, saving response size
Whether it is a vector field

explanation_html: For large text fields that are used for vectorization but don’t need to be shown to the user, setting retrievable to false can reduce response payload and improve performance.

question_html: Which approach can make a RAG system more robust to typos in the user query?

options.text: Using a combination of fuzzy search (for keyword) and semantic vector search, and possibly an LLM-based spell correction step before retrieval

explanation_html: Fuzzy search handles character-level variations, while embeddings are generally resilient to minor misspellings. A pre-processing step can also clean up obvious typos, ensuring higher recall.

question_html: What is the “index projection” capability in a knowledge store actually called in Azure AI Search?
explanation_html: Knowledge store defines projections that shape and export enriched data to Azure Storage. Table projections store flat data, object projections store JSON, and file projections store raw files.

question_html: Why would a RAG system implement a “factuality check” using a separate LLM with a different prompt?

options.text: Because one LLM may be biased; a second independent check with a strict truth-seeking prompt can catch hallucinations that the primary generator missed

explanation_html: Using a dual-LLM setup where one generates and another verifies can improve overall factual accuracy, as the verifier is dedicated to scrutiny and can flag errors.

question_html: What is the primary purpose of “term boosting” in a query?

options.text: To increase the importance of certain query terms in the scoring function, making documents that contain those terms rank higher

explanation_html: In Azure AI Search, you can apply term boosting (e.g., “term^2”) in the simple query syntax to influence the BM25 score, which can be useful when you know certain keywords are more important for relevance.

question_html: How does “context-aware prompt compression” differ from simple summarization?

options.text: It only keeps the first sentence
It uses the query to selectively retain the most relevant sentences from each retrieved passage, rather than blindly summarizing everything

explanation_html: Context-aware compression (e.g., via a cross-encoder selection) extracts or rates sentences based on their relevance to the query, so the compressed prompt is focused exactly on the needed information, preserving nuance.

question_html: What is the purpose of “indexing schedule” in Azure AI Search?

options.text: To define a recurring time window (e.g., every 5 minutes, daily at 2 AM) for running the indexer to keep the search index up to date

explanation_html: Indexer schedules allow periodic automatic updates. For RAG, this ensures new or modified documents become searchable without manual intervention, with the frequency tailored to how often the source content changes.

question_html: Which vector search approach is best suited for a streaming environment where new documents arrive constantly and low-latency availability is critical?

options.text: An index that supports online insertions/upserts with minimal impact on query performance, like a mutable HNSW or DiskANN with incremental build
A static index rebuilt from scratch

explanation_html: Many modern vector databases and Azure AI Search support incremental upserts. Mutable graph indexes can add new nodes without a full rebuild, ensuring queries can access fresh data almost immediately.

question_html: What does the “@odata.type” field define in an Azure AI Search index schema?

options.text: The data type of a field, such as Edm.String, Edm.Int64, or Collection(Edm.Single)

explanation_html: Each field in an index must have a specific EDM type. This typing determines what operations (search, filter, sort) are available and is crucial for defining vector fields.

question_html: In a RAG evaluation, what does “answer coverage” measure?

options.text: How well the generated answer covers all aspects of the expected answer or the information present in the ground truth

explanation_html: Coverage (or completeness) assesses whether the answer leaves out important details. It’s often evaluated using semantic similarity or explicit overlap of key points with a reference answer.

question_html: In a RAG system, what is the benefit of exposing “retrieval confidence” to the end user?

options.text: It provides transparency, letting users know how reliable the sources are, and may include disclaimers when confidence is low

explanation_html: Displaying a confidence indicator or quality score helps users gauge the trustworthiness of the response. For enterprise scenarios, this builds trust and allows humans to double-check when the system is uncertain.

question_html: How can you mitigate the risk of a RAG model generating misinformation when the knowledge base is incomplete?

options.text: Force the model to generate an answer anyway
Implement a confidence score based on retrieval relevance and a generated answer verifier, and have the system admit lack of knowledge if confidence is low

explanation_html: An honest “I don’t know” response is safer than fabrication. By quantifying retrieval quality (e.g., cosine similarity) and validating the answer against context, the system can choose to abstain rather than speculate.

question_html: What does “multi-modal RAG” extend retrieval to include?

options.text: Images, audio, or video whose content is embedded in a common semantic space (e.g., CLIP embeddings for images and text) for cross-modal retrieval

explanation_html: Multi-modal RAG uses models like CLIP or ImageBind to embed images, audio, and text into a shared vector space. A text query can then retrieve relevant images (or vice versa), and a vision-language model can use those retrieved artifacts to ground its answer.

question_html: In Azure AI Search, what is the role of the “api-version” parameter?

options.text: It specifies which version of the REST API to use, enabling access to newer features like vector search and semantic ranking as they are introduced

explanation_html: Azure AI Search evolves over time, adding features behind specific API versions. To use vector search or integrated vectorization, you must specify a recent API version (e.g., 2024-07-01 or later).

question_html: Why is it important to apply “rate limiting” on the embedding service in a high-traffic RAG application?

options.text: To prevent overwhelming the API with too many concurrent requests, staying within TPM/RPM limits and ensuring consistent service for all clients

explanation_html: Embedding APIs have quota limits. Without client-side rate limiting, bursts can cause throttling errors and delays. Implementing a token bucket or retry with backoff ensures smooth, resilient operation.

question_html: What is the purpose of “synthetic data generation” for RAG evaluation?

options.text: To create a large set of question-context-answer triples automatically from documents, enabling robust evaluation of retrieval and generation components
To reduce the number of queries

explanation_html: Using an LLM to generate hypothetical questions that each chunk can answer yields a labeled dataset. These synthetic pairs can then be used to compute recall@k and answer correctness for the RAG pipeline.

question_html: Which technique can reduce the memory footprint of an HNSW index without sacrificing too much accuracy?

options.text: Using product quantization (PQ) on the vectors stored in the graph nodes

explanation_html: Combining HNSW with PQ compresses each vector stored in the graph, drastically reducing memory. The graph structure still guides search, and the compressed vectors are used for distance calculations, offering a good speed-accuracy trade-off.

question_html: In a RAG system, what is the “generator’s faithfulness” evaluated against?

options.text: The provided retrieved context, not the model’s internal knowledge

explanation_html: Faithfulness (or groundedness) specifically checks if the generated response is logically entailed by the context given in the prompt. It’s a key metric to detect hallucinations that contradict the retrieved evidence.

question_html: What is the main advantage of using a “document id” as the partition key in a large vector database?

options.text: It allows for faster retrieval of all chunks belonging to a specific document, enabling operations like fetching the full document context
It replaces the need for chunking

explanation_html: Using a document identifier as a partition or metadata key allows scope-limited queries (e.g., “get all chunks from doc XYZ”) and simplifies context expansion or document-level operations like re-indexing a single updated document.

question_html: Which of the following best describes “intent-aware chunking”?

options.text: Chunking strategies that are adjusted based on the expected downstream queries, such as keeping FAQ pairs together or separating procedure steps

explanation_html: Intent-aware chunking tailors the chunk boundaries to the content type. For example, documentation might keep a heading with its body, while a Q&A dataset might chunk each question-answer pair as a unit, optimizing retrieval for the intended use case.

question_html: How can you implement “multiple hop retrieval” to answer questions requiring sequential information?

options.text: First retrieve a set of chunks, then use that information to form a new query to retrieve further evidence, iteratively building a complete context
Always use the first chunk only

explanation_html: Multi-hop (or iterative) retrieval chains multiple retrieval steps. The initial retrieval provides partial clues, and a re-query with the combined information drills deeper. This is essential for bridging questions like “When did the CEO of the company that acquired X retire?”

question_html: What is the role of “document level embeddings” in a multi-vector retrieval strategy?

options.text: To provide a high-level summary embedding for a document, which can be used to first retrieve the most promising documents, then their chunks are searched

explanation_html: A two-stage approach: a course document embedding stage shortlists documents, and then a fine-grained chunk embedding stage searches within those documents. This improves efficiency for very large corpora.

question_html: In the context of Azure AI Search, what is the “scoring function” for a magnitude profile?

options.text: A function that boosts documents based on a numeric field’s value (e.g., boost by popularity)

explanation_html: Magnitude profiles apply a boost based on a numeric field’s range, like boosting highly rated products. Combined with other scoring profile functions, they customize the relevance score for business needs.

question_html: What is a common approach to prevent RAG models from revealing proprietary system prompts?

options.text: Print the system prompt in the output
Add strict guardrail instructions to the system prompt itself that tell the model to never disclose its instructions, and use input/output filters to detect leak attempts

explanation_html: While not foolproof, combining clear “do not reveal” instructions with a detection layer that scans outputs for known prompt patterns reduces the risk. Defense in depth is necessary.

question_html: Why is “index compaction” an important operational task for a long-running vector database?

options.text: To merge fragmented segments, reclaim space, and improve query performance after many upserts and deletes

explanation_html: Over time, immutable segments accumulate and require compaction to maintain efficient search. This background maintenance ensures consistent latency and optimal resource usage.

question_html: What is the primary function of “entropy-based query routing” in a multi-index RAG setup?

options.text: To measure the uncertainty of a query and route it to a specialized retriever (e.g., vector search) if the intent is ambiguous, or to a precise structured index if it’s clear

explanation_html: By evaluating the ambiguity or domain of the query (often using a classifier), the router can decide which knowledge base or retrieval technique is most likely to succeed, improving first-attempt accuracy.

question_html: What is the function of the “AzureOpenAIEmbedding skill” in Azure AI Search?

options.text: To generate vector embeddings for text using an Azure OpenAI embedding deployment directly within an enrichment pipeline

explanation_html: This skill calls the specified Azure OpenAI embedding model endpoint, vectorizing the text input. It integrates seamlessly with skillsets and indexers, enabling end-to-end vector ingestion without external code.

question_html: Which technique uses an LLM to create a “hypothetical document” to improve retrieval?

options.text: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings): generating a synthetic answer document from the query and then using its embedding to search for similar real documents

explanation_html: HyDE reverses the retrieval problem: it asks the LLM to write a plausible answer, embeds that fabricated document, and uses its vector to find actually relevant passages. This can bridge the vocabulary gap between the query and the knowledge base.

question_html: How does “cross-lingual retrieval” work in a modern RAG system?

options.text: Using a multilingual embedding model that aligns semantic spaces across languages, a query in one language can retrieve documents in other languages
It converts all text to images

explanation_html: Multilingual embedding models like multilingual-E5 or Cohere’s multilingual embed create language-agnostic vectors. This enables a seamless retrieval experience in international enterprises without translating all documents.

question_html: What is the purpose of “session context” in a conversational RAG system?

options.text: To carry forward previously retrieved documents and user intents to provide coherent multi-turn answers without re-retrieving for every turn
To reduce the number of turns

explanation_html: By maintaining a short-term memory of retrieved facts and the conversation state, the system can answer follow-up questions like “Tell me more about that” by using already-fetched context, improving efficiency and consistency.

question_html: In the context of vector search, what does “dynamic rescoring” refer to?

options.text: Using a lightweight model to re-score a subset of results based on additional features (like metadata or user behavior) at query time, without re-indexing

explanation_html: Dynamic rescoring allows a second pass on a shortlist using more current or personalized signals that aren’t encoded in the vector, like real-time inventory or user clicks, improving relevance without a full re-ranking model.

question_html: Which Azure service provides native integration for RAG with enterprise data through a simple drag-and-drop studio experience?

options.text: Azure AI Studio (with prompt flow and data connections)

explanation_html: Azure AI Studio offers tools like prompt flow and “add your data” wizards that connect to Azure AI Search, Cognitive Services, and Azure OpenAI, simplifying the creation, testing, and deployment of grounded RAG applications.

question_html: What is the primary reason to use a “pre-filter” approach in vector search with metadata?

options.text: To guarantee a fixed number of results
To ensure that the vector search is only performed on a subset of vectors that match the filter, which can improve performance if the filter is highly selective

explanation_html: Pre-filtering reduces the search space, potentially speeding up the ANN query. However, it may cause empty results if the filter is too restrictive, so it’s important to consider the selectivity.

question_html: In a RAG system, what is “distillation of the reader”?

options.text: Training a smaller language model to produce grounded answers given the retrieved context, mimicking a larger teacher model’s output

explanation_html: The reader (generator) can be distilled by training a compact LLM on a dataset of context-answer pairs generated by a large, high-quality model. This yields a fast, cost-effective generation step with maintained quality.

question_html: How does the “retriever-generator feedback loop” enable continuous improvement?

options.text: User ratings on answer quality are used to identify poor retrievals, which are then used to fine-tune the embedding model or re-ranker, closing the loop

explanation_html: By collecting feedback (thumbs up/down), the system can mine hard negative examples where retrieval failed. This data refines the retrieval models and chunking strategies over time, adapting to real-world queries.

question_html: What is a “vector search profile” in Azure AI Search?

options.text: A configuration that combines the algorithm, vectorizer, and compression settings for a set of vector fields

explanation_html: A vector search profile bundles the ANN algorithm (e.g., HNSW) and the vectorizer definition. Each vector field in the index references a profile, dictating how its vectors are indexed and queried.

question_html: When would you use “late chunking” over conventional pre-chunking?

options.text: When you want to embed entire documents and then perform chunking in the embedding space after pooling token vectors, preserving more context
When you don’t want any chunks

explanation_html: Late chunking (or embedding then chunk) uses a long-context model to embed the full document, then splits the token-level embeddings into chunk representations. This approach can capture cross-chunk context better than chunking first, according to recent research.

question_html: What is the main purpose of the “enrichment cache” in Azure AI Search?

options.text: To permanently store the final answer
To store intermediate enriched document output to avoid re-processing when skills or documents change partially, reducing pipeline costs

explanation_html: Enrichment caching stores the outputs of skills in a blob container. If only a single skill changes, the indexer can reuse cached results from upstream skills, saving computation and time during incremental updates.

question_html: In a RAG system, what is the benefit of “fact-checking” the generated answer against the original full document (not just the chunk)?

options.text: It can catch context that the chunk missed, such as definitions or disclaimers elsewhere in the document, improving accuracy
It always slows down the system

explanation_html: Chunks may omit broader context. By referencing the full document (or nearby sections) during a verification step, the system can correct misinterpretations that arose from limited chunk context.

question_html: Which vector search index type is specifically designed to handle billion-scale similarity search with minimal RAM by using disk-based storage?

options.text: DiskANN (approximate nearest neighbor with disk-based graph)

explanation_html: DiskANN stores the graph structure and vectors on SSD, allowing very large indexes with low memory usage. It is suitable for huge knowledge bases where keeping everything in RAM is cost-prohibitive.

question_html: What is the primary function of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) in a document intelligence pipeline?

options.text: Converting images of text into machine-readable characters
Identifying the language of a document

explanation_html: OCR extracts printed or handwritten text from images or scanned documents, making it editable and searchable.

question_html: What is the benefit of using “OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-large with Matryoshka” for cost management?

options.text: You can store only a small dimension (e.g., 256) in the index for lower storage and faster search, but dynamically use the full dimension for re-ranking if needed

explanation_html: Matryoshka models allow storing short vectors in the main index for efficiency, but you can still retrieve the larger vector or use it as a re-scoring step, balancing cost and accuracy.

question_html: In Azure AI Search, what is the purpose of the “indexer execution history”?

options.text: To provide logs and status of past indexer runs, including any errors, warnings, and document counts, aiding in pipeline monitoring

explanation_html: The execution history shows the success/failure of each indexer run and detailed error messages. This is essential for debugging ingestion issues in a RAG knowledge base.

question_html: How does “hypothetical document embeddings (HyDE)” differ from “query2doc”?

options.text: HyDE creates an embedding of the hypothetical answer, while query2doc often appends generated text to the query for keyword search

explanation_html: HyDE generates a synthetic document, encodes it, and uses that vector for retrieval. Query2doc often generates a passage and concatenates it to the query for dense or sparse retrieval, but the core idea is similar; however, the classic HyDE is specifically about embedding a hallucinated answer. I’ll clarify: HyDE is about embedding the hypothetical answer to search. Query2doc is about generating a document and then using its terms for sparse search or embedding. So A is correct.

question_html: What is a “graceful degradation” strategy when the vector database is temporarily unavailable?
