question_html:
A marketplace moderates seller-uploaded product images.
The compliance team needs the solution to do all of the following:
classify default harmful visual content such as sexual or violent imagery
tune category thresholds to match company policy
quickly detect a newly emerging prohibited emblem from example images
avoid relying on exact-text matching for image incidents
keep moderators involved when results are disputed
Which design is the best fit?

options.text: A. Standard custom categories plus blocklists
B. Content Safety moderation plus rapid categories
C. Azure AI Search with visual severity thresholds
D. Vision labels with immediate auto-deletion

explanation_html:
B is the best fit because it combines the default image-moderation system with the rapid custom-category capability that Microsoft documents for emerging incidents involving text, image, or other modalities. Microsoft also notes that blocklists allow exact text matching and no image matching, which is why rapid custom categories are the stronger choice for a newly emerging prohibited emblem visible in example images.
It also aligns better with Microsoft’s operational guidance. Microsoft documents configurable severity filters for image moderation and recommends supporting human judgment rather than fully automating the whole process, especially when you need to handle disputed or borderline cases.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Standard custom categories plus blocklists. Microsoft says the standard custom-categories API works on text content, not image content. Microsoft also says blocklists support exact text matching and no image matching. That means this option fails both the “example images” requirement and the “do not rely on exact-text matching” requirement in the stem.
C. Azure AI Search with visual severity thresholds. Azure AI Search is not the moderation service Microsoft documents for harmful-image classification, and the severity-based image moderation flow is documented under Azure AI Content Safety instead. Search infrastructure does not replace built-in unsafe-visual-content classification or rapid incident detection from image samples. This option therefore confuses retrieval technology with moderation controls.
D. Vision labels with immediate auto-deletion. Generic vision labeling is not the documented moderation mechanism for harmful-content severity classification, and immediate auto-deletion ignores Microsoft’s recommendation to support human judgment in the review loop. The stem explicitly asks for policy tuning and disputed-case handling, which requires a more governed moderation workflow than raw labels plus irreversible automated enforcement.

question_html:
A web application lets users upload one DOCX file at a time. The translated file must be returned directly in the response, preserve formatting, and optionally apply a glossary. The team does not want to use Azure Blob Storage for this workflow.
Which translation capability should you include?
explanation_html:
Synchronous document translation is the best fit because Microsoft documents it for single-document translation where the translated document is returned directly to the calling client and Blob Storage is not required. Microsoft also notes that a single document can be translated with a glossary file while preserving the original document’s structure and format.
That combination matches every requirement in the scenario: one file at a time, formatting preserved, direct response, and optional glossary support. The asynchronous batch path is the wrong choice because Microsoft states that batch translation requires Azure Blob Storage containers for source and translated documents.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Text translation. Text translation is intended for translating text strings in real time, not for returning a translated DOCX while preserving document structure and formatting. The question is specifically about a file-based workflow, not a plain-text API call. It therefore lacks the document-preservation behavior the scenario requires.
  • B. Custom Translator. Custom Translator is about building customized neural translation systems for domain-specific terminology. It does not by itself define the single-file response pattern, direct HTTP return, or no-Blob-storage document flow described here. Even if customization were needed, the workflow shape would still be synchronous document translation.
  • D. Asynchronous batch document translation. Microsoft states that batch translation is for multiple documents and large files and requires Azure Blob Storage for source and translated documents. That directly conflicts with the requirement to avoid Blob Storage and return the translated file immediately in the response. It is the right service family but the wrong processing mode.

question_html:
A legal translation workflow must use a published custom translation system. If that exact custom system is unavailable for the language pair, the request must fail instead of falling back to general translation.
Snippet
import requests
params = {

"api-version": "3.0",
"from": "en",
"to": "fr",
"category": custom_category_id,
(MISSING CONFIG): "false"
}
body = [{"text": "The parties agree to binding arbitration."}]
response = requests.post(
endpoint + "/translate",
params=params,
headers=headers,
json=body,
)

Which key should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
“allowFallback” is correct because Microsoft documents allowFallback=false as the setting that prevents the service from falling back to a general system when a matching custom system does not exist. In that case, the request uses only systems trained for the specified category, and if no suitable custom system is found, the request returns a 400 error.
That behavior is exactly what the scenario requires: use the published custom translation system or fail. The category parameter identifies the custom translation system, and allowFallback=false enforces the strict requirement that general translation must not be used as a backup.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. “suggestedFrom”. Microsoft documents suggestedFrom as a fallback language assumption when source-language detection fails and from is omitted. In this snippet, from is already set to en, so source-language fallback is not the problem being controlled. It does not enforce strict use of a custom translation system.
  • C. “includeAlignment”. includeAlignment returns alignment projection between source and translated text. That can be useful for advanced inspection, but it does not control whether the request may fall back to a general translation system. It changes response detail, not model-selection behavior.
  • D. “includeSentenceLength”. includeSentenceLength adds sentence-boundary information to the response. Like includeAlignment, it enriches the output metadata but does not force or prohibit fallback from a custom category to a general system. It is unrelated to the fail-fast requirement in the scenario.

Several specialists debate and iteratively refine the same answer in one shared thread

explanation_html:
Choice A is correct because Microsoft defines sequential orchestration as agents executing one after another in a predefined order, concurrent orchestration as agents executing in parallel, handoff orchestration as dynamic delegation between specialized agents based on context, and group chat orchestration as collaborative work in a shared conversation. Each mapping in A follows those definitions directly.
This question tests whether you can distinguish orchestration patterns by workload shape instead of by generic “multi-agent” wording. Microsoft’s guidance emphasizes choosing the lowest-complexity pattern that meets the requirement and using a pattern that matches the actual coordination model, such as fixed order, parallel work, dynamic transfer, or iterative collaboration.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. This option reverses the first two mappings and swaps the collaboration patterns for items 3 and 4. A fixed draft-review-publish pipeline is sequential, not concurrent, because the later steps depend on earlier output. Likewise, iterative shared-thread collaboration is group chat, while dynamic transfer to a specialist is handoff.
C. This option incorrectly labels the fixed pipeline as handoff and the specialist transfer as sequential. Microsoft distinguishes handoff as context-driven delegation where the next agent is selected based on emerging task needs, not a predefined linear chain. The item about specialists debating in one thread is still group chat, so only one of the four mappings is correct here.
D. This option gets items 1 and 3 right but flips items 2 and 4. Parallel specialist analysis is the defining feature of concurrent orchestration, while group chat is specifically about shared-thread collaboration and iterative refinement.   • C. Remove operationId values. Microsoft requires an operationId for each OpenAPI operation and says those values help the model choose the right function. Removing them would create a separate validation or tool-selection problem rather than fix API-key injection. It makes the specification worse, not better.

question_html:
A company is operating a customer-support copilot built with Foundry and Azure OpenAI.
Users report that responses are “slow sometimes,” and the compliance team wants evidence of blocked or harmful-output trends.
The operations team must be able to:
reconstruct multi-step executions across LLM and tool calls
analyze prompt and completion token consumption over time
distinguish first-response delay from generation speed and total completion time
monitor harmful or blocked-request trends
query telemetry centrally and build dashboards
Which observability design is the best fit?

options.text: B. Application Insights tracing plus Azure OpenAI metrics and safety metrics
C. Azure AI Search analytics plus workbook screenshots
D. Request counts, error rates, screenshots, manual transcript review, and monthly audits

explanation_html:
B is the best fit because it combines the two Microsoft-native observability layers this scenario needs. Foundry observability integrates tracing with Azure Monitor Application Insights for execution visibility, while Azure OpenAI monitoring provides token, latency, request, and safety-related metrics such as Time to Response, Time to Last Byte, Blocked Volume, Harmful Volume Detected, and token usage metrics.
It also supports central analysis workflows. Microsoft documents diagnostic settings and Log Analytics for querying logs and metrics with KQL, and Foundry’s broader observability model explicitly calls out real-time dashboards for token consumption, latency, error rates, quality scores, and alerts on harmful outputs or threshold failures.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Weekly offline evaluation reports. Offline evaluations are useful, but they do not replace runtime observability. The requirement includes traces, token analytics, latency breakdowns, and safety trend monitoring in production, which Microsoft treats as a monitoring and tracing problem, not just an evaluation problem. Weekly reports would also be too delayed for active troubleshooting of intermittent performance issues.
C. Azure AI Search analytics plus workbook screenshots. Azure AI Search analytics can help with search-specific behavior, but the scenario is broader than retrieval and explicitly asks for LLM-tool execution flow, token usage, safety signals, and latency decomposition. Screenshots are not an observability pipeline, and they do not create queriable telemetry. This option misses the core Azure Monitor and Foundry tracing capabilities documented for generative AI operations.
D. Request counts, error rates, screenshots, manual transcript review, and monthly audits. Request counts and error rates are helpful, but they are not enough to explain token economics, first-byte responsiveness, token generation speed, or blocked-content trends. Manual review and monthly audits are also too coarse for near-real-time debugging and operational tuning. Microsoft’s observability guidance emphasizes integrated metrics, traces, and alerts rather than relying on sparse aggregate counts and manual inspection.
Azure OpenAI monitoring data reference
Monitor Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry Models

question_html:
A travel kiosk must listen to spoken Italian and show the translation as English text in near real time.
Which capability is the best fit?
explanation_html:
Speech to text translation is the best fit because Azure Speech supports real-time speech translation and can take spoken input in a specified source language and return translated text in a target language. Microsoft describes this as the standard speech-translation capability for converting input audio streams into translated text.
This matches the scenario better than text-only translation because the input is spoken audio, not already-transcribed text. Azure Speech is the service family in Foundry Tools that handles speech recognition and speech translation workloads, whereas pure text translation starts after speech has already been converted to text.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. Document translation. Document translation is for translating stored documents, not live spoken audio. The scenario needs microphone or audio-stream input and immediate translated text output, which is a speech workload rather than a document-processing workflow. That makes this option the wrong modality and the wrong execution pattern.
C. Text translation. Text translation can translate written text, but it assumes the speech has already been transcribed. The question asks for direct spoken-language handling, so using text translation alone would miss the speech-recognition step that Azure Speech provides. It could be part of a larger pipeline, but it is not the best single answer here.
D. Text to speech. Text to speech synthesizes spoken audio from text. That is the reverse direction of the requirement, because the kiosk must accept speech input and output translated text. It helps with speech-to-speech scenarios, but not for this text-output requirement by itself.

question_html:
A healthcare support app translates spoken consultations from English into Spanish. The team says common medical terms are translated too generically and wants the translated output to reflect domain-specific terminology already used in their bilingual documents.
Which component should they add?
explanation_html:
Custom Translator is the best answer because Microsoft documents that custom translation lets you build translation systems that understand the terminology used in your own business or industry. It is specifically intended to improve translated output by using your domain-specific bilingual material.
That is different from improving recognition of the spoken source audio. The scenario says the translated Spanish terminology is too generic, so the problem is in translation quality and terminology adaptation, not basic speech recognition accuracy.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Phrase list. Phrase lists help speech recognition pay extra attention to expected words or phrases during recognition. Microsoft documents them as a recognition-accuracy aid, not as the main mechanism for customizing translated target-language terminology across a domain.
B. Azure AI Search index. Azure AI Search can support retrieval scenarios, but it is not the documented component for customizing translation output. This option could support grounding in other workloads, but it does not directly solve the translation-terminology problem described here.
D. Custom Speech model. Custom Speech improves speech-to-text accuracy for specialized audio, jargon, or noise conditions. That is useful when transcription is wrong, but this question says the translated output is too generic, which points to translation customization instead.
Create and configure Azure resources for Translator
Improve recognition accuracy with phrase list

question_html:
A team uses Azure Translator text translation with a dynamic dictionary to preserve a brand term during translation. The request relies on source-language autodetection, and the override never applies.
What is the best next step?

options.text: D. Request translated Latin script output

explanation_html:
The best next step is to add the from parameter. Microsoft explicitly states that when you use the dynamic dictionary feature, you must use the from parameter rather than language autodetection. If from is omitted, the service can autodetect the language, but that does not satisfy the documented requirement for dynamic dictionary usage.
This makes the issue configuration-related rather than a problem with the target language, response shape, or translation mode. The service feature being used has a specific prerequisite, and the scenario describes exactly that prerequisite being violated.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Enable sentence boundary output. Sentence-boundary output comes from includeSentenceLength=true, which adds sentence-length metadata to the response. That information can be useful for downstream processing, but it does not make dynamic dictionary substitutions apply. It changes response detail, not dictionary eligibility.
  • C. Use asynchronous document translation. Document translation is for whole-document workflows, especially batch or file-based processing. The issue here is a text translation request using a dynamic dictionary, so switching processing modes would avoid the real root cause instead of fixing it. The documented requirement is to specify from.
  • D. Request translated Latin script output. Transliteration output is controlled with toScript and affects the script used in the translated result. That is useful when you want translated text represented in another script, but it has nothing to do with whether a dynamic dictionary term override is honored. It solves a different problem entirely.

What is Azure Translator in Foundry Tools?
Quickstart: translate text programmatically

question_html:
A platform team is designing a visual moderation workflow.
Match the following:
Classify images into built-in harm categories such as violence and sexual content
Configure which severity levels are accepted or rejected per category
Detect a newly emerging prohibited visual pattern from example images quickly
Keep humans involved for disputed or borderline cases
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Azure AI Content Safety image moderation
Configure category severity filters
Custom categories (rapid) API
Human review workflow

B.
Custom categories (standard) API
Azure AI Search scoring profile
Blocklists
Automatic deletion only

C.
Azure AI Content Safety image moderation
Configure category severity filters
Blocklists
Automatic deletion only

D.
Custom categories (standard) API
Configure category severity filters
Custom categories (rapid) API
Automatic deletion only

explanation_html:
A is the only mapping that matches Microsoft’s documentation end to end. Azure AI Content Safety image moderation is the built-in service for harmful-image classification, the service lets you configure per-category severity filters, the custom categories rapid API works on both text and image content for emerging incidents, and Microsoft recommends designing the system to support human judgment rather than fully automating moderation decisions.
This mapping also reflects the real operational split between default moderation, policy tuning, rapid custom detection, and human escalation. Microsoft’s transparency guidance explicitly notes that severity thresholds should be tuned for your use case and that meaningful human review helps detect and resolve misidentification and other failures.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. This choice fails in multiple places. Microsoft documents that the custom categories standard API works on text content, not image content, so it is not the right answer for built-in unsafe visual classification. Azure AI Search scoring profiles are unrelated to moderation thresholds, blocklists do exact text matching rather than image matching, and “automatic deletion only” ignores Microsoft’s guidance to support human judgment in moderation workflows.
C. The first two mappings are correct, which makes this distractor plausible. However, Microsoft explicitly notes that blocklists allow exact text matching and no image matching, so they are not the right tool for emerging prohibited visual patterns from image examples. It also ends with automatic deletion only, which is weaker than the documented recommendation to keep meaningful human review in the system.
D. This choice gets the second and third lines partly aligned, but it still breaks the first and fourth requirements. Microsoft says the standard custom-categories API does not work on image content, so it cannot serve as the main built-in visual-classification mechanism here. It also replaces human review with automatic deletion only, which conflicts with Microsoft’s guidance on using Content Safety to support people making judgments rather than fully automating the process.
Custom categories in Azure AI Content Safety
Transparency Note and use cases for AI Content Safety

question_html:
A team is testing a video-editing workflow in Foundry and keeps receiving 400 Bad Request with a dimension error. Their request uses a width of 1024 and a height of 1024.
What is the best next step?
explanation_html:
The best next step is to switch to a supported resolution. Microsoft’s troubleshooting guidance for Sora 2 explicitly says a 400 Bad Request with a dimension error means the requested resolution is unsupported, and it lists supported sizes such as 480×480, 720×720, 1080×1080, 1280×720, and 1920×1080.
This is the most direct fix because the failure is tied to an invalid render size, not to data access, variation count, or request timing. Changing the request to one of the supported dimensions aligns the workflow with the documented constraints of the video-generation service.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Increase n_variants to 4. n_variants controls how many alternate outputs are produced from the same prompt, not whether the chosen dimensions are valid. Raising it would increase output variation but would not resolve a dimension validation failure. It addresses a creative-output setting instead of the actual cause of the error.
  • B. Add a SharePoint connector. Connectors can matter in other Foundry workflows, but this scenario is failing on video render dimensions. Microsoft’s Sora 2 troubleshooting table ties this specific error to unsupported resolution, not to missing content connectors or external data sources. Adding a connector would leave the invalid width and height unchanged.
  • D. Switch to synchronous rendering. Microsoft describes video generation as an asynchronous process where you create a job, poll for status, and retrieve the finished video. The problem here is not the polling model or job lifecycle. It is the unsupported resolution, so switching architectural style would not fix the request validation error.

Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry Models v1 API
Choose an Azure AI image and video processing and generation technology

question_html:
An application receives short customer messages and must translate each message into French, German, and Japanese before passing the text to an LLM for summarization. The translations must be returned in real time, and no industry-specific customization is required.
Which component should perform the translation?
explanation_html:
Text translation is the best fit because Azure Translator’s text translation capability is the real-time API for source-to-target text translation, and the v3 Translate method supports translating to multiple target languages in one request by repeating the to parameter. That matches a workflow where short text is translated immediately before it continues through a larger LLM-powered pipeline.
This is also the generic choice when the content is not industry-specific. Microsoft’s architecture guidance maps generic text translation to Text translation, while Custom Translator is for domain-specific or industry-specific terminology and style.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure Language. Azure Language is for NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis, entity extraction, summarization, and question answering. It is not the primary Microsoft service for direct neural machine translation of text into multiple target languages. Choosing it would misplace the core translation step in the workflow.
  • C. Custom Translator. Custom Translator is used when you need a customized neural translation system that understands business-specific terminology and style. The scenario explicitly says no domain-specific customization is required, so the added training and deployment overhead is unnecessary. Standard text translation is the simpler and more direct fit.
  • D. Asynchronous document translation. Document translation is designed for translating whole documents while preserving their structure and formatting. The scenario is about short chat-style text that must be translated in real time before an LLM step, not about translating files asynchronously. Using document translation would be the wrong workload shape.

Azure Translator in Foundry Tools 3.0: Translate
Choose an Azure AI Targeted Language Processing Technology

question_html:
A team is building a Foundry-based voice workflow. They plan to use Azure Speech for speech recognition, then use an LLM-based translation deployment such as GPT-4o-mini instead of standard NMT for the translation stage.
Problem:
The design must use a language-model-based translation deployment inside Foundry.
Proposed solution:
Use only a multi-service Foundry Tools resource, because it already exposes prebuilt translation APIs and no Foundry resource is required.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
The proposed solution does not meet the goal. Microsoft documents that you can use either standard NMT or a language model deployment such as GPT-4o-mini or GPT-4o for text translation, but using a language model deployment requires a Foundry resource.
A multi-service Foundry Tools resource gives access to prebuilt translation capabilities, but that is not the same as meeting the requirement for an LLM-based translation deployment inside Foundry. The requirement is specifically about the model-backed translation path, so the Foundry resource is required.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Yes. This would be defensible for a standard prebuilt translation workflow that uses the usual Translator capability without an LLM deployment. But Microsoft explicitly states that a Foundry resource is required when you want to use a language model deployment for translation.
Choose an Azure AI targeted language processing technology
Text translation REST API preview reference guide

question_html:
Match the following:
A Foundry agent queries an existing Azure AI Search index
A Foundry agent searches user-uploaded documents
A custom application invokes a retrieval pipeline directly without using an agent
An MCP-compatible agent connects to a knowledge base endpoint
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Azure AI Search tool
File Search
Retrieve action
knowledge_base_retrieve via MCP

B.
File Search
Azure AI Search tool
Web search
Retrieve action

C.
Azure AI Search tool
Web search
File Search
knowledge_base_retrieve via MCP

D.
Retrieve action
File Search
Azure AI Search tool
Web search

explanation_html:
A is the only mapping that aligns with Microsoft’s documented integration patterns. The Azure AI Search tool connects a Foundry agent to an existing Azure AI Search index, File Search lets a Foundry agent retrieve from uploaded files, the retrieve action lets an application call the knowledge-base retrieval pipeline directly, and each knowledge base exposes an MCP endpoint with the knowledge_base_retrieve tool for MCP-compatible agents.
This is the core distinction behind the dot point: the retrieval pipeline can be connected in different ways depending on whether the caller is a Foundry agent, an app workflow, or another MCP-compatible client. Microsoft’s docs split these paths clearly rather than treating them as interchangeable.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. This option swaps the first two mappings and misuses Web search for direct retrieval-pipeline invocation. File Search is for uploaded documents, not for querying an existing Azure AI Search index. Web search is also not the direct app-side retrieve method for a knowledge base; Microsoft documents the retrieve action for that purpose.
C. The first and fourth lines are correct, which makes this distractor plausible. However, Web search is for public-web grounding, not for agent retrieval over uploaded user documents, and File Search is not the direct workflow API for invoking a knowledge-base retrieval pipeline. Microsoft documents those as separate capabilities with different data-source assumptions.
D. This option treats the retrieve action as though it were the normal agent-side tool for an existing Azure AI Search index, which is not how Microsoft documents that integration. It also assigns Azure AI Search tool to the direct application retrieval path and Web search to MCP knowledge-base integration, both of which are incorrect. The result mixes up agent tools, workflow APIs, and public-web grounding.
File search tool for Microsoft Foundry agents
Query a knowledge base using the retrieve action or MCP endpoint

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wSTDGPPYkobjsp-NYn4OyjyuT_nnw1iF7VBmLnWAZYE/edit?usp=sharing
Aurelia Mutual is preparing the agent for production. The Azure AI Search service and the claims API will have public network access disabled. The Foundry project must authenticate to Azure AI Search by using its managed identity and must access all dependencies through the organisation’s virtual network.
The architecture must satisfy TR1, TR2, and C1 with the least custom hosting responsibility.
Which agent deployment design should you use?

options.text: A. Basic agent with an Azure AI Search private endpoint
B. Hosted agent with public Search firewall access
C. Standard agent with VNet injection
D. Prompt flow endpoint using storage access keys

explanation_html:
A Standard agent setup with virtual network injection is the appropriate design. It provides an isolated agent environment that can access private Azure resources through the organisation’s virtual network while keeping the agent runtime managed by Microsoft. This directly supports private access to Azure AI Search and the claims API without requiring Aurelia Mutual to operate its own agent-hosting platform.
The Azure AI Search connection should use the Foundry project managed identity rather than a search key. Microsoft specifically requires managed-identity authentication when a Foundry agent connects to a private Azure AI Search service through a virtual network. The identity must also receive the required Azure AI Search data-plane roles.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. A basic agent can use an Azure AI Search tool, but it does not satisfy the private Azure AI Search requirement when public network access is disabled. Adding a private endpoint to Search does not place the basic agent runtime inside a network path that can reach that endpoint. The design would therefore fail TR1 even if its Search permissions were correct. A Standard agent setup with network injection is required for this private architecture.
B. Allowing a hosted agent to reach a public Search endpoint through firewall rules contradicts the requirement to disable public network access. Firewall restrictions can limit which public clients connect, but they do not convert the connection into private network traffic. This option therefore fails the explicit private-connectivity requirement. It also introduces an unnecessary exception to Aurelia Mutual’s network-isolation policy.
D. Storage access keys violate TR2 because they are stored credentials. A prompt flow endpoint would also introduce another deployment surface without resolving the agent’s need to privately access Azure AI Search and the claims API. Key rotation would create additional operational overhead and potential service interruption. Managed identities and RBAC are the required authentication model.
Connect an Azure AI Search index to Foundry agents
Configure a managed identity for Azure AI Search

question_html:
Refer to:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wSTDGPPYkobjsp-NYn4OyjyuT_nnw1iF7VBmLnWAZYE/edit?usp=sharing

The Azure AI Search service uses its system-assigned managed identity to read the approved storage container. A shared private link provides private outbound connectivity from the search service to the storage account.

The indexer currently runs only when an administrator starts it. You must satisfy BR2 with minimal operational overhead.

Snippet

{
  "name": "policy-document-indexer",
  "dataSourceName": "approved-policy-storage",
  "targetIndexName": "policy-knowledge-index",
  "parameters": {
    "configuration": {
      "dataToExtract": "contentAndMetadata",
      "parsingMode": "default"
    }
  },
  "schedule": {
    (MISSING CONFIG)
  }
}

Which configuration should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
An Azure AI Search indexer can be scheduled as frequently as every five minutes. Azure Storage provides built-in change detection based on source changes, so each scheduled execution can process new and modified documents rather than rebuilding the complete index. A five-minute interval gives sufficient time for indexing to finish within the 15-minute business target under normal operating conditions.
The data-source connection can identify the storage account by resource ID and use the search service’s managed identity instead of an account key. When the storage account is private, a shared private link enables the indexer’s outbound connection to remain on a private path. This design meets the freshness, private-networking, and credential-free requirements without introducing an Event Grid and Azure Functions ingestion pipeline.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. One minute is below the minimum supported Azure AI Search indexer schedule interval. The configuration would not be accepted as a valid schedule. Reducing the interval below the service limit is therefore not a valid way to meet BR2. A supported five-minute schedule provides adequate time for several attempts within the business window.
C. A 30-minute schedule cannot guarantee that a document becomes searchable within 15 minutes. A document committed immediately after an indexer run could wait almost 30 minutes before the next execution even begins. Indexing time would add further delay. This option therefore fails BR2 despite being operationally simple.
D. The 15-minute interval is theoretically close to the business limit, but setting disabled to true suspends scheduled execution. The indexer would not run automatically after the configuration is saved. Even without the disabled property, a document could wait almost 15 minutes before indexing begins. The design leaves no allowance for processing duration or a transient failed run.
Connect Azure AI Search to Storage using managed identity
Make outbound connections through a shared private link

question_html:
Refer to:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wSTDGPPYkobjsp-NYn4OyjyuT_nnw1iF7VBmLnWAZYE/edit?usp=sharing

Testing produces the following findings:

Vector-only retrieval frequently ranks conceptually similar documents above an exact policy identifier.
Keyword-only retrieval performs poorly when employees paraphrase policy language.
The agent’s managed identity can query the complete search index.
Document visibility must be determined by the signed-in employee’s Microsoft Entra group memberships.

You must satisfy BR1, BR3, and TR3.

Which search design should you implement?

options.text: A. Hybrid search with a group filter
B. Vector search with private endpoint and larger top-k
C. Semantic search with index-level RBAC assignment
D. Keyword search with storage-container SAS filtering

explanation_html:
Hybrid search combines full-text and vector queries in one request. The text portion can match exact policy identifiers, while the vector portion retrieves conceptually similar passages when employees use different wording. Azure AI Search merges the result sets by using Reciprocal Rank Fusion, after which semantic ranking can rerank the strongest candidates.
The application must also pass the employee’s group identifiers in an OData security filter that matches the index’s allowedGroupIds field. This trims unauthorised results during retrieval, before any document content is passed to the model. Authentication of the agent to the search service and authorisation of an employee to individual documents are separate controls; the project managed identity handles the former, while the query filter handles the latter.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. Increasing top-k can return more vector candidates, but it does not improve exact lexical matching for policy codes. A private endpoint protects the network path but does not enforce document-level authorisation. The model could still receive documents that the employee is not permitted to view. This option therefore fails both the exact-match and access-filtering requirements.
C. Semantic ranking can improve the ordering of an initial result set, but it does not replace the combined lexical and vector retrieval required by the scenario. Assigning an Azure AI Search role grants a principal permission to query an index or service; it does not dynamically filter documents based on the employee’s group membership. The agent’s identity would continue to retrieve content across all operational groups. This design therefore fails BR3.
D. Keyword search can match exact policy identifiers but remains weak for semantically similar employee questions. A storage SAS controls access to source storage and is not evaluated when users query documents already stored in the search index. It also violates the prohibition on stored credentials. This option cannot provide runtime document trimming for the signed-in employee.
Configure semantic ranking
Implement security filters for result trimming

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wSTDGPPYkobjsp-NYn4OyjyuT_nnw1iF7VBmLnWAZYE/edit?usp=sharing
The claims API is added to the agent as an OpenAPI tool. Aurelia Mutual replaces the pilot API key with managed-identity authentication.
Every claims API call now returns HTTP 401. The agent successfully obtains a Microsoft Entra token, but trace metadata shows that the OpenAPI tool requests a token for the Foundry project endpoint. The claims API validates tokens whose audience is api://aurelia-claims.
What should you change?

options.text: A. Set the audience to the API Application ID URI
B. Assign Search Service Contributor to the agent identity
C. Add a Key Vault reference to the OpenAPI connection
D. Enable anonymous authentication on the claims API

explanation_html:
For an OpenAPI tool that uses managed-identity authentication, the configured audience identifies the service for which Microsoft Entra ID must issue the access token. A custom API normally uses the Application ID URI exposed by its app registration. Because the claims API expects api://aurelia-claims, the OpenAPI tool must request a token for that audience.
The Foundry project endpoint identifies the Foundry project and is not the audience of the external claims API. A token issued for the wrong audience can be validly signed and unexpired but will still be rejected by the API with HTTP 401. After correcting the audience, Aurelia Mutual must also ensure that the agent identity has any app role or API permission required by the claims API.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. Search Service Contributor grants management permissions associated with Azure AI Search. It has no effect on token validation performed by the claims API. The trace already proves that the agent can obtain a token, so adding an unrelated Search role does not correct its audience. This change would increase privileges without resolving the HTTP 401 response.
C. Adding a Key Vault reference would reintroduce a stored credential and violate TR2. The claims API already supports Microsoft Entra authentication, so a secret-based connection is unnecessary. Key Vault can protect secrets but does not make a secretless design. It also would not correct the audience of the managed-identity token currently being rejected.
D. Anonymous authentication would remove the API’s ability to verify which workload is making the request. It would expose claim-status operations to any caller that can reach the endpoint unless additional custom controls were introduced. Private networking does not replace application-layer authentication. This option would weaken the security architecture and violate TR2.
Microsoft Foundry agent tools overview
Expose an application API in Microsoft Entra ID

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wSTDGPPYkobjsp-NYn4OyjyuT_nnw1iF7VBmLnWAZYE/edit?usp=sharing
After production deployment, end-to-end 95th-percentile latency increases from 3.2 seconds to 7.1 seconds. Operations staff must determine whether the delay occurs during search retrieval, model generation, or the claims API call.
The monitoring solution must retain durations, token usage, exceptions, dependency outcomes, and correlation identifiers. It must not retain message content, retrieved passages, claim identifiers, or tool arguments.
Which configuration should you use?

options.text: A. Foundry tracing with production content capture
B. Application Insights request logging without agent spans
C. OpenTelemetry tracing with content recording disabled
D. Azure Activity Log with diagnostic settings

explanation_html:
Microsoft Foundry tracing uses OpenTelemetry and Application Insights to capture agent execution spans. These spans can expose the duration and outcome of retrieval, model, and tool operations, allowing operators to isolate which dependency causes the latency regression. Tracing also supports operational information such as exceptions, token consumption, timestamps, and correlated execution steps.
Content recording must remain disabled in production. With message-content capture disabled, the solution can retain execution metadata without intentionally recording prompts, responses, and tool arguments. Aurelia Mutual should also avoid adding claim identifiers to custom span attributes, apply suitable sampling and retention policies, and use a de-identified test dataset for detailed quality evaluations.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Production content capture can record user messages, model outputs, retrieved material, and tool-call arguments. These fields could contain claim identifiers and other customer information prohibited by C4. Although full content is useful during controlled development, it creates an unacceptable production telemetry risk here. The organisation needs execution metadata rather than complete message payloads.
B. Standard Application Insights request logging can show the duration of the outer application request, but it does not automatically provide the complete internal agent span hierarchy. Operations staff would struggle to distinguish search latency from model latency or claims API latency. Additional manual instrumentation would effectively recreate the OpenTelemetry tracing design. This option therefore does not satisfy the diagnostic requirement with the least operational effort.
D. Azure Activity Log records subscription-level control-plane events such as resource creation, deletion, and configuration changes. It is not intended to trace individual agent executions or measure model, retrieval, and tool-call durations. Diagnostic settings can route supported logs and metrics, but they do not turn Activity Log into an agent tracing system. This option cannot provide the required request-level dependency correlation.
Microsoft Foundry tracing and data handling
Configure tracing for AI agent frameworks

question_html:
A development team wants a customer-support assistant that can plan multistep responses, invoke tools, call external APIs, and scale in production without building its own agent runtime.
Which Foundry service should they choose as the primary workflow platform?
explanation_html:
Foundry Agent Service is the correct choice because Microsoft documents it as a fully managed platform for building, deploying, and scaling AI agents. That maps directly to the scenario, which is about agent workflows, runtime hosting, and production operation rather than just retrieval or model catalog access.
Microsoft’s tool documentation further explains that agents in Foundry Agent Service can use tools to search the web, run code, query data, and call APIs. That is exactly the workflow posture described here: multistep reasoning plus tool invocation plus operational hosting, which is broader than search, knowledge, or model deployment alone.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Search. Azure AI Search is the right choice for grounded retrieval, vector search, and knowledge access patterns. However, the scenario is centered on hosting and running an agent workflow that can decide when to invoke tools and APIs. Search can be attached to an agent, but it is not the managed agent runtime itself.
  • B. Foundry IQ. Foundry IQ is a managed knowledge layer for enterprise data and is valuable when agents need permission-aware knowledge access. But the question is asking for the primary workflow platform for an operational agent. Knowledge access is just one part of the design, while Agent Service is the broader execution platform.
  • C. Foundry Models. Foundry Models helps you discover, compare, evaluate, and deploy models. That is important for model choice, but it does not by itself provide the managed agent workflow platform described in the stem. A model catalog is not the same thing as an agent runtime with tools and orchestration.

Agent tools overview for Foundry Agent Service
Microsoft Foundry Models overview

question_html:
A company is creating a common AI platform for legal, HR, finance, and engineering agents.
The platform must:
Support tool-using agents.
Allow multiple agents to consume the same enterprise knowledge layer.
Combine knowledge from multiple governed data sources.
Support permission-aware retrieval.
Support query planning and retrieval for complex questions.
Return grounded answers with source attribution.
Keep model inference available through managed Foundry deployments.
Avoid creating a separate duplicate vector store for every agent.
Which architecture best satisfies the requirements?

options.text: A. Agent Service + per-agent File Search + duplicated vector stores
B. Agent Service + Search knowledge base + model deployment
C. Prompt flow + Azure SQL retrieval + hosted model endpoint
D. Azure Functions + Blob Storage + shared model deployment

explanation_html:
Microsoft Foundry Agent Service provides the agent execution layer, while a Foundry IQ knowledge base backed by Azure AI Search provides a reusable enterprise knowledge layer. Microsoft describes Foundry IQ as turning enterprise content into reusable, permission-aware knowledge bases that agents can consume, while Azure AI Search knowledge bases can orchestrate retrieval across knowledge sources.
This separation is important architecturally. Agent definitions can focus on behavior, tools, and workflows while the knowledge base centrally manages grounding and retrieval. Model deployments then provide the inference capability used by the agents and retrieval orchestration, avoiding unnecessary duplication of knowledge storage across every individual agent.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Agent Service + per-agent File Search + duplicated vector stores. File Search is a valid grounding mechanism for files uploaded to an agent and can automatically handle parsing, chunking, embeddings, and retrieval. It is less appropriate when the organization specifically wants a reusable, centrally governed knowledge layer shared across many agents and multiple enterprise sources. Duplicating vector stores for each agent also increases synchronization and lifecycle overhead.
C. Prompt flow + Azure SQL retrieval + hosted model endpoint. Azure SQL can store structured enterprise information and could participate in a larger retrieval solution. This design does not naturally provide the reusable permission-aware knowledge-base abstraction, agent-focused query planning, or multi-source retrieval model described in the requirements. It also substitutes a flow-oriented architecture for the explicit tool-using agent requirement.
D. Azure Functions + Blob Storage + shared model deployment. Blob Storage is suitable for storing source documents, and Azure Functions could implement custom orchestration code. Neither component by itself provides vector retrieval, hybrid search, query decomposition, citations, or reusable permission-aware knowledge management. The organization would have to build much of the required retrieval platform itself instead of using the Foundry and Search capabilities designed for it.
Create a knowledge base in Azure AI Search
Study guide for Exam AI-103

question_html:
A company has been granted enough Global Provisioned PTU quota to create a planned production deployment.
When the team attempts to create the deployment in its preferred region, Foundry reports that the requested provisioned capacity is currently unavailable.
Finance proposes purchasing a one-year Azure Reservation immediately because the subscription already has sufficient PTU quota.
The application can run from another supported region, and no strict regional processing requirement exists.
What should the team do next?

options.text: A. Purchase an Azure Reservation before creating the deployment
B. Request additional PTU quota in the same region
C. Test provisioned capacity in another eligible region
D. Add application replicas and retry the deployment

explanation_html:
PTU quota and deployable capacity are separate concepts. Quota defines how many PTUs the subscription is allowed to deploy for a provisioned deployment type in a region, but actual service capacity must still be available when the deployment is created. Microsoft explicitly warns that capacity might not be available even when quota exists.
Because the application has no strict regional requirement, checking another supported region is the appropriate next action. The team should first successfully establish the provisioned deployment and verify the required PTU capacity, then purchase an Azure Reservation if long-term discounted billing is appropriate. Microsoft specifically states that reservations do not guarantee capacity and recommends creating deployments before purchasing the reservation.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Purchase an Azure Reservation before creating the deployment. An Azure Reservation is a financial discount applied to provisioned-throughput billing rather than a mechanism for reserving physical model-serving capacity. Purchasing it does not make unavailable regional capacity suddenly become deployable. Microsoft recommends establishing the deployment first and purchasing reservation coverage afterward.
B. Request additional PTU quota in the same region. Additional quota is useful when the requested PTU deployment exceeds the subscription’s allocation. The scenario explicitly says sufficient PTU quota already exists, so increasing that policy limit does not address the reported capacity shortage. More permission to consume capacity does not create physical capacity where it is unavailable.
D. Add application replicas and retry the deployment. Scaling application hosts can increase the application’s ability to issue requests, but it has no effect on whether Foundry can allocate provisioned model capacity. In fact, app-layer scaling and model-serving capacity are separate controls. The failure is occurring during deployment creation, before application request processing is relevant.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/concepts/provisioned-throughput
Operate provisioned throughput deployments

question_html:
A production customer-support agent has maintained:
99.95% endpoint availability.
Stable P95 latency.
Stable HTTP error rates.
Normal token consumption.
After a large policy-document refresh, customer complaints increase.
A sampled evaluation shows:
Lower groundedness.
Lower answer relevance.
Occasional new safety failures.
The operations team must detect similar regressions automatically and be able to investigate which retrieval, tool, or agent step contributed to a bad response.
Which monitoring design is most appropriate?

options.text: A. Continuous evaluations, traces, and operational metrics
B. Azure Monitor availability metrics and error alerts
C. Monthly transcript sampling without trace correlation
D. Search index health dashboards and replica metrics

explanation_html:
Operational metrics alone cannot establish whether an AI response is grounded, relevant, or safe. Microsoft Foundry observability combines evaluation metrics, logs, traces, model outputs, and operational signals so teams can monitor both conventional service health and AI-specific quality behavior. Continuous evaluation can identify quality and safety regressions in production traffic.
Tracing then provides the diagnostic depth needed to determine why a failed interaction occurred. Foundry traces can capture agent inputs, outputs, tool usage, retries, latency, and other execution details, allowing an operator to move from a degraded evaluation metric to the particular retrieval or tool step involved.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. Azure Monitor availability metrics and error alerts. These signals are important because they reveal uptime, request failures, and infrastructure-performance problems. The scenario already demonstrates that those metrics are healthy while answer quality has deteriorated. They therefore cannot independently detect the groundedness, relevance, and safety regressions described.
C. Monthly transcript sampling without trace correlation. Manual transcript review can reveal qualitative failures and remains useful for targeted investigation. A monthly cadence is too slow for the requirement to detect future regressions automatically, and plain transcripts do not reveal the complete execution path behind the response. Without trace correlation, it can be difficult to determine whether retrieval, a tool call, or the generation step caused the problem.
D. Search index health dashboards and replica metrics. Search health is important for a grounded application because indexing failures and retrieval issues can reduce response quality. It represents only one layer of the complete agent system, however, and would not identify generation safety failures or incorrect tool behavior. The requested design needs both AI-quality evaluation and end-to-end execution observability.
Agent tracing overview
Monitor agents with the Agent Monitoring Dashboard

question_html:
A team has initialized a hosted agent by using:

azd ai agent init –infra=bicep

The generated azure.yaml and infra/ Bicep files are committed to Git.

The agent:

Runs correctly locally.
Has already been deployed successfully with azd up.
Must be promoted through development, test, and production.
Must use GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps rather than manual portal deployments.

Snippet

azd ai agent init –infra=bicep

git add azure.yaml infra/
git commit -m "Add hosted agent infrastructure"
(MISSING CONFIG)

Which command should replace (MISSING CONFIG) to configure the deployment pipeline?
explanation_html:
Microsoft documents azd pipeline config as the Azure Developer CLI command for configuring continuous delivery for hosted agents. It detects the Git provider, creates the CI/CD authentication identity, sets repository variables or secrets, and generates the appropriate GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines workflow.
Using –infra=bicep during initialization also materializes the agent infrastructure into an infra/ directory so it can be version controlled and customized. Together, the committed azure.yaml, Bicep infrastructure, and generated deployment workflow support repeatable environment promotion instead of relying on portal drift.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. azd provision –from-portal –manual-sync. azd provision is associated with provisioning infrastructure, but the additional flags in this option do not represent the documented pipeline-configuration workflow. Provisioning resources once does not create GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps automation. The requirement is to configure CI/CD rather than manually synchronize portal state.
B. az agent create –manual –no-pipeline. This command does not represent the documented Azure Developer CLI hosted-agent pipeline workflow. The requirement explicitly calls for automated source-controlled deployment rather than manual agent creation. Even if an agent were successfully created manually, the promotion mechanism across environments would remain missing.
C. azd deploy –skip-infra –environment production. An azd deployment can participate in a delivery process, but running a deployment command locally is not the same as configuring the repository’s CI/CD integration. Skipping infrastructure would also undermine the requirement to keep the Bicep-defined environment synchronized when infrastructure changes. The documented command that establishes the pipeline is azd pipeline config.
Hosted agent infrastructure with Azure Developer CLI
azure.yaml reference for hosted agents

question_html:
A Foundry project must connect to an internal MCP endpoint.
Requirements:
the MCP service is protected by Microsoft Entra ID
no client secret can be stored
all agents in the project can share the same project service identity
the target endpoint expects the Cognitive Services audience
the identity will receive the required RBAC role on the target resource
Which connection configuration should you use?
explanation_html:
The connection should be configured with the target audience, for example:
azd ai connection create internal-mcp \
–kind remote-tool \
–target https://.cognitiveservices.azure.com/language/mcp \
–auth-type project-managed-identity \
–audience https://cognitiveservices.azure.com
Overall explanation:
project-managed-identity uses the project’s system-assigned managed identity. It is therefore appropriate when agents in the project should share the same service identity and secrets must be avoided. Microsoft also requires the corresponding identity to receive the necessary RBAC permissions on the destination resource.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. custom-keys stores a header credential such as an API key or PAT in a connection. That conflicts with the requirement to use Entra identity without stored secrets.
B. user-entra-token passes a user’s Entra identity and is appropriate for delegated user scenarios. The requirement calls for a shared project service identity.
D. agentic-identity uses an agent-specific identity. It would be appropriate where individual agents require separate security principals, not where the entire project should share one identity.

question_html:
A team is grounding a chatbot on large technical manuals.
They want Azure AI Search to chunk the content and generate embeddings during indexing, and they also want vector encoding support in the query pipeline.
Which feature should they use?
explanation_html:
Integrated vectorization is the best answer because Microsoft defines it as an extension of both the indexing and query pipelines in Azure AI Search. It adds vector encoding during indexer-driven indexing and also during queries, which directly matches the requirement in the scenario.
It also fits the chunking requirement. Microsoft’s integrated-vectorization documentation states that a skillset can chunk and vectorize content from a supported data source, using Text Split or Document Layout for chunking and an embedding skill for vectorization. Microsoft’s RAG overview also notes that large documents commonly require automatic chunking and that integrated vectorization is the built-in answer for similarity search.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Semantic ranker configuration. Semantic ranker improves relevance by reranking results, but it does not chunk documents or generate embeddings during indexing. Microsoft positions it as a relevance feature, not as a content-ingestion and vectorization mechanism. It can complement a grounding pipeline, but it does not replace integrated vectorization.
  • B. Knowledge store projections. A knowledge store is useful for persisting enriched outputs, but it is not the feature Microsoft documents for automatic chunking and vector generation in the index pipeline. The scenario specifically asks for chunking and embeddings in Azure AI Search itself. That points to integrated vectorization instead of storage projections.
  • C. Shaper skill output. The Shaper skill helps reshape in-memory enrichments, but it is not the primary feature for end-to-end chunking and vector encoding. Microsoft’s integrated-vectorization articles center on skillsets, chunking skills, and embedding skills, not on Shaper as the main answer. Shaper can participate in some pipelines, but it does not satisfy the full requirement on its own.

Integrated vectorization using REST APIs
RAG in Azure AI Search

question_html:
A legal team is building a grounding index for scanned contracts and reports.
Requirements:
Extract both text and images from the files.
Keep image location metadata so the application can relate figures to nearby content.
Output tables and figures in a format that is easier for LLMs to consume.
Avoid adding a separate Text Split skill for chunking.
Which design best meets the requirements?

options.text: B. OCR skill plus Text Split
C. Document Layout skill with plain text

explanation_html:
Azure Content Understanding skill is the strongest fit because Microsoft says this skill analyzes unstructured documents and other content types, extracts both text and images, and preserves each image’s location within the document. Microsoft also states that the skill can be used for both content extraction and chunking, so there is no need to add a Text Split skill in the same skillset.
It also matches the table-and-figure requirement better than the alternatives. Microsoft documents that the Azure Content Understanding skill outputs tables and figures in Markdown, can recognize cross-page tables as a single unit, and allows chunks to span multiple pages instead of forcing page-bounded chunks. Those behaviors are especially aligned to RAG and grounding workflows for rich documents.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. OCR skill plus Text Split. OCR is useful for extracting printed and handwritten text from image files, but the requirement is broader than OCR alone. Microsoft positions the Azure Content Understanding skill as a richer content-extraction-and-chunking option that preserves image position and handles tables and figures more effectively for LLM consumption. OCR plus Text Split would usually require more pipeline assembly and still would not match the Markdown and cross-page-table advantages described by Microsoft.
  • C. Document Layout skill with plain text. This is a plausible distractor because it can parse documents, but Microsoft explicitly contrasts it with Azure Content Understanding skill and says the Content Understanding skill outputs tables and figures in Markdown while Document Layout outputs them as plain text. Microsoft also notes that Document Layout restricts chunks to a single page, which is weaker for semantic units that span pages. That makes it a less complete match to the requirements.
  • D. Query-time semantic reranking. Semantic reranking happens after indexing and improves relevance of retrieved results, but it does not extract text and images from source files, preserve location metadata, or create Markdown-rich chunks. The scenario is fundamentally about ingestion and indexing design, not about ranking after the index is built. This option therefore addresses the wrong stage of the pipeline.

RAG in Azure AI Search
OCR skill

question_html:
Match the following:
High-resolution OCR text, paragraphs, and lines from scanned documents
Tables, selection marks, and structural regions for downstream understanding
Standard invoice fields from known invoice documents
One model ID that routes mixed document types to the right trained extractor
Choices:

options.text:
A.
prebuilt-layout
prebuilt-read
Custom extraction model
Query fields

B.
prebuilt-read
prebuilt-layout
prebuilt-invoice
Composed custom model

C.
prebuilt-invoice
prebuilt-layout
prebuilt-read
Composed custom model

D.
prebuilt-read
Query fields
prebuilt-invoice
prebuilt-layout

explanation_html:
Choice B is correct because Microsoft documents the Read model as the OCR engine that extracts printed and handwritten text, paragraphs, lines, and words from document files. Microsoft documents the Layout model as the structure-analysis model for tables, selection marks, and layout regions, the Invoice model as the pretrained model for invoice field extraction, and composed custom models as the way to expose multiple trained models behind one model ID for mixed document types.
This mapping reflects a realistic multimodal extraction pipeline. OCR comes first through Read, structural understanding is handled by Layout, standard business fields for invoices come from the invoice model, and mixed-type custom routing is handled by a composed custom model. That is the cleanest stage-to-capability mapping for this exact subtopic.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This option swaps the first two stages and then misuses Custom extraction model and Query fields. Layout includes structure and OCR-related output, but Microsoft specifically documents Read as the OCR-first model for extracting text, paragraphs, and lines from scanned documents. Query fields also do not replace a composed custom model for mixed-type routing behind one model ID.
  • C. This option incorrectly assigns invoice extraction to the OCR-first stage and moves Read into the invoice-field slot. Microsoft documents the invoice model as the pretrained field extractor for invoices, not the general OCR-first stage. The result is a broken mapping of document-processing responsibilities.
  • D. This option begins correctly with Read for OCR, but it then assigns Query fields to the structure-analysis role and Layout to the one-model-ID routing role. Microsoft documents Query fields as an add-on for targeted field extraction, not as a replacement for layout analysis, and Layout is not the mechanism for mixed-document routing across several trained schemas. Those roles belong to different features and models.

Document layout analysis
Composed custom models

question_html:
A team is preparing MP4 training videos for a grounding pipeline.

They want the analyzer to return keyframes, transcripts, and chapter segments before the content is indexed.

Snippet

from azure.ai.contentunderstanding.models import (
AnalysisInput,
AudioVisualContent
)

video_url = “https://contoso.example/training/video1.mp4”

poller = client.begin_analyze(
analyzer_id=(MISSING CONFIG),
inputs=[AnalysisInput(url=video_url)],
)

result = poller.result()

video_content: AudioVisualContent = result.contents[0] # type: ignore

print(video_content.markdown)

Which value should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
“prebuilt-videoSearch” is correct because Microsoft’s Content Understanding quickstart uses that analyzer to extract keyframes, transcript, and chapter segments from video. Microsoft’s video overview also says the prebuilt video analyzer packages the content into richly formatted Markdown and JSON so that a search index or chat agent can ingest it without custom glue code.
Microsoft’s prebuilt-analyzers reference also describes prebuilt-videoSearch as the analyzer that extracts transcripts and segment descriptions and automatically splits videos into meaningful sections based on topic shifts, scene changes, or visual cues. That aligns exactly with the workflow in the question.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. “prebuilt-imageSearch”. Microsoft documents prebuilt-imageSearch for images, where it generates a one-paragraph description and extracts visual content for search and retrieval. It does not provide the video-specific outputs the scenario asks for, such as chapter segments and transcript-aware video analysis. That makes it the wrong modality.
  • B. “prebuilt-document”. Document-oriented analyzers are for document extraction workflows, not for MP4 video analysis. The scenario requires a video analyzer that understands time-based media and can return segments and keyframes. Microsoft’s examples point to prebuilt-videoSearch, not a document analyzer, for this pattern.
  • D. “prebuilt-audioSearch”. prebuilt-audioSearch is a strong distractor because it supports transcripts and summaries, but Microsoft describes it as optimized for conversation analysis and content extraction from audio and video files, not for video scene segmentation and keyframe-oriented outputs. The quickstart specifically uses prebuilt-videoSearch when the requirement includes keyframes and chapter segments.

Prebuilt analyzers in Azure Content Understanding
Azure Content Understanding video overview

question_html:
A procurement platform receives large uploaded PDFs that can contain one or more document types in the same file.
The solution must:
detect and split mixed files into component documents
identify whether each component is a purchase order, supplier form, or invoice
extract different business fields for each document type
call one model endpoint from the application layer
minimize custom routing code in the application
Which design is the best fit?
explanation_html:
A composed custom model is the best fit because Microsoft documents composed models as grouping multiple custom models behind a single model ID. Microsoft also explains that some scenarios require classifying the document first and then analyzing it with the model best suited to extract the fields, especially when the uploaded file contains multiple document types or when the document type is not known in advance. That maps directly to the requirements in the stem.
This design also minimizes routing logic in the app because the application can call one composed model endpoint instead of maintaining separate branching logic for each document type. Microsoft states that the response includes a docType property indicating which component model handled the extraction, which is exactly what you want in a mixed-document intake pipeline.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. prebuilt-layout with query fields. Query fields can extend layout or prebuilt models so you can request specific fields in addition to structure. That is useful when you want targeted field extraction without full custom training. However, it does not solve the central problem in this stem, which is automatic document-type identification and routing across several different business schemas inside one endpoint.
  • C. prebuilt-read with searchable PDF. Read is the OCR layer and searchable PDF is helpful when you need searchable output. But the stem requires document-type recognition plus different field schemas per document type, which Microsoft addresses through classification and custom extraction rather than plain OCR output. Searchable PDF improves usability, not schema routing.
  • D. prebuilt-invoice with key-value pairs. The invoice model is excellent for invoice extraction, and Microsoft documents optional key-value-pair return for invoices. But the upload stream includes purchase orders and supplier forms as well, each with different extraction needs. A single invoice model is too narrow for the mixed-type routing requirement in this scenario.

Custom document models
Choose the right Azure AI tool for document processing

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KL5r5lDcN4JDa45bROfDFuAS9anguaQi4BCFAtn4_p4/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy TR1 and TR2.
The evaluation team has generated responses from both candidate language models by using the same representative Meridian dataset. The JSONL file contains the engineering question, retrieved context, generated response, approved reference response, latency, and token usage for every test case.
The team must apply quality and safety evaluators to the existing responses without invoking either candidate model again.
Which evaluation target should you select in Microsoft Foundry?
explanation_html:
Dataset evaluation is designed for evaluating pre-existing model or agent outputs stored in a CSV or JSONL dataset. Meridian can map the question, generated response, retrieved context, and approved reference response to the fields required by evaluators such as groundedness, relevance, response completeness, and safety. Neither candidate model needs to be invoked again because the generated outputs already exist.
Latency and token usage recorded in the dataset can be analysed alongside the evaluator scores. This allows Meridian to determine whether any quality improvement from the larger model justifies its additional latency and consumption. Using the same dataset and evaluator configuration for both models also provides the controlled comparison required by TR1 and TR2.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Benchmark evaluation uses standard benchmark datasets and scoring methods to compare general model capabilities. It can help Meridian identify candidate models before workload testing. It does not directly evaluate the existing responses against Meridian’s approved engineering answers and retrieved maintenance context. The organisation still requires a dataset evaluation using its representative data.
B. Continuous evaluation is used to monitor application or agent quality after deployment by evaluating production interactions or sampled operational data. Meridian is making a predeployment model-selection decision and does not yet have production traffic. Continuous evaluation would therefore occur too late to satisfy TR1. It also would not make direct use of the prepared response dataset as the evaluation target.
D. Trace-based agent evaluation analyses historical agent executions captured through Application Insights. It is appropriate when Meridian needs to inspect tool selection, agent decisions, or previously recorded conversations. The current task compares existing model responses rather than complete agent executions. No agent traces are required to score the prepared JSONL data.
Built-in evaluators in Microsoft Foundry
View evaluation results

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KL5r5lDcN4JDa45bROfDFuAS9anguaQi4BCFAtn4_p4/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E4, BR3, TR3, and C4.
The agent already uses Azure AI Search to retrieve approved maintenance procedures. You must enable the agent to retrieve the current state of a work order directly from the existing REST API.
The agent must select the appropriate API operation, supply the required parameters, and authenticate by using the Foundry managed identity. Meridian must not implement another service to execute the API request.
Which tool should you add to the agent?
explanation_html:
An OpenAPI tool enables a Foundry agent to discover and invoke operations described by an OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 specification. The agent can select the appropriate work-order operation, construct its parameters, invoke the endpoint, and use the returned current state in its response. This directly uses the API described in E4 without requiring Meridian to write a separate dispatch service.
OpenAPI tools support managed-identity authentication for APIs protected by Microsoft Entra ID. Meridian must configure the work-order API’s Application ID URI as the audience and grant the Foundry identity the required API access. This meets TR3 while avoiding API keys, client secrets, and custom orchestration.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. Azure AI Search retrieves indexed content from a search index. It is appropriate for maintenance manuals, but it does not invoke arbitrary operations from the work-order API specification. Indexing the work-order data would also create a delay between an operational change and the agent’s response. That would not reliably satisfy BR3’s requirement for the current work-order state.
C. A function tool allows an agent to request execution of a function defined by the application. Meridian would still need to host code that receives the tool request, calls the work-order API, and returns the result. This adds custom orchestration that C4 requires the implementation team to minimise. The existing OpenAPI specification makes that additional function layer unnecessary.
D. An MCP tool connects the agent to capabilities exposed by a Model Context Protocol server. Meridian does not have an MCP server in the case-study environment. Introducing one solely to wrap the existing REST API would add another hosted component and security boundary. It would not be the most direct solution under C4.
Foundry Agent Service tool catalogue
Secure OpenAPI calls from Foundry Agent Service

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1KL5r5lDcN4JDa45bROfDFuAS9anguaQi4BCFAtn4_p4/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E1, BR1, BR2, and C2.
A training image can contain several defect categories and multiple instances of the same defect. The production application must identify the category and location of every detected instance.
Which Custom Vision project configuration should you use?
explanation_html:
Object detection is required because BR1 requires a bounding box for every visible defect instance. An object-detection model can identify several regions within one image, including multiple instances of the same trained category. Image classification would instead assign labels to the complete image without returning each defect’s location.
The General (compact) domain is required because E1 specifies a local ONNX runtime and BR2 requires disconnected inference. Custom Vision models trained with compact domains can be exported and run locally, including through ONNX-compatible runtimes. The non-compact General domain is intended for hosted prediction and does not meet the offline deployment requirement.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Multilabel classification can assign several defect labels to a complete image. It does not return bounding boxes for individual defect instances. It also cannot distinguish two separate instances of the same defect by location. Although the compact domain supports export, the selected project type still fails BR1.
B. Object detection with the General domain would identify and locate multiple defects correctly. However, the model would remain dependent on the hosted Custom Vision prediction service.
