question_html:
A team already has an Azure AI Search index that stores product titles, long descriptions, tags, and embeddings.
They want to improve grounding quality by using semantic ranking over the human-readable fields in the index.
The solution must meet these requirements:
identify the title, content, and keyword fields used for semantic ranking
avoid rebuilding the index
support query-time selection of the ranking setup
Which component should the team configure?
explanation_html:
A semantic configuration is the correct component because Microsoft defines it as the part of an index that establishes the field inputs used for semantic ranking. Microsoft also states that you can add or update a semantic configuration at any time with no rebuild required, and that a query can specify which semantic configuration to use or fall back to the default.
This lines up directly with the scenario. The team already has an index and wants to point semantic ranking at the right title, content, and keyword fields for grounding. Microsoft further says those fields must be searchable and retrievable string fields, which reinforces that semantic configuration is the right index-level setup for this requirement.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. HNSW algorithm. HNSW is relevant to vector retrieval because Azure AI Search uses vector ranking algorithms such as HNSW and eKNN. But HNSW controls how nearest-neighbor vector matching works, not which title, content, and keyword fields semantic ranking should use. It addresses vector retrieval mechanics, not semantic field configuration.
  • B. Scoring profile. Scoring profiles can boost certain fields or criteria in text and hybrid search, and Microsoft lists them as a relevance-tuning option. But they are not the configuration that defines semantic title, content, and keyword inputs. The scenario is explicitly about semantic ranking field setup, which Microsoft assigns to semantic configurations.
  • C. Vectorizer. A vectorizer is useful for generating embeddings for vector search workflows. However, the question is about configuring semantic ranking over human-readable text fields, not generating embeddings. Microsoft separates vectorization concerns from semantic configuration, so this option addresses a different layer of the retrieval pipeline.

Semantic Ranking Overview – Azure AI Search
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) in Azure AI Search

question_html:
A developer is testing a hybrid query for a grounding pipeline.

The team wants semantic reranking plus extractive captions and answers from the returned chunks.

Snippet

{
  "search": "reset a leaked service principal credential",
  "vectorQueries": [
    {
      "kind": "vector",
      "fields": "contentVector",
      "vector": [0.018, -0.044, 0.012, 0.009],
      "k": 50
    }
  ],
  "captions": "extractive|highlight-true",
  "answers": "extractive|count-3",
  "select": "title, content, source",
  (MISSING CONFIG)
}

Which missing configuration best completes the query?
explanation_html:
This is the correct completion because Microsoft says semantic ranking queries need semantic parameters, and examples show queryType set to semantic together with semanticConfiguration. Microsoft also documents that captions and answers are returned as part of semantic ranking requests, not plain hybrid retrieval without semantic setup.
The existing snippet is already close to a valid hybrid grounding query because it includes both search and vectorQueries. Adding semantic query settings is what enables semantic reranking and the extractive caption and answer behavior the team wants. Microsoft’s hybrid examples also show k of 50 when semantic ranker is used so the reranker has enough input candidates.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. “orderBy”:”lastUpdated desc”. Microsoft says explicit ordering on specific fields overrides relevance scores and is incompatible with semantic ranking. If you apply semantic ranking over ordered results, Azure AI Search returns an HTTP 400 error. So this option actively conflicts with the goal of semantic grounding quality.
  • C. “search”:”*”. Microsoft states that search=* or an empty search string bypasses relevance scoring and therefore cannot be semantically ranked. Semantic ranking requires plain-text query input that can be evaluated for relevance. This would break the intended semantic behavior instead of enabling it.
  • D. “suggest”:”reset”. Suggest functionality is for suggestion-style experiences, not semantic reranking in a search request. Microsoft’s semantic query documentation and hybrid query examples do not use suggest to enable semantic captions, answers, or reranking. It is unrelated to the missing grounding configuration here.

Create a Hybrid Query – Azure AI Search
Create a Vector Query – Azure AI Search

question_html:
Match each Azure AI Search concept to its primary role in a grounding pipeline.
Match the following:
Vector search
Hybrid search
Semantic ranker
Semantic configuration
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Reranks fused results using language models
Defines title, content, and keyword fields
Finds nearest embeddings by similarity
Combines keyword and vector retrieval

B.
Combines keyword and vector retrieval
Finds nearest embeddings by similarity
Defines title, content, and keyword fields
Reranks fused results using language models

C.
Finds nearest embeddings by similarity
Combines keyword and vector retrieval
Reranks initial results for better relevance
Defines title, content, and keyword fields

D.
Defines title, content, and keyword fields
Reranks initial results for better relevance
Combines keyword and vector retrieval
Finds nearest embeddings by similarity

explanation_html:
Choice C is correct because Microsoft describes vector search as nearest-neighbor matching over embeddings, hybrid search as the combination of keyword and vector queries in one request, semantic ranker as a reranking layer that improves the quality of initial results, and semantic configuration as the index section that specifies title, content, and keyword fields for semantic ranking.
These roles are distinct but complementary in grounding pipelines. Vector search expands recall through conceptual similarity, hybrid search combines that with keyword precision, semantic ranker improves the final ordering, and semantic configuration tells the reranker which fields carry the human-meaningful text.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This option swaps several responsibilities. Semantic ranker does rerank results, but it is incorrectly assigned to vector search here, while semantic configuration is incorrectly assigned to hybrid search. Microsoft documents these as separate capabilities with different roles in the pipeline.
  • B. This option incorrectly maps vector search to hybrid behavior and hybrid search to vector behavior. Microsoft is clear that vector search matches embeddings by similarity, while hybrid search runs text and vector queries together and merges them. Because the first two mappings are reversed, the full choice is incorrect.
  • D. This choice incorrectly assigns semantic configuration to vector search and vector matching to semantic configuration. It also flips semantic ranker and hybrid search. Microsoft’s documentation separates index field selection, retrieval mode, and reranking stage, so these mappings do not align with the actual architecture.

Hybrid search using vectors and full text in Azure AI Search
Configure Semantic Ranker – Azure AI Search

question_html:
A team runs a hybrid grounding query with semantic ranker enabled.
The query uses a restrictive filter and vectorFilterMode set to postFilter. After filtering, the reranker often receives too few candidate chunks and answer quality drops.
What is the best next step?
explanation_html:
vectorFilterMode=preFilter is the best next step because Microsoft explains that post-filtering can reduce the number of documents that reach semantic ranker after vector retrieval, leaving fewer than 50 documents for reranking. Microsoft also notes that semantic ranker works best when it has 50 documents as input, which is why post-filtering can harm grounding quality in filtered hybrid queries.
Pre-filtering changes where the restriction is applied. Microsoft says that with preFilter, the vector query runs only over the filtered subset first, and the resulting candidates then continue through hybrid merging and semantic ranking. In this scenario, that is the most direct fix for preserving reranker input quality under filtering constraints.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. search=*. Microsoft states that search=* bypasses relevance scoring and therefore cannot be semantically ranked. That would undermine the semantic grounding pipeline rather than improve it. It removes meaningful text-query relevance instead of fixing the filtered candidate problem.
  • B. Remove semanticConfiguration. Removing semantic configuration would disable the intended semantic reranking setup instead of solving the low-candidate problem. The issue is not that semantic ranking is configured incorrectly; the issue is that post-filtering is starving the reranker of inputs. Removing semantic configuration would usually reduce grounding quality even further.
  • C. k=5. Microsoft recommends giving semantic ranker up to 50 candidates, and specifically notes that using less than 50 deprives semantic models of necessary inputs in vector-based scenarios. Lowering k would shrink the candidate set even more and make the problem worse.

Create a Vector Query – Azure AI Search

question_html:
A team is building an agent over policy PDFs, screenshots, and Office documents. They need clean markdown for reasoning workflows and grounded structured fields for auditability.
Which service is the best fit?
explanation_html:
Azure Content Understanding is the best fit because Microsoft documents that it turns messy multimodal inputs into predictable, standardized inputs, delivers clean markdown representations for reasoning and knowledge workflows, and provides schema-aligned key-value fields with confidence scores and grounding. Those capabilities align directly with the requirement for agent-ready and RAG-ready outputs rather than raw extraction alone.
This is also the most complete match for mixed document types and downstream agent use. Microsoft states that Content Understanding supports documents, images, video, and audio, and that its output can be consumed by downstream systems for reasoning with LLMs in RAG scenarios. That makes it stronger here than a standalone search index, OCR engine, or document parser by itself.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Azure AI Search. Azure AI Search is an excellent retrieval layer and index store for RAG, but it is not the primary service that transforms messy source files into the clean, grounded representations described in the question. Microsoft’s Content Understanding documentation places the extraction, markdown generation, field extraction, grounding, and confidence logic in Content Understanding, while search comes later as the index and retrieval layer. Search helps retrieve prepared content efficiently, but it does not replace the content preparation step itself.
C. Azure AI Vision OCR. OCR is useful for extracting text from images and documents, but the requirement goes beyond text recognition. The question asks for clean markdown, grounded structured fields, and outputs suitable for agents and RAG. Microsoft describes Content Understanding as combining OCR, layout understanding, grounding, confidence, and structured output, so OCR alone is too narrow.
D. Azure AI Document Intelligence. Document Intelligence is a strong distractor because it also works with documents, but the user’s dot point is specifically about using Content Understanding to produce clean, grounded representations for agents and RAG. Microsoft’s current Content Understanding documentation explicitly calls out clean markdown for reasoning workflows, schema-aligned structured output, and RAG ingestion scenarios, which is the more direct match here.
Build a retrieval-augmented generation solution with Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools
Transparency Note and use cases for Content Understanding

question_html:
A team is building a Foundry agent over internal policy manuals. User questions are conversational, often span multiple concepts, and the business wants grounded answers with citations.
Which retrieval method should the team choose?
explanation_html:
Agentic retrieval is the best fit because Microsoft positions it for agent and chatbot scenarios, especially when queries are conversational, relevance requirements are high, and the response should include grounding data, citations, and query details. It adds query planning, parallel focused subqueries, and structured retrieval output, which is stronger than a single-query pattern for this workload.
Classic RAG is still valid, but Microsoft describes it as the simpler, faster pattern when you want to preserve existing orchestration code or stay with GA-only features. In this case, the requirement is not just retrieval speed, but richer retrieval behavior for an agent, so agentic retrieval is the more appropriate choice.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Classic RAG pipeline. Classic RAG uses the original single-query execution architecture. Microsoft recommends it when simplicity, speed, or preserving existing orchestration is the main priority. It does not provide the same agent-oriented query planning and structured retrieval output that agentic retrieval adds.
  • C. Push API ingestion. The push API is an indexing and ingestion method, not a retrieval strategy. It controls how documents get loaded into an index, but it does not decide how the application retrieves or plans searches at query time. It therefore solves the wrong part of the problem.
  • D. Semantic ranker. Semantic ranker improves relevance by reranking search results, but it is a ranking feature rather than a full retrieval architecture. Microsoft notes that semantic ranker is built into agentic retrieval, which means it complements that pattern rather than replaces it. Choosing semantic ranker alone would not satisfy the broader requirement for agent-style retrieval behavior.

Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and indexes in Microsoft Foundry

question_html:
A team created a custom document analyzer for contract ingestion. They now need each extracted field to include both source grounding and a confidence value so reviewers can verify where values came from before feeding them to an agent.

Snippet

{
  "analyzerId": "contract-rag",
  "baseAnalyzerId": "prebuilt-document",
  "config": {
    "returnDetails": true,
    "enableOcr": true,
    "enableLayout": true,
    "(MISSING CONFIG)": true,
    "omitContent": false
  },
  "fieldSchema": {
    "fields": {
      "effectiveDate": { "type": "date" },
      "terminationClause": { "type": "string" }
    }
  }
}

Which property should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
The correct property is estimateFieldSourceAndConfidence. Microsoft documents that confidence scores and source grounding for structured analyzers are enabled by the estimateFieldSourceAndConfidence setting, and shows it in the document analyzer configuration example. That directly matches the requirement to return both confidence and traceable source regions for extracted fields.
This is especially important for grounded agent and RAG workflows because the extracted output is not just being stored. It is being passed into downstream reasoning systems, where verifiability matters. Microsoft’s Content Understanding documentation ties grounding to tracing field values back to their origin in source content, which is the exact behavior this team wants before handing data to an agent.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. enableLayout. enableLayout is important when you want layout-aware extraction, but it is not the switch that enables source grounding and confidence on extracted fields. Layout improves structural understanding of paragraphs, sections, and tables, while the question specifically asks for field-level provenance and confidence. Microsoft documents that those are enabled through estimateFieldSourceAndConfidence.
B. returnDetails. returnDetails sounds plausible because it suggests richer output, but Microsoft does not describe it as the setting that computes field source grounding and confidence. The explicit property for that behavior is estimateFieldSourceAndConfidence. In exam terms, this is a close-but-wrong configuration choice because it sounds helpful without being the actual feature that satisfies the requirement.
D. omitContent. omitContent controls whether content is omitted from the output, which is a very different concern from grounding and confidence. In fact, using it here would not solve the reviewer’s need to verify field origins. The question is about traceability and reliability scores, not minimizing output payload.

question_html:
A team is building an in-car voice assistant. They want the spoken responses to sound clearer on car speakers without changing the text content.

Snippet

<speak version=”1.0″
xmlns=”http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis”
xml:lang=”en-US”>

Turn left in 200 meters, then take the exit on your right.

Which fragment should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
Correct

Option A. effect="eq_car"

The eq_car audio effect is designed to improve speech clarity when audio is played through car speakers. It adjusts the audio output to suit the car listening environment without changing the spoken text.

This is useful for in-car voice assistants because navigation instructions need to remain clear and understandable despite road noise and speaker characteristics.

Option B. effect="eq_telecomhp8k"

This effect is intended for telephone-style audio playback, particularly narrowband telecommunications audio. It is not specifically optimized for car speakers.

Option C. xml:lang="fr-FR"

This attribute specifies French (France) as the language. It changes the language configuration rather than improving audio clarity for car speakers.

Option D. name="my-custom-voice"

The name attribute identifies a voice to use for speech synthesis. It does not apply an audio equalization effect or optimize sound for car speakers.

question_html:
A team connected a Foundry agent to an Azure AI Search index for RAG. The search resource has public network access disabled and is reachable through a private virtual network. The team configured the connection with an API key, and retrieval now fails.
What is the best next step?

options.text: C. Rotate the API key daily
D. Add a private DNS zone

explanation_html:
The best next step is to use Microsoft Entra project managed identity for the Azure AI Search connection. Microsoft’s Foundry agent documentation explicitly states that when the Azure AI Search tool is used with private virtual network access, key-based authentication is not supported and the connection must use managed identity instead.
This matters directly to a RAG application because the retrieval connection is part of the runtime grounding path. If the authentication method is unsupported for the network design, the application cannot reliably retrieve context from the index, so fixing identity is the correct action before tuning relevance or other behaviors.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Enable semantic ranker. Semantic ranker can improve result ordering, but it does not solve a connection failure caused by unsupported authentication over private networking. The issue is access configuration, not retrieval quality. Tuning ranking before restoring connectivity would leave the RAG app unable to fetch grounding data.
  • C. Rotate the API key daily. Key rotation is a security hygiene step, but Microsoft’s guidance here is not about key freshness. The issue is that key-based authentication is not supported for this private network scenario, so rotating the key does not change the underlying incompatibility. This would preserve the same broken design.
  • D. Add a private DNS zone. DNS configuration can be important in private networking, but the documented blocker in this scenario is the authentication method. Even with correct name resolution, the connection would still be using an unsupported key-based pattern. That makes this a plausible infrastructure distractor, but not the best next step.

question_html:
A team is using gpt-image-1-mini to edit portrait photos from a reference image. They set input_fidelity=high because they want the generated result to preserve facial structure closely. The output still drifts away from the source face.
What is the best next step?
explanation_html:
The best next step is to deploy gpt-image-1, because Microsoft documents input_fidelity as the parameter that increases effort to match the style and features of input images, especially facial features. Microsoft also states that input_fidelity is not supported by gpt-image-1-mini, so the team is currently depending on a setting their selected model cannot use.
Switching to a model that supports the feature is the correct fix because the problem is not prompt wording alone or response formatting. The team chose a mini model for an edit scenario where close preservation of facial structure is a core requirement, and Microsoft’s documentation makes that limitation explicit.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Add semantic ranker. Semantic ranker is an Azure AI Search relevance feature and has no role in how an image generation model preserves facial structure from a reference image. This option belongs to retrieval scenarios, not image-edit fidelity scenarios. It is a classic Microsoft-service confusion distractor.
  • B. Use JSON request body. Microsoft documents the image edit API as taking multipart form data, not JSON data. Moving to JSON would not enable input_fidelity, and it would actually conflict with the documented request pattern for edits. So this would not solve the unsupported-model problem and could introduce a second implementation mistake.
  • C. Increase partial_images. Microsoft documents partial_images as part of streaming behavior that provides faster visual feedback during generation. That affects how intermediate images are returned, not whether facial features are preserved more accurately. It therefore changes latency experience, not edit fidelity capability.

question_html:
A team wants a repeatable promotion path for a Foundry solution across environments.
Steps
Review the cloud evaluation results stored in the Foundry project.
Configure the repository pipeline by running azd pipeline config.
Trigger the pipeline stage that provisions the environment and runs evaluation.
Export or author the Foundry resource and project as parameterized Bicep.
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
The correct order is 4, 2, 3, 1. 4 is first because the team needs a repeatable, version-controlled infrastructure definition before building the release workflow; Microsoft recommends Bicep for deploying Foundry resources and projects and for reusing the same configuration across environments. 2 is second because once the infrastructure definition exists in the repo, azd pipeline config is the step that configures the CI/CD provider, authentication, pipeline files, and required variables.
3 is third because the actual pipeline run is what provisions and deploys the selected environment. 1 is last because cloud evaluation results are reviewed after the stage runs; Microsoft documents cloud evaluation as useful for CI/CD and predeployment testing, and those results are stored in the Foundry project for review.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. 2, 4, 3, 1. This starts by configuring the pipeline before the reusable infrastructure definition is established. That is backwards for an enterprise setup where the pipeline should deploy versioned infrastructure-as-code rather than an undefined or portal-only state. It also weakens repeatability because the deployment model is not fully expressed before pipeline setup.
  • C. 4, 3, 2, 1. This gets the infrastructure step right, but it tries to trigger the deployment stage before the repository pipeline is configured. Microsoft documents azd pipeline config as the mechanism that provisions the pipeline files, authentication, and secrets needed for CI/CD execution. Without that setup, the deployment stage is not correctly established.
  • D. 2, 3, 4, 1. This sequence delays the Bicep definition until after the pipeline is already configured and run. That undermines the purpose of infrastructure as code and makes the CI/CD workflow less reproducible across environments. In Microsoft’s Foundry guidance, the reusable resource and project definition belongs up front, not after deployment execution.

question_html:
A developer is defining a function tool for an agent that checks order status.

The tool must require an order_id argument and should not accept unexpected extra fields.

Snippet

from azure.ai.projects.models import PromptAgentDefinition, Tool, FunctionTool

func_tool = FunctionTool(
name=”lookup_order”,
parameters={

        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "order_id": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "Customer order identifier"
            }
        },
        (MISSING CONFIG)
    },
    description="Get order status for a specific order.",
    strict=True,
)

tools: list[Tool] = [func_tool]

definition = PromptAgentDefinition(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    instructions="You are a support agent that checks order status when needed.",
    tools=tools,
)

Which missing configuration best completes the tool schema?
explanation_html:
This is the best completion because Microsoft’s function-calling documentation shows function tools defined with a name, parameters, and description, and the example schema marks the needed property as required while setting additionalProperties to False. That documented pattern matches a schema where order_id is mandatory and unexpected extra arguments are rejected.
The same Microsoft example also uses strict=True, which reinforces the intent that the tool schema should be explicit and constrained. In Foundry, the agent can request function calls based on the defined schema, and your application then executes the function and returns the output. A precise schema improves reliability because the model sees exactly which fields are expected.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. “required”: [], “additionalProperties”: True. This makes order_id optional even though the scenario says it must be required. It also allows unexpected extra arguments, which conflicts with the stated goal of a tightly defined tool schema. That is the opposite of the pattern shown in Microsoft’s example, where required fields are explicitly listed and extra properties are disallowed.
  • C. “items”: [“order_id”], “type”: “array”, “minItems”: 1. Microsoft’s example defines function parameters as an object with named properties, not as an array of items. This option changes the top-level schema shape away from the documented pattern for a function call that expects a named argument such as order_id. It therefore does not model the intended function input cleanly.
  • D. “required”: [“order_id”], “type”: “string”, “nullable”: False. This conflicts with the documented object-based schema pattern because the parameters container is already defined as an object with properties. Replacing that with a top-level string type would not align with the example Microsoft provides for function definitions. The result would no longer express a structured function schema with named inputs.

question_html:
A team already checked in its Foundry project, azure.yaml, and Bicep files.

The GitHub Actions job signs in to Azure successfully and selects the target environment.

Which command should replace the missing line so the job provisions and deploys the Foundry solution?

Snippet

name: azure-dev
on:
push:
branches: [ main ]

jobs:
deploy:
runs-on: ubuntu-latest
steps:
– uses: actions/checkout@v4

  • name: Install Azure Developer CLI
    uses: Azure/setup-azd@v1
  • name: Azure login
    uses: azure/login@v2
    with:
    client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
    tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
    subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
  • name: Select environment
    run: azd env select prod
  • name: Provision and deploy Foundry app
    run: |
    (MISSING CONFIG)

Select only one answer.
explanation_html:
azd up is the best replacement because Microsoft’s Foundry azd guidance says that azd up orchestrates the deployment workflow end to end: it provisions infrastructure, deploys models, builds and pushes containers when needed, and publishes the agent or application endpoint. In other words, it is the command intended to turn a checked-in azd-based Foundry solution into a deployed environment.
By contrast, azd pipeline config is the setup command that creates the CI/CD pipeline configuration itself. Microsoft documents it as the command that selects the provider, configures authentication, copies pipeline files, sets secrets and variables, and pushes the pipeline definition to the repository. That is a configuration step, not the deployment command executed inside the configured pipeline job.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. azd pipeline config. This is a real azd command, so it is a credible distractor. But Microsoft describes it as the command that creates or configures the pipeline, including provider selection, auth setup, and pipeline file creation. Once the pipeline already exists and is running, this is not the command you use for the actual deployment step.
  • C. az deployment group create. This can deploy a Bicep template at resource-group scope, so it is technically relevant. However, Microsoft’s Foundry azd workflow covers more than raw Bicep deployment by also coordinating azure.yaml, model deployment, environment handling, and application publishing. Using az deployment group create alone would bypass the broader azd orchestration the checked-in solution is built around.
  • D. azd auth login. This is used to authenticate azd, primarily in development or setup flows. In the snippet, Azure authentication has already been handled earlier in the job, and the missing line is specifically inside the deploy step. So this command would not provision or deploy the Foundry solution.

question_html:
A manufacturer wants to analyze live assembly-line video feeds and recorded clips at the factory. The design must meet these requirements:
process video close to the data source
support real-time analysis of live streams
satisfy strict data residency requirements
minimize latency for operational decisions
Which service should the team choose?

options.text: A. Azure Content Understanding with segment extraction
B. Cloud-based Azure AI Video Indexer
C. Azure AI Vision with custom detection
D. Video Indexer via Azure Arc

explanation_html:
Video Indexer via Azure Arc is the best answer because Microsoft says Azure AI Video Indexer enabled by Arc runs video and audio analysis on edge devices through Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes and supports both uploaded and live video streams. Microsoft also says this model is particularly suited for strict data residency requirements and low-latency operational needs, which matches this scenario directly.
This is stronger than the cloud-based alternative because the requirement is not just video analysis in general, but analysis directly at or near the source with operational latency constraints. Microsoft specifically describes real-time live-stream analysis and edge deployment as core Arc-enabled Video Indexer strengths, which is why it is the best-fit implementation choice here.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure Content Understanding with segment extraction. Content Understanding is excellent for uploaded multimodal content when you need structured extraction, segment-level summaries, and RAG-ready output. However, Microsoft positions it around extraction and schema-based understanding rather than live stream analysis at the edge. This answer misses the real-time and on-premises operational requirements that point to Arc-enabled Video Indexer.
  • B. Cloud-based Azure AI Video Indexer. Cloud-based Video Indexer can extract deep insights from uploaded and live content, so it is a plausible distractor. But Microsoft distinguishes the Arc-enabled option as the one suited for edge deployment, strict data residency, and low-latency operational use. Because those are central requirements here, the cloud-based deployment is not the best answer.
  • C. Azure AI Vision with custom detection. Azure AI Vision can be useful for targeted image or video analysis tasks, and Microsoft even notes it can be more cost-effective for some basic scenarios. But this question asks for a complete workflow across live streams and recorded clips with edge deployment, operational latency, and residency constraints. Vision does not match the documented end-to-end live and uploaded video analysis positioning that Arc-enabled Video Indexer provides.

question_html:
A release pipeline can deploy code to an existing Foundry project, but it fails whenever the workflow tries to create a new Foundry project for a fresh environment.
The pipeline identity currently has Azure AI User on an existing project. A separate platform team already handles subscription setup and broad resource governance.
What is the best next step?

options.text: D. Subscription Owner with shared credentials

explanation_html:
The best next step is to grant the pipeline identity the Azure AI Project Manager role. Microsoft’s Foundry prerequisites say that to create and manage Foundry resources, you need a role such as Azure AI Project Manager or Owner, whereas Azure AI User is the least-privilege role for using projects rather than creating new resources. Since the scenario says the platform team already handles wider governance, Azure AI Project Manager is the least-privilege role that matches the pipeline’s missing capability.
The RBAC model also reinforces that Foundry separates permissions by scope and role. Project-scope access for using an existing project is not the same as the permissions needed to create or manage projects during deployment automation. That is why the current Azure AI User assignment is insufficient for this CI/CD task.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Foundry resource API key. This might look like a quick workaround because it avoids a role assignment change. But Microsoft recommends Entra ID-based RBAC over key-based access, and key-based authentication grants full access without role restrictions. More importantly, swapping to an API key does not address the root issue that the pipeline lacks the correct management permissions for the deployment operation.
  • B. Project-scope Azure AI User. This is already close to the current state, which is why it is plausible. However, Microsoft explicitly describes Azure AI User as the least-privilege role for using projects, not for creating and managing Foundry resources or new projects. Reapplying the same level of access at project scope would not solve the project-creation failure.
  • D. Subscription Owner with shared credentials. Owner can be necessary in some scenarios, especially when additional role assignments are required, so this option is not nonsense. But the scenario says broad platform governance is already handled elsewhere, and shared credentials are a poor CI/CD pattern. Azure AI Project Manager is the better least-privilege fit for a pipeline that needs project-management capability without overbroad standing access.

Role-based access control for Microsoft Foundry
Authentication and authorization in Microsoft Foundry

question_html:
A customer support chatbot accepts free-form prompts from the public. The team wants to detect and block adversarial prompt attacks before the model generates a response.
Which control should you configure?
explanation_html:
Prompt Shields is the documented control for detecting and blocking adversarial user input attacks on large language models before content is generated. That makes it the best fit when the requirement is specifically to stop jailbreak-style or policy-bypassing prompt attacks at input time, rather than to do general monitoring or unrelated AI processing.
Azure AI Content Safety provides broader harmful-content moderation capabilities, but Prompt Shields is the feature called out for adversarial prompt attack detection. In practice, this question is asking for the most specific responsible AI control for malicious prompt input, not a retrieval component, observability signal, or document-processing service.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. Azure AI Search. Azure AI Search is useful when you need indexing, retrieval, and grounding support, but the requirement here is to inspect incoming prompts for adversarial attacks before generation occurs. Nothing in the requirement asks for search or retrieval behavior. Prompt Shields is the control specifically documented for adversarial prompt detection and blocking.
C. Azure Monitor alerts. Alerts help operators observe issues after telemetry is produced, and Foundry observability integrates with Azure Monitor for dashboards, metrics, and alerts. That is valuable for production monitoring, but it is not the primary safety filter that analyzes and blocks malicious prompts before the model responds. This question asks for a prevention control, not an observability layer.
D. Document Intelligence. The scenario is not about extracting text, layout, or fields from files. It is about preventing adversarial prompt attacks against an LLM. Prompt Shields directly matches that responsible AI requirement, while document-processing capability does not.
What is Azure AI Content Safety?
Guardrails and controls overview in Microsoft Foundry

question_html:
A team wants to build a workflow that turns uploaded videos into a retrieval-ready knowledge asset by using Azure Content Understanding.
Steps
Configure default model deployments for the Content Understanding resource.
Send an analyze request to prebuilt-videoSearch with the video URL.
Poll the analysis operation until the result succeeds.
Ingest the returned Markdown or JSON segments into the search or chat layer.
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
1 is first because Microsoft’s quickstart says you must set up default model deployments for the Content Understanding resource, including the required Foundry model deployments, before running analysis requests. 2 is second because the actual video workflow begins by sending the file to prebuilt-videoSearch for analysis.
3 is third because Microsoft says the analyze call is asynchronous and returns an Operation-Location header that you use to retrieve the results. 4 is last because Microsoft describes prebuilt-videoSearch output as an immediately usable knowledge asset packaged as Markdown and JSON for ingestion into a search index or chat agent, which naturally happens after the operation completes successfully.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. 2, 1, 3, 4. This sequence starts analysis before the resource is prepared with the required default model deployments. Microsoft’s quickstart puts model deployment setup before running the analysis workflow, so this order skips an important prerequisite. It might look close because the later steps are reasonable, but the opening sequence is backwards.
  • C. 1, 3, 2, 4. Polling for an analysis result before the analyze request is sent is not logically valid. Microsoft’s workflow clearly shows that the asynchronous analyze call happens first, and only then do you use the returned operation reference to retrieve results. This sequence reverses the core request-and-poll pattern.
  • D. 2, 3, 1, 4. This option delays prerequisite model configuration until after the analyze request and polling steps, which conflicts with Microsoft’s setup guidance. It also assumes you can complete the full analysis loop before the resource has been properly prepared. That makes it the weakest operational sequence of the four.

Azure Content Understanding video overview
Azure Content Understanding prebuilt analyzers

question_html:
A team is building a chat workflow over uploaded training videos. They need segment-based multi-frame analysis, a custom schema for extracted fields, and RAG-ready Markdown and JSON for downstream retrieval.
Which service should they implement?
explanation_html:
Azure Content Understanding is the best fit because Microsoft says to use it when you need schema-defined extraction, scene segmentation, or RAG-ready video output. Microsoft also describes it as generating structured JSON or RAG-ready Markdown from video, with confidence scores and grounding that support downstream automation.
This question is specifically about processing and interpreting video segments, not just analyzing whole videos at a high level. Microsoft’s video overview for Content Understanding highlights segment-based multi-frame analysis and shows that prebuilt-videoSearch can produce an immediately usable knowledge asset for a search index or chat agent without custom glue code.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Vision. Azure AI Vision is appropriate for image analysis, OCR, and related visual tasks, but Microsoft’s video-processing guidance does not position it as the tool for schema-defined video segmentation and RAG-ready output. It is a weaker fit when the requirement is to interpret uploaded video in segments and return structured, retrieval-ready results. This option confuses general visual analysis with multimodal video-segmentation workflows.
  • C. Azure OpenAI. Azure OpenAI can handle broad multimodal reasoning, and Microsoft notes that GPT models have image, video, and audio capabilities. However, the guidance does not position Azure OpenAI as the dedicated service for schema-defined extraction, segment-based video interpretation, or RAG-ready video output. This scenario needs a purpose-built video understanding workflow, which is why Content Understanding is the stronger Microsoft-aligned choice.
  • D. Azure AI Video Indexer. Video Indexer is strong for deep video insights across live and uploaded content, including transcription, translation, object detection, and summarization. But Microsoft explicitly says to use Content Understanding when you need schema-defined extraction, scene segmentation, or RAG-ready video output. That makes Video Indexer plausible, but not the best fit for this exact requirement set.

Azure Content Understanding video overview

question_html:
Match each requirement to the best responsible AI control or service. The items below reflect different parts of Microsoft’s responsible AI stack for generative AI and agents.
Match the following:
Moderate harmful text and images from user or model content
Detect adversarial prompt attacks in prompts or documents
Check whether an answer is based on provided source material
Run automated predeployment adversarial scans and review a scorecard
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Groundedness detection
Azure AI Content Safety
Prompt Shields
AI Red Teaming Agent

B.
Azure AI Content Safety
Groundedness detection
Prompt Shields
Azure Monitor

C.
Prompt Shields
Azure AI Content Safety
Groundedness detection
AI Red Teaming Agent

D.
Azure AI Content Safety
Prompt Shields
Groundedness detection
AI Red Teaming Agent

explanation_html:
This mapping is correct because Azure AI Content Safety is the service for detecting harmful user-generated and AI-generated content across text and images. Prompt Shields is the control for adversarial prompt attacks, groundedness detection checks whether model responses stay based on provided source material, and the AI Red Teaming Agent performs automated adversarial scans and produces reporting such as attack success metrics and scorecards.
The value of this question is that it separates runtime moderation, prompt-attack defense, hallucination-style grounding checks, and predeployment adversarial testing. AI-103 candidates need to recognize that these are related responsible AI capabilities, but they are not interchangeable. Each one addresses a different risk surface in the lifecycle of a generative AI or agentic system.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Item 1 is wrong because groundedness detection is not the primary service for moderating harmful text and images. Item 2 is also wrong because Azure AI Content Safety is broader than the specific prompt-attack control the requirement asks for. This option confuses general moderation with prompt-injection defense and swaps two distinct responsibilities.
B. Item 2 is wrong because groundedness detection is about whether responses are based on provided source material, not about blocking adversarial prompt attacks. Item 3 is wrong because Prompt Shields is not the tool for checking whether a response stays grounded in source documents. Item 4 is also wrong because Azure Monitor is observability infrastructure, not the automated adversarial scanning tool described in the requirement.
C. Item 1 is wrong because Prompt Shields does not replace content moderation for harmful text and images. Item 2 is wrong because Azure AI Content Safety is broader than the specific prompt-attack feature needed there. This option partly recognizes groundedness and red teaming correctly, but it still misassigns the first two capabilities.

question_html:
A team is building a new Foundry application for legal research over internal contracts and policy documents. The application will be chat-based, queries are often multi-part, and users want answers grounded with citations.
The solution must:
handle conversational questions
improve coverage for complex queries
return structured retrieval details with citations
favor the highest relevance over the simplest pipeline
Which retrieval pattern should the team implement?
explanation_html:
Agentic retrieval is the best choice because Microsoft describes it as a multi-query retrieval pipeline designed for complex questions from users or agents in chat and copilot applications. It uses an LLM to break down a complex query into focused subqueries, which improves coverage over indexed content and makes it a strong fit for a new RAG application with conversational input.
Microsoft’s RAG guidance also says to prefer agentic retrieval when you are building a new RAG implementation, need the highest relevance and accuracy, and want structured responses with citations and query details. Those requirements match this scenario more closely than classic RAG, which Microsoft frames as the simpler and faster option when advanced relevance is less important.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Classic RAG pipeline. Classic RAG is still a valid Microsoft pattern, but the guidance says it is better when simplicity, speed, GA-only features, or preserving existing orchestration code are the main priorities. In this scenario, the application is new and explicitly prioritizes higher relevance for conversational, multi-part questions. That makes classic RAG reasonable but not the best-fit answer.
  • C. Semantic ranking alone. Semantic ranker reranks results and can improve relevance, but it is not a full retrieval architecture. Microsoft notes that semantic ranker is built into agentic retrieval, which shows it is a supporting capability rather than a replacement for the retrieval pattern itself. Using semantic ranking alone would not satisfy the requirement for multi-query planning and structured retrieval output.
  • D. Push API ingestion. Push API ingestion is about how documents are loaded into an index, not how the application retrieves grounding information at runtime. It helps with indexing workflows, but it does not address conversational query planning, citations, or high-relevance retrieval behavior. This option solves a different stage of the RAG pipeline.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) in Azure AI Search
Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and indexes

question_html:
A team is building a RAG application that accepts plain-text questions and searches an index that already stores chunk embeddings. They want Azure AI Search to convert the user’s text query into a vector at query time by using the same embedding model family used during indexing.

Snippet

{
  "name": "kb-index",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "chunk",
      "type": "Edm.String",
      "searchable": true
    },
    {
      "name": "chunkVector",
      "type": "Collection(Edm.Single)",
      "searchable": true,
      "dimensions": 3072,
      "vectorSearchProfile": "rag-profile"
    }
  ],
  "vectorSearch": {
    "algorithms": [
      {
        "name": "hnsw-config",
        "kind": "hnsw"
      }
    ],
    "profiles": [
      {
        "name": "rag-profile",
        "algorithm": "hnsw-config",
        "vectorizer": "aoai-vectorizer"
      }
    ],
    (MISSING CONFIG)
  }
}

Which section should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
The missing section is vectorizers because Microsoft states that a vectorizer handles query-time vectorization. When an index contains vector fields and a configured vectorizer, text input can be converted into vectors during query execution, which is exactly what this RAG application needs.
Microsoft’s integrated vectorization guidance also explains that the index schema must include the vectorizer definition and that the vectorizer should correspond to the embedding model used for the indexed data. Without that section, the profile refers to a vectorizer name that has not actually been defined.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. semantic configuration block. Semantic configuration is used for semantic ranking behavior, captions, and related query features. It does not define the model-backed component that converts incoming text into an embedding vector at query time. In other words, it may improve ranking, but it does not complete the vectorization path required here.
  • B. custom analyzers block. Analyzers are part of text processing for searchable string fields, such as tokenization and linguistic analysis. They are useful for full-text search behavior, but they do not generate embeddings for vector search. This answer mixes lexical text processing with vector query encoding.
  • C. scoring profiles block. Scoring profiles adjust ranking behavior using weights and scoring logic. They can influence ordering in text-oriented retrieval, but they do not define a query-time vectorizer. The missing requirement is query encoding, not ranking customization.

Integrated vector embedding in Azure AI Search

question_html:
A team wants to build a RAG application over PDF files in Azure Blob Storage by using integrated vectorization and minimal custom code.
Steps
Create a data source connection for the blob content.
Create a skillset that chunks text and generates embeddings.
Create an index with vector fields and a vectorizer.
Run ingestion, then query the index to ground model responses.
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
1 is first because the indexing pipeline needs a source connection before content can be pulled into the enrichment flow. Microsoft’s integrated vectorization guidance starts with creating a data source connection to a supported source for indexer-based indexing.
2 is second because chunking and embedding are part of the enrichment pipeline, so the skillset must be defined before ingestion can process content correctly. 3 is third because the index must then provide the vector fields and vectorizer used for storage and query-time vectorization. 4 is last because the application can only retrieve grounding content after the source, enrichment, and index definitions are in place and ingestion has populated the index.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. 3, 1, 2, 4. Creating the index before the data source is possible in some workflows, but this sequence does not reflect the documented integrated vectorization setup flow Microsoft gives for indexer-based ingestion. More importantly, it places the source connection after the target index without establishing the content pipeline first. For an exam-style implementation question, that makes it the weaker sequencing choice.
  • C. 2, 1, 3, 4. A skillset is meant to operate on ingested content and is tied to the indexing workflow. Defining enrichment before the source connection reverses the normal setup logic and makes the pipeline harder to reason about. Microsoft’s documented order begins with the data source, not with the chunking skillset.
  • D. 1, 3, 2, 4. This sequence gets the source connection first, which is reasonable, but it places the index definition before the skillset that performs chunking and vector creation. Microsoft’s integrated vectorization guidance explicitly places the skillset step before the index step in the standard flow it documents. That is why this sequence is close, but still not the best answer.

question_html:
A company is building a support agent for a live billing chat.
During one active chat session, the agent must automatically remember earlier user turns and use them in follow-up answers. The design does not require remembering the user after the session ends.
Which conversation-tracking approach is the best fit?
explanation_html:
A conversation is the best fit because Microsoft’s runtime model says a conversation persists history across turns for stateful, multi-turn interactions. The same guidance says that an agent defines model, instructions, and tools, while the conversation is the component that keeps prior messages available so the agent can continue the exchange in context.
This requirement is different from long-term personalization. Microsoft’s memory documentation says memory is intended for long-term knowledge across sessions, while the runtime guidance says that if you do not use a conversation, you would need to carry context forward manually from a previous response. For a single live support session, a conversation is the cleanest built-in approach.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Managed memory store. Memory is for persistent, cross-session knowledge rather than the immediate turn-by-turn context of one active chat. Microsoft describes memory as long-term continuity that can retain user preferences and facts across sessions, devices, and workflows. That makes it useful for personalization, but broader than the session-scoped requirement in this question.
  • B. Response output reuse. Microsoft does say that if you do not use a conversation, you can carry forward context by using the output from a previous response. However, that is the fallback pattern when a conversation is not being used, not the best built-in way to track a normal multi-turn chat session. It is less direct than simply creating a conversation that persists history across turns.
  • D. Agent tracing. Tracing is for observability and debugging, not conversation state. Microsoft’s Foundry documentation describes tracing as a way to inspect model calls, tool invocations, and decisions. That helps diagnose behavior, but it does not serve as the conversation-tracking mechanism for end-user chat continuity.

What is Memory?
Microsoft Foundry Agent Service overview

question_html:
A platform team wants one repository to promote the same Foundry setup through dev, test, and prod.
They must version-control the Foundry resource, project creation, network settings, identity settings, and project associations.
Which component should be added to the CI/CD solution?
explanation_html:
A Bicep template is the right component because Microsoft documents Bicep as a way to deploy a Foundry resource and project together in one coordinated deployment and to reuse the same configuration across environments. Microsoft also states that exporting an existing Foundry resource to Bicep captures settings such as network rules, identity configuration, and project associations, which is exactly what a repeatable CI/CD pipeline needs.
This also matches the Foundry architecture model. The Foundry resource is the top-level governance boundary for security, networking, and model deployments, while the project is the development boundary where teams build and evaluate. Infrastructure as code is therefore the cleanest way to reproduce both layers consistently across environments.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure Monitor workbook. A workbook is useful for visualization and monitoring after deployment. It does not define or recreate Foundry resources, projects, network rules, or identity configuration. That makes it operationally useful, but not the core CI/CD component the scenario asks for.
  • B. Prompt flow tracing. Tracing helps with runtime diagnostics and flow behavior analysis. It is not an infrastructure definition mechanism and does not version-control project associations, resource topology, or security settings. So it supports observability, not environment reproduction.
  • C. Static .env file. Environment variable files are helpful for per-environment values, and azd stores environment-specific variables in .azure//.env. However, those files do not replace infrastructure as code, and they do not model the Foundry resource, project objects, or security configuration themselves. They complement Bicep; they do not substitute for it.

Microsoft Foundry architecture
Use the Microsoft Foundry azd agent extension

question_html:
Match each Foundry agent design element to its primary responsibility.
Match the following:
Instructions
Conversation
Memory
Function tool schema
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Retains user preferences across sessions
Persists multi-turn chat history
Defines function parameters and description
Sets goals and behavioral constraints

B.
Persists multi-turn chat history
Sets goals and behavioral constraints
Defines function parameters and description
Retains user preferences across sessions

C.
Defines function parameters and description
Retains user preferences across sessions
Persists multi-turn chat history
Sets goals and behavioral constraints

D.
Sets goals and behavioral constraints
Persists multi-turn chat history
Retains user preferences across sessions
Defines function parameters and description

explanation_html:
Choice D is correct because Microsoft’s Foundry documentation assigns these responsibilities clearly. Instructions define goals, constraints, and behavior; conversations persist history across turns; memory retains durable knowledge across sessions; and function tools are defined through a schema that includes the function name, parameters, and description.
This mapping is useful because these pieces often seem similar during design, but they solve different problems. Instructions shape agent behavior, conversations handle short-term interaction state, memory handles long-term continuity, and tool schemas describe callable capabilities. Mixing them up leads to poorly controlled agents or the wrong persistence design.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This choice swaps several responsibilities. Memory, not instructions, retains user preferences across sessions, and instructions, not the function schema, set goals and behavioral constraints. Microsoft documents instructions, conversations, memory, and function-tool definitions as distinct concepts, so this mapping blends them incorrectly.
  • B. This option incorrectly assigns conversation behavior to instructions and long-term memory behavior to the function tool schema. A conversation persists history across turns, while a function schema describes callable inputs and descriptions for a tool. Those responsibilities are documented separately in Microsoft Foundry and are not interchangeable.
  • C. This mapping places function-schema responsibility onto instructions and moves conversation state into memory. Microsoft distinguishes short-term conversation state from long-term memory, and it separately shows function tools as having explicit parameters and descriptions. Because of those documented separations, this choice misaligns all four concepts.

Build with agents, conversations, and responses

question_html:
A team created an agent in the Foundry portal and can chat with it successfully.
They now need to add a new function definition and update an existing function schema, but they cannot find a portal option that supports those edits.
What is the best next step?

options.text: A. Edit the portal tool definition
D. Enable a managed memory store

explanation_html:
The best next step is to use the SDK or REST API. Microsoft’s function-calling guidance states that while you can run agents with function tools in the Foundry portal, the portal does not support adding, removing, or updating function definitions on an agent. The same guidance explicitly says to use the SDK or REST API to configure function tools.
This is a configuration problem, not a state-management problem. Conversations are for maintaining history across turns, and memory is for long-term continuity across sessions. Neither of those changes the documented limitation that function definitions themselves must be configured through code or REST rather than through the current portal editing experience.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Edit the portal tool definition. This is the tempting answer because the team is already using the portal successfully for chat. However, Microsoft explicitly says the portal does not support adding, removing, or updating function definitions on an agent. So this path does not address the actual limitation described in the question.
  • C. Create another conversation thread. A new conversation thread would affect session history, not the agent’s function schema. Microsoft documents conversations as the mechanism for maintaining turn history, which is unrelated to authoring or editing function definitions. It would therefore change the chat state without solving the configuration issue.
  • D. Enable a managed memory store. Memory provides long-term knowledge retention across sessions and devices. Microsoft describes it as a persistence feature for continuity and personalization, not as a way to define or revise function-tool schemas. It is useful for agent memory, but irrelevant to the missing function-definition editing capability.

Tool best practices for Microsoft Foundry Agent Service
Build with agents, conversations, and responses

question_html:
A media workflow must process documents, images, audio, and video.
The solution must extract structured JSON that matches a defined schema and should support complex field generation for downstream automation.
Which component should be included?

options.text: A. Azure AI Search multimodal index

explanation_html:
Azure Content Understanding is the best fit because Microsoft describes it as a Foundry tool that uses generative AI to process documents, images, video, and audio into a user-defined output format. Microsoft also says the final result can be returned as structured JSON matching your defined schema for automation and analytics workflows. That matches this requirement almost exactly.
Microsoft also says analyzers are the core building blocks of Content Understanding and combine content extraction, AI-powered analysis, and structured data output in a reusable configuration. That makes an analyzer the right component when the workflow needs schema-driven extraction rather than just a one-off multimodal answer.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Search multimodal index. Azure AI Search is excellent for multimodal ingestion and retrieval, especially in RAG scenarios. But this question is about producing schema-defined structured JSON for downstream automation, which Microsoft assigns to Content Understanding and its analyzers rather than to the search index itself. Search is retrieval-centric, not the primary extraction component here.
  • B. GPT-4o deployment. A multimodal chat model can analyze images and answer questions, so this option sounds reasonable. However, Microsoft’s Content Understanding documentation specifically covers user-defined output formats, structured JSON, and analyzer-based extraction. A plain model deployment does not provide that full schema-governed extraction framework by itself.
  • D. OCR endpoint. OCR is useful for reading text from visual content. But the requirement spans documents, images, audio, and video and calls for structured JSON aligned to a defined schema. Microsoft’s Content Understanding documentation clearly goes beyond OCR and supports multimodal processing with structured outputs for automation workflows.

What is a Content Understanding analyzer?
Multimodal Search Concepts and Guidance

question_html:
A manufacturing company is building a grounded chat application in Foundry over repair manuals, parts catalogs, and service bulletins. The index already contains both text fields and vector fields.
The retrieval layer must satisfy these requirements:
match exact part numbers and maintenance codes
handle natural-language questions from technicians
return conceptually similar passages even when wording differs
maximize grounding quality for generated answers
Which retrieval method should the team use?

options.text: B. Pure vector search with embeddings
C. Keyword search with scoring profiles

explanation_html:
Hybrid search is the strongest choice because Azure AI Search runs full-text and vector queries in parallel in a single request, then merges the results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. That design is ideal when the workload needs both exact matching for identifiers like part numbers and conceptual matching for natural-language questions.
Microsoft also recommends hybrid queries for maximum recall in RAG-style implementations, and notes that semantic ranker can further improve relevance on top of that. In this scenario, pure keyword search is too narrow for concept matching, while pure vector search can miss exact text-heavy cases such as codes, dates, or specialized jargon.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Pure vector search with embeddings. Vector search is excellent for conceptual similarity, multilingual matching, and semantic closeness. However, Microsoft specifically notes that some scenarios such as product codes, dates, names, and specialized jargon perform better with keyword search. Using vector search alone would weaken exact-match behavior that this scenario clearly requires.
  • C. Keyword search with scoring profiles. Keyword search handles exact matching well and scoring profiles can boost fields or business criteria. But it does not provide the semantic similarity behavior needed when technicians ask questions in language that differs from the source documents. That makes it incomplete for a modern grounded chat experience.
  • D. Semantic ranker without vectors. Semantic ranker is a reranking layer, not a substitute for vector retrieval. It can improve the ordering of text results, but without vector search the system still lacks a core mechanism for embedding-based similarity matching. This answer again confuses relevance enhancement with the primary retrieval method.

Semantic Ranking Overview

RAG and Generative AI

question_html:
A retail app must generate a new hero image from a text prompt plus nine reference product shots. The team wants one deployed model to handle this through an API-driven workflow.
Which model is the best fit?
explanation_html:
FLUX.2-flex is the best fit because Microsoft documents it as supporting text-to-image generation and multi-reference image editing with up to 10 reference images. That directly matches a workload that needs a text prompt plus nine reference images in a single implementation.
It is a better fit than the other choices because this question is specifically about combining text prompts with a large set of reference media. Microsoft’s FLUX guidance also notes that multi-reference support for FLUX.2-flex is available through the API, which aligns with the app-driven implementation requirement in the scenario.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. FLUX.1-Kontext-pro. This model is documented for in-context generation and editing with character consistency, which makes it useful for reference-aware editing scenarios. However, Microsoft’s FLUX capability table does not position it as the model for up to 10 reference images. That specific multi-reference scale is called out for FLUX.2-flex instead.
  • C. MAI-Image-2 model. MAI-Image-2 is documented as a text-to-image generation model that accepts text input and returns one PNG image. Microsoft does not describe it here as a multi-reference image editing model, so it does not meet the reference-media requirement in this question. It is a strong text-to-image option, but not the best fit for this particular implementation.
  • D. gpt-image-1-mini deployment. Microsoft documents GPT-image models as accepting text plus image inputs, so this option can participate in image generation and editing workflows. But the Microsoft FLUX documentation specifically calls out FLUX.2-flex for multi-reference editing up to 10 images, which is the key requirement here. The question asks for the best fit, and the FLUX model is the more directly aligned choice.

question_html:
A team wants to edit only the background of an existing product photo while leaving the subject unchanged.

Snippet

curl -X POST “[https://$RESOURCE.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT/images/edits?api-version=2025-04-01-preview](https://$RESOURCE.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT/images/edits?api-version=2025-04-01-preview)” \

  • H “api-key: $API_KEY” \
  • H “Content-Type: multipart/form-data” \
  • F “image[]=@shoe.png” \

(MISSING CONFIG) \

  • F “prompt=Replace the background with a white studio backdrop” \
  • F “model=gpt-image-1” \
  • F “size=1024×1024” \
  • F “n=1”

Which line should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
The missing line is the mask parameter because Microsoft documents the mask as the way to define the specific area that should be edited. The mask uses fully transparent pixels to indicate editable regions, so it is the correct mechanism when the team wants to change only the background and preserve the rest of the image.
Microsoft also states that the image edit API is separate from the generation API, uses the images/edits endpoint, and requires multipart form data with an input image. The mask must be a PNG file and must have the same dimensions as the input image, which makes it the exact configuration element needed for this targeted edit workflow.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. -F “background=transparent”. Microsoft documents transparent background generation as a GPT-image-1 image generation option that requires background=transparent and output_format=PNG. That is useful when the goal is generating an image with transparency, but it does not define the edit region inside an existing image. This question is about selective editing, so the mask is still required.
  • C. -F “response_format=url”. Microsoft states that GPT-image-1 series models always return base64-encoded image data and do not support the response_format parameter. Even if it were supported, response format would affect output handling rather than which part of the image gets edited. It therefore fails both technically and conceptually for this scenario.
  • D. -F “guidance=7”. Microsoft documents guidance as part of the BFL provider-specific API for FLUX workflows, where it controls prompt adherence. It is not the mechanism that marks editable regions in the Azure OpenAI image edit flow shown in this snippet. This distractor mixes a FLUX-specific generation control with a GPT-image edit scenario.

question_html:
You already created a guardrail named prod-rai. You now want a Foundry model deployment to enforce that guardrail at runtime. Microsoft documents that a guardrail is represented as a RAI policy and is assigned to a deployment through a specific deployment property.

Snippet

{
  "name": "gpt4o-prod",
  "sku": {
    "name": "Standard",
    "capacity": 10
  },
  "properties": {
    "model": {
      "format": "OpenAI",
      "name": "gpt-4o",
      "version": "2024-11-20"
    },
    "versionUpgradeOption": "OnceCurrentVersionExpired",
    "dynamicThrottlingEnabled": true,
    "(MISSING CONFIG)": "prod-rai"
  }
}

Which property should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
In the Foundry guardrails model, the guardrail is a RAI policy resource, and Microsoft’s guidance says you assign it to a deployment by setting the raiPolicyName property on that deployment. That is why raiPolicyName is the correct missing configuration in this deployment body.
This is a good AI-103 style distinction because it separates creating a guardrail from actually binding it to a runtime deployment. The platform can return annotations for guardrail results, but the deployment must first reference the named RAI policy for those controls to apply in the first place.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. contentFilterRef. This name sounds plausible because the scenario is about safety filtering, but it is not the property Microsoft documents for assigning a guardrail to a deployment. The documented property is raiPolicyName. In certification terms, this is a classic near-correct label that does not match the actual deployment contract.
B. moderationName. This option sounds like it might point to a moderation policy, but Microsoft’s guardrail assignment guidance does not use that property name. The question is about Foundry guardrails as RAI policies, not an arbitrary moderation label. The deployment property documented for this purpose is raiPolicyName.
D. guardrailProfile. This is another believable invented property, which is why it works as a distractor. However, the platform guidance specifically says to include the guardrail name in deployment properties by using raiPolicyName. A candidate who remembers the exact binding property will avoid this trap.

question_html:
Match each requirement to the most appropriate model or capability.
Match the following:
Support up to 10 reference images in one API workflow
In-context generation and editing with character consistency
High-volume text-to-image generation with greater efficiency
Transparent background generation on an image generate request
Choices:
explanation_html:
Choice B is the strongest mapping. Microsoft documents FLUX.2-flex as supporting multi-reference image editing with up to 10 reference images, FLUX.1-Kontext-pro as supporting in-context generation and editing with character consistency, and MAI-Image-2e as the faster and more efficient MAI text-to-image option for scale-oriented workloads.
For item 4, Microsoft documents transparent background generation as a GPT-image-1 capability when background is set to transparent and output_format is PNG on an image generation request. That makes gpt-image-1 the correct match for the final requirement in the list.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Choice A. Item 1 is wrong because FLUX.2-pro supports up to eight reference images, not 10. Item 2 is wrong because FLUX-1.1-pro is documented for fast text-to-image generation rather than in-context generation and character consistency. Item 4 is also wrong because Microsoft documents the transparent background generation setting specifically for GPT-image-1, not gpt-image-1-mini.
  • C. Choice C. MAI-Image-2 is documented as a text-to-image model, so mapping it to multi-reference editing is incorrect. FLUX.2-flex is not the model Microsoft documents for character consistency; that capability is called out for FLUX.1-Kontext-pro. The last two mappings are also reversed relative to the documented capabilities.
  • D. Choice D. gpt-image-1 is not the documented answer for up to 10 reference images; FLUX.2-flex is. MAI-Image-2e is also not the in-context editing model with character consistency, and FLUX.2-pro is not the high-efficiency MAI text-to-image model. This option scrambles four different capability families and is therefore fully inconsistent with Microsoft’s model guidance.

question_html:
A moderation workflow must review both the poster artwork and any printed slogan embedded in the poster image. The team is calling the Content Safety multimodal endpoint.

Snippet

{
  "image": {
    "content": ""
  },
  "categories": ["Hate", "Sexual", "Violence", "SelfHarm"],
  "(MISSING CONFIG)": true,
  "text": "Launch this campaign worldwide"
}

Which property should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
The correct property is enableOcr. Microsoft’s multimodal quickstart shows the imageWithText:analyze request using “enableOcr”: true when you want the service to analyze image content together with text extracted from the image and any provided text. That is the exact configuration needed when moderation depends on visible printed text inside the poster.
This is an important implementation detail because without OCR enabled, the moderation workflow would not directly include text embedded in the image as part of the multimodal evaluation path. In a visual-policy scenario, that could let harmful slogans or prohibited textual symbols inside posters slip through even if the surrounding image is analyzed.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. includeText. This looks plausible because the request also has a text field, but Microsoft’s documented multimodal request uses enableOcr for extracting text from the image itself. The question is about reading printed text inside the poster, not merely passing an already separate text field. includeText is not the documented property for this API.
  • B. readText. This name sounds close to OCR terminology, especially because Microsoft uses “Read” for OCR capabilities in Vision and Document Intelligence. However, the multimodal Content Safety API does not use readText as the request property. The documented flag for OCR within the multimodal moderation request is enableOcr.
  • C. ocrMode. This is another believable invented property, but Microsoft’s example request does not use it. The actual documented property is enableOcr, which turns OCR extraction on for multimodal analysis. In AI-103 style, this is the kind of near-correct configuration label that you have to reject in favor of the real API contract.

OCR – Optical Character Recognition
