question_html:
A production model deployment is accessed through a Foundry AI Gateway.
During short traffic bursts, clients receive:
429 Too Many Requests
Later in the same day, after sustained usage, every request begins returning:
403 Forbidden
The application already implements exponential backoff for transient throttling.
The operations team confirms that both a tokens-per-minute limit and a daily total-token quota are configured for the deployment.
What should the team do?

options.text: A. Raise TPM and total-token quota independently
B. Increase model max completion tokens
D. Convert the deployment to Global Batch

explanation_html:
Foundry AI Gateway treats the two limits separately. Exceeding the configured TPM rate limit returns 429 Too Many Requests, while exhausting the total-token quota for the configured period returns 403 Forbidden. If both are constraining the workload, each control must be reviewed and adjusted independently.
Why the other options are incorrect
B. Increasing maximum completion length can increase token consumption and therefore worsen the problem.
C. More application replicas do not increase the gateway’s token limits and can increase pressure against the constrained deployment.
D. Global Batch is intended for asynchronous workloads rather than correcting real-time gateway quota policy.
Microsoft Foundry Models quotas and limits
AI-103 Study Guide

question_html:
A company has approved use of the currently documented Azure OpenAI custom blocklist preview.

An internal project codename must be blocked whenever a user submits it in a prompt, but the model must still be able to include that codename in an approved compliance warning generated as output.

The current policy contains:

{
  "properties": {
    "basePolicyName": "Microsoft.Default",
    "completionBlocklists": [
      {
        "blocklistName": "internal-project-names",
        "blocking": true
      }
    ]
  }
}

What should you change?

options.text: A. Add another entry to completionBlocklists
B. Raise the prompt harm-category threshold
C. Disable the default content filter
D. Move the blocklist to promptBlocklists

explanation_html:
Microsoft distinguishes blocklists applied to user prompts from blocklists applied to model completions. completionBlocklists applies the list to generated content, whereas promptBlocklists applies the list to incoming prompts. Because the codename must remain permitted in approved output, the blocklist belongs on the prompt side only. Custom blocklists are currently documented as preview functionality for Azure OpenAI models.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. This would continue blocking model-generated completions, which conflicts with the requirement.
B. Harm-category severity filtering and organization-specific blocked terms are separate controls.
C. Disabling the default filter weakens the broader safety configuration and does not correctly scope the custom term.
Content filtering in Azure OpenAI

question_html:
A subscription contains two Global Standard deployments of the same model and model version:
Deployment1 in East US
Deployment2 in West Europe
In the Foundry Quota page, the model’s Scope value is Global.
Deployment1 has consumed the remaining available quota. An engineer proposes creating Deployment3 in Australia East to obtain a separate quota allocation.
What should you recommend instead?

options.text: A. Create another Global Standard deployment
B. Increase or reallocate the shared subscription quota
C. Move Deployment2 to East US
D. Create the deployment in another Foundry resource

explanation_html:
For models onboarded to Foundry’s subscription-level quota system, a Global scope means Global Standard deployments of the same model and version share a quota pool across regions within the subscription. Moving the deployment to another region or resource does not create a fresh independent Global quota pool.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. The additional deployment would consume the same applicable subscription-level Global quota.
C. Changing regions does not change the quota scope when the model’s scope is explicitly Global.
D. Subscription-level quota is broader than the individual Foundry resource, so creating another resource does not bypass it.

question_html:
A team is packaging custom agent code as a Foundry Hosted agent.
The agent must receive GitHub webhook payloads directly.
Requirements:
GitHub controls the incoming JSON structure
the payload cannot be reformatted as a chat message
the handler must return a custom JSON response
application code owns any conversational state
OpenAI-compatible conversation threading is unnecessary
Which protocol should the Hosted agent expose?
explanation_html:
The Hosted agent Invocations protocol is designed for arbitrary JSON payloads, webhook-style endpoints, and non-conversational processing. The platform passes the payload to the container without interpreting it as an OpenAI Responses request. Conversation history is also not automatically managed by the protocol.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Responses is the preferred protocol for OpenAI-compatible conversational agents where platform-managed conversation behavior is useful.
B. Activity relates to channel integrations rather than an arbitrary webhook payload contract.
D. A2A supports agent-to-agent interoperability and delegation rather than general incoming webhook processing.

question_html:
A Hosted agent successfully starts and can call its Foundry model.

At runtime, its code attempts to write a generated report to an Azure Blob container and receives:

403 AuthorizationPermissionMismatch

The environment has these properties:

Storage networking permits the runtime path
the Foundry project’s managed identity has Storage Blob Data Contributor
the deployed Hosted agent has its own dedicated agent identity
the application must use Microsoft Entra authentication
Storage shared keys are prohibited

What should you do next?

B. Grant the calling user Foundry Project Manager
C. Increase the project identity's Storage role

explanation_html:
A deployed Hosted agent receives its own dedicated Microsoft Entra agent identity for runtime calls to downstream Azure services. The project managed identity is used for different project/platform purposes and does not automatically authorize the Hosted agent’s runtime principal to access external Storage. The Storage data-plane RBAC role must be assigned to the agent identity.
Why the other options are incorrect
B. Changing the human caller’s Foundry role does not authorize the agent’s runtime identity against Blob Storage.
C. Making the project identity more privileged does not grant permission to a different Entra principal.
D. Shared-key authentication contradicts the explicit keyless requirement and fails to correct the RBAC root cause.
