question_html:
An engineer uses az rest to list Hosted agents.

The Foundry account, project name, API version, user authentication, and feature header are correct.

ACCOUNT_NAME=”contoso-foundry”
PROJECT_NAME=”production-ai”

BASE_URL=”https://${ACCOUNT_NAME}.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/${PROJECT_NAME}”

az rest \
  --method GET \
  --url "${BASE_URL}/agents?api-version=v1" \
  --headers "Foundry-Features=HostedAgents=V1Preview"

The request fails during Microsoft Entra authentication because Azure CLI cannot derive the correct token audience from the data-plane URL.

Which configuration should be added?
explanation_html:
Microsoft’s Hosted-agent REST guidance explicitly requires the –resource argument for az rest calls against Agent Service data-plane endpoints and defines the resource as https://ai.azure.com. Without it, az rest cannot derive the required Entra audience from the URL.
The corrected command is:
ACCOUNT_NAME=”contoso-foundry”
PROJECT_NAME=”production-ai”
BASE_URL=”https://${ACCOUNT_NAME}.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/${PROJECT_NAME}”
az rest \
–method GET \
–url “${BASE_URL}/agents?api-version=v1” \
–resource “https://ai.azure.com” \
–headers “Foundry-Features=HostedAgents=V1Preview”
Why the other options are incorrect
A. az rest uses the –resource parameter for this documented pattern rather than the –scope syntax shown.
B. https://management.azure.com is the Azure Resource Manager audience, not the Foundry data-plane audience.
C. https://search.azure.com is the Azure AI Search audience and would produce a token for the wrong target service.
Manage Hosted agent sessions
Hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service

question_html:
A Foundry agent calls Azure AI Search through an OpenAPI tool using managed identity authentication.
The following have been verified:
the OpenAPI operation contains a valid operationId
network connectivity succeeds
the managed identity has the required Search data-plane role
the Search endpoint is correct
the target service returns 401 Unauthorized
decoding the token shows that its audience is the Foundry project instead of Azure AI Search
Which audience should be configured for the OpenAPI tool?

options.text: D. The individual Search service hostname

explanation_html:
For managed-identity OpenAPI authentication, the audience must identify the downstream API that receives the token. Microsoft explicitly lists the Azure AI Search audience as https://search.azure.com and identifies an audience mismatch as a cause of 401 Unauthorized even when RBAC is otherwise configured correctly.
Example configuration:
{
“auth”: {
“type”: “managed_identity”,
“security_scheme”: {
“audience”: “https://search.azure.com”
}
}
}
Why the other options are incorrect
A. https://ai.azure.com is the Foundry data-plane audience, not the Azure AI Search audience.
C. https://management.azure.com is used for Azure Resource Manager operations.
D. The Search service hostname identifies the network endpoint but is not the documented Entra resource identifier for Azure AI Search.
Azure AI Search role-based access
Agent identity concepts

question_html:
A support workflow contains:
a triage agent
an identity specialist
a billing specialist
Requirements:
triage chooses the specialist from conversation context
responsibility transfers to the selected specialist
agents should not collaboratively debate every answer
the billing specialist can call issue_refund
every issue_refund invocation must pause before execution until a human approves it
Which design best satisfies the requirements?

options.text: A. Concurrent orchestration with unrestricted tools
B. Sequential orchestration with final manual review
C. Handoff orchestration with an approval-required function
D. Group Chat orchestration with retry middleware

explanation_html:
Handoff orchestration is designed for scenarios where agents transfer control based on context. Microsoft Agent Framework also supports approval-required tools inside handoff workflows: when the specialist requests the sensitive tool, execution pauses and a human approval request is surfaced before the function runs.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Concurrent orchestration runs agents in parallel and does not model contextual transfer of responsibility.
B. Sequential orchestration follows a predefined order rather than dynamically choosing a specialist, and a final review occurs too late to protect the refund execution.
D. Group Chat is intended for agents collaborating in a shared conversation. This workflow instead needs triage followed by responsibility transfer to one specialist.
Handoff orchestration
Tool approval

question_html:
Match each requirement to the best capability or component.
Match the following:
Reusable definition that controls extraction behavior and schema
Output style best suited to reasoning and knowledge workflows
Ability to trace a generated field back to source content
Retrieval store used after extraction for fast grounded lookup
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Analyzer
Markdown
Grounding
Azure AI Search index

B.
Azure AI Search index
JSON Web Token
Grounding
Analyzer

C.
Markdown
Analyzer
OCR
Azure AI Search index

D.
Analyzer
Grounding
Markdown
Azure AI Search index

explanation_html:
A is the correct mapping. Microsoft defines an analyzer as the reusable processing unit that determines how content is analyzed and what gets extracted. It also states that Content Understanding delivers clean markdown representations for reasoning and knowledge workflows, uses grounding to identify the specific regions where values came from, and works with Azure AI Search as the indexing and retrieval layer in RAG solutions.
This question reflects the real workflow split in AI-103: Content Understanding prepares the content, grounding makes it auditable, and Azure AI Search supports retrieval after preparation. Mixing those roles up leads to weak designs where retrieval is expected to do extraction work, or extraction output is not prepared in a way that helps downstream agents reason over it.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. This option incorrectly uses Azure AI Search index as the reusable definition for extraction behavior, even though Microsoft defines that role as the analyzer. It also inserts JSON Web Token, which is unrelated to the output style used for reasoning workflows in this Content Understanding scenario. The fourth mapping is also wrong because an analyzer is not the retrieval store used after extraction.
C. This option swaps analyzer and markdown, which breaks the first two mappings. Markdown is an output representation, not the reusable processing definition. It also uses OCR for tracing a generated field back to its source, but Microsoft documents that source verification comes from grounding, not from OCR alone.
D. The first and fourth mappings are correct here, but the middle two are reversed. Grounding is not the output style for reasoning workflows, and markdown is not the mechanism for tracing a field back to its origin. Microsoft clearly separates markdown output formatting from grounding and confidence calculations.
Build a retrieval-augmented generation solution with Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools
Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) and indexes in Microsoft Foundry

question_html:
A manufacturing application receives 14 inspection photographs for one asset.
The application currently sends all 14 photographs in a single vision-enabled chat request.
Requirements:
every photograph must be analyzed
each intermediate finding must retain its photograph identifier
the application must produce one final asset-level conclusion
no photographs may be discarded
The request fails before inference.
What is the best design change?

options.text: B. Set every image to detail: low
C. Store the photos in one Azure AI Search document
D. Process compliant image batches and then synthesize the findings

explanation_html:
Microsoft currently documents a limit of 10 images per vision-enabled chat request. The application must therefore divide the 14 images across multiple requests, retain structured results associated with each photo, and then perform a final synthesis over those intermediate findings.
For example, an intermediate structure could be:
[
{
“imageId”: “asset-42-photo-01”,
“finding”: “Corrosion visible around the lower mounting bracket.”
},
{
“imageId”: “asset-42-photo-02”,
“finding”: “No visible damage to the cable termination.”
}
]
The final model call can then reason over the accumulated text findings rather than attempting to resend all 14 images simultaneously.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Output-token limits do not increase the allowed number of image inputs.
B. Low-detail processing can reduce image-token consumption but does not increase the image-count limit.
C. Azure AI Search can support image-related retrieval architectures, but storing the photos in Search does not change the native per-request image-input limit.
Azure OpenAI chat model
AI-103 Study Guide

question_html:
A Python service must translate speech from an English WAV file into German, Italian, and French in one recognition workflow.

The developer has created the translation configuration:

import os
import azure.cognitiveservices.speech as speechsdk

translation_config = speechsdk.translation.SpeechTranslationConfig(
subscription=os.environ[“SPEECH_KEY”],
region=os.environ[“SPEECH_REGION”]
)

translation_config.speech_recognition_language = “en-US”

targets = [“de”, “it”, “fr”]

# (MISSING CONFIG)

result = recognizer.recognize_once()

Which implementation should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?

options.text: A. Create one SpeechConfig and three separate SpeechRecognizer objects
B. Add each target language, create file AudioConfig, then create TranslationRecognizer
C. Create AutoDetectSourceLanguageConfig and use a standard SpeechRecognizer
D. Create TranslationRecognizer using the default microphone

explanation_html:
The Speech SDK supports multiple translation targets by calling add_target_language() for each language. File-based input should be supplied through AudioConfig(filename=…), and that audio configuration is then passed to TranslationRecognizer.
The missing code is:
for lang in targets:
translation_config.add_target_language(lang)
audio_config = speechsdk.audio.AudioConfig(
filename=”support-call.wav”
)
recognizer = speechsdk.translation.TranslationRecognizer(
translation_config=translation_config,
audio_config=audio_config
)
Why the other options are incorrect
A. One translation recognizer can return multiple target translations, so separate speech recognizers are unnecessary.
C. The source language is already known, and SpeechRecognizer is not the required translation workflow.
D. The requirement specifies an existing WAV file, not live microphone input.
Speech translation quickstart
SpeechTranslationConfig Python API

question_html:
A service is migrating from Translator Text API v3.0 to the current GA 2026-06-06 API.

The existing implementation sends:

POST /translate?api-version=3.0&to=de&to=fr

with:

[
  {
    "Text": "The maintenance window starts at 22:00."
  }
]

The application also assumes that the response root itself is an array.

The developer changes only the API version:

api-version=2026-06-06

Requests now fail schema validation.

What should the developer change?

options.text: A. Keep the to parameters and continue parsing the root array
B. Move the target languages into HTTP headers
C. Use the new inputs/targets request structure and parse value
D. Call BreakSentence before every translation request

explanation_html:
Translator 2026-06-06 is a breaking API revision rather than a drop-in version change. Microsoft documents that to is replaced by a targets array and that the newer JSON contract uses top-level inputs in the request and value in the response. BreakSentence is also no longer supported in the new version.
A revised request follows this shape:
{
“inputs”: [
{
“text”: “The maintenance window starts at 22:00.”,
“language”: “en”,
“targets”: [
{
“language”: “de”
},
{
“language”: “fr”
}
]
}
]
}
The application must also update its response parsing to read the new top-level response structure rather than assuming the v3.0 response shape.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Both assumptions belong to the older API contract and are part of what must change.
B. Target languages are represented in the request JSON schema, not moved into arbitrary HTTP headers.
D. BreakSentence is not required for migration and is specifically listed as unavailable in 2026-06-06
Azure text translation overview
Languages API 2026-06-06

question_html:
A RAG pipeline uses Azure AI Search index projections to create one searchable document for every chunk.

The target index contains:

chunk_id as the document key
parent_id as a filterable string
chunk
chunk_vector
title

The skillset currently contains:

{
  "indexProjections": {
    "selectors": [
      {
        "targetIndexName": "rag-chunks",
        "parentKeyFieldName": "parent_id",
        "sourceContext": "/document/pages/*",
        "mappings": [
          {
            "name": "parent_id",
            "source": "/document/metadata_storage_path"
          },
          {
            "name": "chunk",
            "source": "/document/pages/*"
          },
          {
            "name": "chunk_vector",
            "source": "/document/pages/*/chunk_vector"
          },
          {
            "name": "title",
            "source": "/document/title"
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "parameters": {}
  }
}

Search results contain additional parent-shaped documents whose chunk fields are null.

The team also requires synchronized refresh behavior when source documents change.

What should you change?

options.text: A. Remove the explicit parent-key mapping and use skipIndexingParentDocuments
B. Keep the mapping and add semantic ranking
C. Make parent_id the document key
D. Add an indexer outputFieldMapping for every chunk

explanation_html:
For the recommended single-index RAG pattern, Microsoft recommends projectionMode: “skipIndexingParentDocuments” so only the uniform chunk-shaped search documents are indexed. Without it, the default includes extra parent documents whose child fields can be null. Microsoft also explicitly warns not to create a field mapping for the parent key because the projected key is managed by the indexer for change tracking and synchronized refresh.
The corrected projection resembles:
{
“indexProjections”: {
“selectors”: [
{
“targetIndexName”: “rag-chunks”,
“parentKeyFieldName”: “parent_id”,
“sourceContext”: “/document/pages/*”,
“mappings”: [
{
“name”: “chunk”,
“source”: “/document/pages/*”
},
{
“name”: “chunk_vector”,
“source”: “/document/pages/*/chunk_vector”
},
{
“name”: “title”,
“source”: “/document/title”
}
]
}
],
“parameters”: {
“projectionMode”: “skipIndexingParentDocuments”
}
}
}
Why the other options are incorrect
B. Semantic ranking affects query-time relevance and does not correct projection shape or projected-key lifecycle behavior.
C. parent_id repeats across chunks and therefore must not be the unique document key.
D. Selector mappings already define the projected child fields. Output field mappings do not solve the unwanted parent documents.
Map fields in Azure AI Search indexers

question_html:
A Content Understanding custom document analyzer must produce three fields from insurance policies.

Requirements:

policyNumber must reproduce the literal identifier appearing in the source document
riskClass must be selected from low, medium, or high
rationale must be newly written from the evidence in the document rather than copied verbatim

The field schema contains:

{
  "fieldSchema": {
    "fields": {
      "policyNumber": {
        "type": "string",
        "method": "(METHOD 1)"
      },
      "riskClass": {
        "type": "string",
        "enum": [
          "low",
          "medium",
          "high"
        ],
        "method": "(METHOD 2)"
      },
      "rationale": {
        "type": "string",
        "method": "(METHOD 3)"
      }
    }
  }
}

Which mapping should you use?
explanation_html:
Content Understanding supports three field-generation methods. Extract is for values that appear directly in the source, classify is for selecting from predefined categories, and generate is for newly inferred or summarized values. The three requirements therefore map directly to extract, classify, and generate.
The completed schema is:
{
“fieldSchema”: {
“fields”: {
“policyNumber”: {
“type”: “string”,
“method”: “extract”
},
“riskClass”: {
“type”: “string”,
“enum”: [
“low”,
“medium”,
“high”
],
“method”: “classify”
},
“rationale”: {
“type”: “string”,
“method”: “generate”
}
}
}
}
Why the other options are incorrect
A. It would generate the literal identifier, attempt extraction for an enum classification, and classify the free-form rationale.
B. The identifier is not a category, the enum should not be freely generated, and the rationale does not need to appear verbatim.
C. The identifier is correct, but riskClass and rationale have their methods reversed.

question_html:
You are selecting Foundry agent capabilities for a customer-service assistant.
Match each requirement to the most appropriate capability.
Match the following:
Answer from uploaded troubleshooting guides
Create a CRM case through an API
Preserve context during follow-up turns
Remember user preference across sessions
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Function calling
File Search
Code Interpreter
Web Search

B.
Web Search
Code Interpreter
File Search
Function calling

C.
Code Interpreter
Memory store
Function calling
File Search

D.
File Search
Function calling
Conversation
Memory store

explanation_html:
Choice D is correct because it maps each requirement to the Foundry capability designed for that job. File Search supports retrieval over uploaded documents, function calling supports external API actions, conversations preserve context across turns, and memory stores support longer-term retained information such as user preferences.
This distinction is important because “memory” is not the same as “retrieval.” Retrieval brings in external knowledge at response time, while conversation context and memory deal with user/session state. A strong agent design combines these capabilities without using one as a substitute for all the others.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This choice reverses retrieval and action capabilities. Function calling is not intended to search uploaded troubleshooting guides. File Search is not the mechanism for creating a CRM case through an API. Code Interpreter and Web Search also do not directly satisfy the conversation and long-term preference requirements.
  • B. This choice uses Web Search where the requirement is uploaded internal content. Web Search can ground answers in public web information, but that is not the same as searching internal troubleshooting guides. Code Interpreter is also not the correct tool for creating a CRM case. The mapping fails because it confuses external public grounding, code execution, and business API actions.
  • C. This choice incorrectly maps Code Interpreter to uploaded troubleshooting-guide retrieval. Code Interpreter is useful for analysis tasks, not primary document grounding. It also maps Memory store to API case creation, which is not the function of memory. Function calling belongs with the CRM API action, not preserving follow-up context.

Use function calling with Microsoft Foundry agents
Create and use memory in Foundry Agent Service

question_html:
A warranty agent must remember customer preferences across separate sessions, search uploaded warranty PDFs, and start an RMA request in a claims system. The solution must avoid storing long-term preferences inside document chunks.
Problem:
You need to choose the appropriate memory, knowledge, and tool integrations.
Proposed solution:
Configure file search with the warranty PDFs, and store all customer preferences and RMA request details as vector store metadata.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
The proposed solution does not meet the goal because file search addresses only the knowledge-retrieval part of the design. It can help the agent retrieve relevant warranty PDF content, but it is not the right service for durable user preferences or workflow execution.
The design needs separate capabilities: agent memory for long-term preference continuity, file search or another knowledge integration for warranty PDFs, and a callable tool such as function calling or Azure Functions for the RMA workflow. Storing preferences and workflow state in vector metadata would blur responsibilities and create governance, retrieval, and lifecycle problems.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• A. Yes is incorrect because the proposal satisfies only one major requirement. File search can support document grounding, but it does not provide managed long-term memory. It also does not execute the RMA request in the claims system. Treating vector store metadata as the main place for preferences and workflow details is the wrong integration pattern.
Memory in Microsoft Foundry Agent Service
Integrate Azure Functions with Foundry Agents

question_html:
You are choosing integration services for a customer service agent.
Match each requirement to the most appropriate capability.
Match the following:
Retain user preferences across sessions
Retrieve private manuals from uploaded files
Answer using current public web content
Execute custom order-cancellation workflow
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Thread messages
Agent memory
File search
Code Interpreter

B.
File search
Web search tool
Agent memory
Azure AI Search

C.
Code Interpreter
File search
Azure Functions tool
Web search tool

D.
Agent memory
File search
Web search tool
Azure Functions tool

explanation_html:
The correct mapping separates memory, knowledge, web grounding, and action execution. Agent memory handles long-term preferences, file search handles uploaded private documents, web search handles current public web grounding, and an Azure Functions tool can execute custom business workflows.
This distinction is important for AI-103 because agent design is not just about picking a model. You must choose the right supporting capability for each part of the agent: memory for continuity, knowledge tools for grounding, and action tools for business operations.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This choice confuses thread history with managed memory. Thread messages can preserve conversation context, but they are not the best capability for long-term preferences across sessions. It also maps private manuals to agent memory, which is the wrong purpose. Code Interpreter is not the right integration for a governed order-cancellation workflow.
  • B. This choice maps user preferences to file search, which is a knowledge-retrieval feature. It also maps uploaded private manuals to web search, which would be inappropriate for private documents. Agent memory is incorrectly used for current public web content. Azure AI Search can support knowledge grounding, but it is not the best direct match for executing a workflow.
  • C. This choice incorrectly uses Code Interpreter for user preference retention. Code Interpreter is for sandboxed computation, not durable personalization. It also maps current public web content to an Azure Functions tool, which would require custom implementation instead of using the built-in web grounding capability. The workflow action is then incorrectly mapped to web search.

File search tool for agents
Agent tools overview for Foundry Agent Service

question_html:
A support agent uses an Azure OpenAI model deployment in Microsoft Foundry.
The app containers scale correctly, but users still receive 429 responses during peak token usage.
Which setting should you manage first?
explanation_html:
Deployment TPM allocation is the best answer because model throughput is constrained by Azure OpenAI quota and rate limits, not by the number of application containers. Azure OpenAI quota is assigned around model, region, subscription, and deployment characteristics, and rate limits are enforced through token and request limits.
Scaling the hosting layer can increase the number of callers, but it does not increase the backend model deployment’s allowed throughput. For AI-103, this is a key distinction: application scale and model quota are separate controls, especially for model and agent workloads that call deployed models.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. App Service autoscale rules increase or decrease app instances, but they do not raise model TPM. This option is plausible because the symptom appears during peak load. However, adding more app instances can make throttling worse if more callers hit the same model deployment quota. The limiting factor in this scenario is the model deployment’s rate limit.
  • C. Azure AI Search replicas can help query throughput for search indexes. This is useful when retrieval latency or search capacity is the bottleneck. It does not increase Azure OpenAI model TPM or RPM. The 429 responses are coming from model rate limits, not search query capacity.
  • D. Blob Storage lifecycle policy manages storage retention and cost over time. It can reduce storage costs for old files or logs. It does not affect model inference throughput, token limits, or request throttling. It is unrelated to this peak model usage issue.

Manage and increase quotas for Foundry resources
Foundry Agent Service limits, quotas, and regional support

question_html:
A claims-processing agent runs at high volume every business day.
Usage is predictable, latency must remain stable, and the finance team wants clearer capacity planning than variable pay-per-token spikes.
Which deployment approach best supports reserved model capacity?
explanation_html:
Provisioned throughput is the best fit because it is designed for workloads that need reserved capacity and more predictable throughput planning. Microsoft describes standard deployments as pay-per-token and provisioned deployments as reserved capacity, with provisioned throughput billed based on deployed PTUs.
This does not automatically mean provisioned throughput is always cheaper. It is strongest when demand is sustained and predictable enough to justify reserved capacity. For a workload with steady business-day usage and latency expectations, it is a better capacity-management choice than relying entirely on variable standard deployment behavior.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Standard deployment is suitable for many variable or lower-volume workloads. It uses consumption-style billing and can be cost-effective when usage is inconsistent. However, it does not provide the same reserved capacity planning model as provisioned throughput. In this scenario, the requirement is predictable high-volume capacity.
  • B. Serverless model endpoint can reduce operational overhead for some model access patterns. It is not the best answer for reserved Azure OpenAI capacity planning in this scenario. The question is asking for a model deployment approach that supports predictable throughput. Serverless access does not directly satisfy that reserved-capacity requirement.
  • C. Azure Functions autoscale can scale application orchestration code. It does not reserve model inference capacity. This is a common confusion because the app layer and model layer both affect performance. Here, the constraint is model workload capacity and cost planning, not function execution scale.

Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models
Plan and manage costs in Microsoft Foundry

question_html:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1.
Sub1 contains a Microsoft Foundry project named Project1.
Project1 contains an agent named Agent1.
Agent1 must support tool use, runtime troubleshooting, evaluation, and controlled approval for high-impact actions.
You need to recommend the correct Microsoft Foundry capability or configuration for each requirement.
Requirements
1. Allow Agent1 to request a custom operation that is executed by the application and returned to the agent.
2. Review agent execution details, including inputs, outputs, tool usage, retries, latency, and cost.
3. Run a test dataset against Agent1 to measure quality, safety, task completion, and tool-call behavior.
4. Pause a high-impact agent workflow until a user or reviewer approves the action.
Answer bank
A. Agent tracing
B. Azure AI Search index
C. Function calling tool
D. Human approval workflow
E. Model catalog benchmark
F. Agent evaluation
G. Code Interpreter tool
H. Content Understanding analyzer
Which mapping should you use?

options.text:
A.
C = Requirement 1
F = Requirement 2
A = Requirement 3
D = Requirement 4

B.
C = Requirement 1
A = Requirement 2
F = Requirement 3
D = Requirement 4

C.
G = Requirement 1
A = Requirement 2
F = Requirement 3
D = Requirement 4

D.
C = Requirement 1
A = Requirement 2
E = Requirement 3
F = Requirement 4

explanation_html:
A function calling tool satisfies Requirement 1 because Microsoft Foundry agents can request custom functions that are executed by the application and returned to the agent. This allows the agent to perform custom operations, call business logic, or retrieve real-time data from external systems instead of relying only on generated text.
Agent tracing satisfies Requirement 2 because Microsoft Foundry tracing captures execution details such as inputs, outputs, tool usage, retries, latency, and costs. Agent evaluation satisfies Requirement 3 because evaluations can run test datasets against agents and measure quality, safety, task completion, and tool behavior. A human approval workflow satisfies Requirement 4 because high-impact semiautonomous actions should pause for review before execution.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping correctly uses function calling for Requirement 1 and human approval workflow for Requirement 4, but it reverses tracing and evaluation. Agent evaluation is used to run test datasets and measure agent behavior. Agent tracing is used to inspect what happened during execution, including tool calls, retries, latency, and costs.
  • C. This mapping incorrectly uses Code Interpreter for Requirement 1. Code Interpreter allows an agent to run Python code in a sandboxed environment, which is useful for data analysis and file-based computation. The requirement asks for a custom operation executed by the application and returned to the agent, which aligns better with function calling.
  • D. This mapping correctly uses function calling and tracing for the first two requirements, but it incorrectly uses a model catalog benchmark for Requirement 3. Benchmarks help compare models, but the requirement is to evaluate a specific agent against a test dataset. It also incorrectly maps agent evaluation to Requirement 4; evaluation measures quality and behavior, while approval workflow controls execution of high-impact actions.

What is Microsoft Foundry Agent Service?
Use function calling with Microsoft Foundry agents

question_html:
An engineer is updating an agent gateway call to reduce unnecessary completion tokens.

The app already retries 429 responses with exponential backoff.

Snippet

import os
import time
from openai import AzureOpenAI, RateLimitError

client = AzureOpenAI(
azure_endpoint=os.environ[“AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT”],
api_key=os.environ[“AZURE_OPENAI_KEY”],
api_version=”2024-10-21″
)

def call_model(messages):
for attempt in range(5):
try:
return client.chat.completions.create(
model=os.environ[“AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT”],
messages=messages,
temperature=0.2,
(MISSING CONFIG)
)
except RateLimitError:
wait_seconds = min(2 ** attempt, 16)
time.sleep(wait_seconds)

raise RuntimeError(“Model request failed after retries”)

Which configuration should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
“max_tokens”: 300 is the best completion because it directly limits the maximum output size for the model response. Since token-based metering and token-based rate limits are central to Azure OpenAI and Foundry model workloads, controlling output length helps reduce both cost footprint and pressure on token-per-minute limits.
The existing retry loop helps handle transient rate-limit responses, but retries alone do not reduce token demand. A well-managed production workload usually combines retry behavior with request shaping, output limits, quota planning, and monitoring. That is the AI-103 distinction being tested: handling 429s is useful, but controlling token consumption is also part of managing scale and cost.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. “stream”: true changes how tokens are delivered to the client. It can improve perceived responsiveness because output can begin before the full response is complete. However, it does not cap the number of generated tokens. It therefore does not directly reduce the completion token footprint.
  • B. “temperature”: 0.1 changes randomness and response variability. It can make responses more deterministic, which is useful for some enterprise workflows. It does not set a maximum completion size. A deterministic response can still be long and consume unnecessary tokens.
  • D. “n”: 3 requests multiple completions for a single prompt. That can increase token usage rather than reduce it. It is especially risky in cost-controlled workloads because each generated candidate can add completion tokens. It works against the requirement to reduce unnecessary token consumption.

Plan and manage costs in Microsoft Foundry
Access Azure OpenAI through a gateway

question_html:
You are designing controls for several production AI workloads.
Match each requirement to the most appropriate control.
Match the following:
Increase allowed model tokens per minute
Reserve predictable model inference capacity
Investigate agent tool latency and cost
Prevent one tenant exhausting shared usage
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Deployment TPM allocation
Provisioned throughput
Agent tracing
Gateway rate limiting

B.
Agent tracing
Standard deployment
Deployment TPM allocation
Blob lifecycle policy

C.
Azure AI Search replicas
Key Vault secret rotation
Provisioned throughput
Agent tracing

D.
Gateway rate limiting
Blob Storage lifecycle policy
Azure Functions autoscale
Deployment TPM allocation

explanation_html:
Choice A is correct because each mapping targets the actual operational control. TPM allocation is used for model quota management, provisioned throughput is used for reserved capacity, tracing helps investigate agent execution behavior, and gateway rate limiting helps protect shared backends from tenant-level spikes.
This item tests the difference between model capacity, application scale, observability, and consumer throttling. These controls often work together, but they are not interchangeable. AI-103 questions commonly reward choosing the control that matches the precise bottleneck or operational goal.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. This choice incorrectly maps agent tracing to token capacity. Tracing helps with observability, debugging, latency analysis, and execution visibility, not raising TPM. Standard deployment also does not reserve capacity in the same way as provisioned throughput. Blob lifecycle policy is unrelated to tenant-level model usage throttling.
  • C. This choice confuses search scaling and secret governance with model quota and throughput controls. Azure AI Search replicas can improve search query capacity, but they do not increase model TPM. Key Vault secret rotation is important for security hygiene, not reserved inference capacity. Agent tracing belongs with investigation and observability, not shared tenant throttling.
  • D. This choice incorrectly uses gateway rate limiting as the way to increase backend token capacity. Rate limiting protects the service from excessive usage; it does not raise quota. Blob lifecycle policy affects storage retention and cost, not inference capacity. Azure Functions autoscale can scale orchestration code but not agent tool tracing or model telemetry.

Set up tracing in Microsoft Foundry
Azure API Management rate-limit-by-key policy

question_html:
You need to choose the correct Content Understanding task configuration for each workflow.
Match the following:
Extract fields from one receipt image
Analyze one call recording for summary fields
Validate invoice details against a contract
Compare mortgage documents for consistency
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Pro mode
Pro mode
Single-file Standard task
Azure AI Search

B.
Single-file Standard task
Single-file Standard task
Pro mode
Pro mode

C.
Azure AI Search
Document Intelligence model
Single-file Standard task
Pro mode

D.
Document Intelligence model
Pro mode
Azure AI Search
Single-file Standard task

explanation_html:
Choice B is correct because single-file Standard tasks are appropriate for straightforward extraction from individual files, including receipt images and call recordings. Pro mode is appropriate when the workflow must reason across documents, validate consistency, or use related documents to make a decision.
The important distinction is not whether the input is “AI content,” but whether the pipeline needs cross-file reasoning. Single-file Standard tasks handle independent content analysis across supported content types. Pro mode is reserved for advanced document workflows that need multi-step reasoning, multiple inputs, or reference data.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping incorrectly uses pro mode for simple single-file extraction tasks. Pro mode adds complexity for scenarios that do not need cross-document reasoning. It also assigns single-file Standard processing to invoice-versus-contract validation, which is exactly where pro mode is more appropriate. Azure AI Search is not the Content Understanding task mode for comparing mortgage documents.
  • C. This mapping confuses downstream indexing and separate document services with Content Understanding task configuration. Azure AI Search can support retrieval after content is extracted or indexed, but it is not the correct task mode for a receipt image. Document Intelligence can process documents, but the question asks for Content Understanding pipeline configuration. The mapping partially identifies pro mode for mortgage comparison, but the other assignments are misaligned.
  • D. This mapping overuses unrelated or misplaced services. Document Intelligence may extract fields from documents, but it is not the Content Understanding single-file task configuration requested here. Pro mode is not the right choice for one call recording because pro mode is focused on advanced document reasoning. Assigning a single-file Standard task to mortgage document comparison misses the need for cross-document consistency reasoning.

What is Azure Content Understanding?
Create Content Understanding Standard and Pro tasks

question_html:
A support application translates short English messages into German by using the Translator API.
The organization maintains approximately 30 approved product terms whose translations change frequently.
Requirements:
provide the approved term translation dynamically
affect specified words or phrases inside otherwise variable sentences
keep using the ordinary Translator API
do not train or publish a Custom Translator model
do not require the entire source sentence to exactly match a dictionary entry
Which capability should you implement?

options.text: A. Neural phrase dictionary through a trained Custom Translator model
B. Dynamic dictionary with the Translator API
C. Phrase dictionary incorporated into Custom Translator training
D. Sentence dictionary containing complete source and target sentence pairs

explanation_html:
Microsoft distinguishes dynamic dictionaries from dictionaries used to train Custom Translator systems. Dynamic dictionary functionality is used with the Translator API and lets applications provide specific terminology translations dynamically, which directly matches the requirement to change approved product terminology without model training.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Neural phrase dictionaries are a strong option when the organization is already creating a customized Translator model and wants better contextual fluency around defined terminology. Microsoft describes the neural phrase dictionary as part of the Custom Translator path rather than an ad-hoc per-request substitute for model customization. The scenario explicitly prohibits training and publishing a Custom Translator model. This option therefore provides sophisticated terminology handling but through the wrong lifecycle and deployment model.
C. Phrase dictionaries let a Custom Translator project supply preferred translations for particular expressions and are therefore relevant to terminology control. However, they belong to a customized translation model and aren’t the request-time Translator API mechanism requested here. Maintaining a trained Custom Translator system would also add the publication lifecycle that the scenario explicitly seeks to avoid. This option solves the terminology problem with a heavier customization architecture than required.
D. Sentence dictionaries can enforce translation pairs when the complete input sentence matches a supplied entry. The support messages in this scenario vary while containing only a relatively small number of controlled product terms. Requiring entire-sentence matches would therefore provide poor coverage for normal conversational variation. This option is useful for fixed sentence mappings but not for dynamic term substitution inside changing messages.
Neural dictionary
Azure Translator overview

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OOAvXtRkR0_VHHsLi486CG0AFxyqZVTDWRz1Kfq2KK0/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E4, TR4, and C4.
A Document Intelligence custom classifier has been trained for each document class. An uploaded PDF can contain several consecutive documents, and each identified document can contain one or more pages.
The application submits the following request:
POST {endpoint}/documentintelligence/documentClassifiers/maintenance-classifier:analyze
?api-version=2024-11-30
&(MISSING CONFIG)
Which configuration should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
The auto split mode instructs the custom classifier to identify individual documents and their associated page ranges within the input file. It supports a file that contains multiple document classes or multiple instances of the same document class. This allows Pinnacle to route each detected document and its complete page range to the appropriate extraction model.
This configuration is important because some documents span multiple pages. The classifier must determine where each document starts and ends rather than treating the whole PDF as one document or treating every page as an independent document. Using the built-in split behaviour eliminates custom page-boundary code and satisfies C4.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. The none mode treats the entire input file as one document. The classifier would return a classification for the complete PDF rather than identifying the individual work orders, certificates, release forms, and sign-off sheets. Pinnacle would still need custom logic to locate document boundaries. This fails TR4.
C. The perPage mode treats every page as a separate document. This could classify individual pages, but it would break documents that span several pages into unrelated results. The application would then need to determine which adjacent pages belong together. That additional grouping logic conflicts with C4.
D. single is not a supported Document Intelligence split mode. The supported behaviours are none, auto, and perPage. Supplying an unsupported value would cause the request to fail validation. It cannot satisfy the document-classification requirement.
Build a custom classifier
Classify Document REST API

question_html:
You are selecting evaluators for a generative app and an agent workflow.
Match the following:
Detect unsupported claims against source context
Check whether an answer addresses the user query
Assess harmful or inappropriate generated content
Assess whether an agent chose suitable tools
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Groundedness
Relevance
Risk and safety
Tool selection

B.
Relevance
Groundedness
Tool selection
Risk and safety

C.
Content filtering
Token usage
Semantic ranking
Availability testing

D.
Tool selection
Risk and safety
Groundedness
Relevance

explanation_html:
Groundedness is the correct evaluator for detecting unsupported claims because it checks whether a generated response is supported by the provided context. Relevance checks whether the answer addresses the user’s query, while risk and safety evaluators assess harmful or inappropriate content.
For agent workflows, tool selection evaluates whether the agent selected the correct and necessary tools. This mapping separates RAG output quality, safety risk, and agent behavior instead of treating them as one generic quality score.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. This mapping swaps groundedness and relevance, which changes the meaning of both evaluations. Relevance is about whether the response answers the user’s query, not whether every claim is supported by context. Groundedness is about source support, not general query fit. It also swaps safety and tool selection, confusing output risk with agent tool behavior.
  • C. This mapping uses operational or pipeline concepts instead of the requested evaluator concepts. Content filtering can be a runtime safety control, but it is not the best match for all four evaluation goals. Token usage and availability testing do not measure response quality or agent tool choice. Semantic ranking can affect retrieval, but it is not the evaluator for the generated answer.
  • D. This mapping assigns tool selection to unsupported claims, which is incorrect. Tool selection evaluates agent tool choice rather than factual support in the final response. It also assigns groundedness to harmful content, but groundedness does not classify harmful categories. The option mixes evaluator responsibilities and would lead to misleading evaluation results.

Risk and Safety Evaluators for Generative AI
Agent Evaluators for Generative AI

question_html:
A customer-service application sends approximately 6,000 tokens of shared policy instructions and examples with every request.
Requests are currently constructed in this order:
tenant-specific metadata
user-specific preferences
shared policy instructions
shared few-shot examples
user message
The deployed model supports Azure OpenAI prompt caching. However, monitoring shows that cached-token utilization is much lower than expected even though the policy instructions and examples are identical across most requests.
The team must improve cache utilization without changing the intended model behaviour or introducing an application-managed semantic cache.
Which change should you make?

options.text: A. Generate a consistent prompt_cache_key from the shared policy content but leave the current message order unchanged
B. Move the shared policy and examples before tenant-specific content and use a stable cache key for requests sharing that prefix
C. Split the shared policy into several system messages while keeping tenant metadata at the beginning of the messages array
D. Move the shared policy after the user message so that only the user-specific portion is evaluated before cache lookup

explanation_html:
Azure OpenAI prompt caching works by matching identical content at the beginning of the prompt. Microsoft specifically recommends placing stable, reusable content first and dynamic content later, and it also recommends a consistent prompt_cache_key for requests sharing a prefix. The existing design breaks prefix reuse because tenant-specific data appears before the otherwise identical 6,000-token block.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. A consistent prompt_cache_key can improve affinity for requests that already share a reusable prefix. It does not make two different prompt prefixes identical when tenant-specific data appears before the shared policy. Leaving the dynamic content first therefore preserves the main cause of the low cache-hit rate. This approach becomes useful after the reusable prefix itself has been stabilized.
C. Splitting shared content into several system messages does not remove the requirement for repeated content to occur at the beginning. Tenant metadata would still change the initial token sequence before the reusable policy content is reached. Multiple system messages can be useful for instruction organization, but they do not inherently improve prefix identity. The cache problem therefore remains even though the message structure looks more organized.
D. Moving the policy after the user message places reusable content even farther from the beginning of the request. Prompt caching does not search the entire prompt for arbitrary repeated blocks and then cache them independently. The model could still receive the same semantic instructions, but the repeated prefix would remain ineffective for caching. This change therefore moves the architecture in the opposite direction from Microsoft’s optimization guidance.
Azure OpenAI latency guidance

question_html:
A production application uses a Global Standard deployment.
Traffic contains two request classes:
ordinary requests use standard performance and pricing
premium requests require priority processing for lower latency
Requirements:
continue using the existing deployment
do not change the deployment-level service tier
do not create another model deployment
do not purchase provisioned throughput
select the higher service tier only for premium requests
Which configuration should you use?

options.text: A. Keep the deployment at default; submit both classes with service_tier="auto" and use different client timeouts
B. Change the deployment to priority; submit premium requests with auto and ordinary requests with default
C. Keep the deployment at default; submit premium requests with priority and ordinary requests with default
D. Keep the deployment at default; submit premium requests with auto and ordinary requests with priority

explanation_html:
Microsoft supports priority processing as a request-level override on compatible Global Standard and Data Zone Standard deployments. When a deployment remains default, a request specifying service_tier=”priority” uses priority processing, while one specifying default receives standard processing. This satisfies the requirement without changing the deployment itself or purchasing provisioned capacity.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. service_tier=”auto” follows the service tier configured on the deployment. Because the existing deployment remains default, both classes would continue to receive standard processing. Client-side timeouts can change how long the application waits, but they do not select Azure’s priority inference tier. This option therefore changes application behaviour without changing the processing class that Microsoft uses.
B. This configuration could technically separate premium and ordinary traffic because default can override a priority deployment back to standard processing. However, the scenario explicitly requires the deployment-level configuration to remain unchanged. Changing the entire deployment to priority would therefore violate a stated operational constraint even though the request overrides themselves are valid. It introduces an unnecessary deployment change when the request-level priority override already solves the problem.
D. This option reverses the required service tiers. auto on the unchanged default deployment would process the premium request as standard traffic. priority would then incorrectly assign the higher tier to the ordinary workload. Both values are legitimate Microsoft settings, but they are attached to the wrong traffic classes.
Foundry model deployment types
AI-103 Study Guide

question_html:
A production application records two different outcomes from Azure OpenAI.

Event 1

HTTP 400

error.code = content_filter

No model output is generated.

Event 2

HTTP 200

finish_reason = content_filter

Generation began before the response was filtered.

The application’s compliance policy states that content-policy events must not be automatically resubmitted unchanged.

Which handling strategy should you implement?

options.text: A. Treat the HTTP 400 as a blocked prompt and the HTTP 200 content_filter result as filtered generation, then handle each explicitly without generic retry
B. Apply the same exponential-backoff retry policy to both events because both indicate transient inference failure
C. Handle only HTTP 400 as filtering and treat any HTTP 200 response as successful regardless of finish_reason
D. Ask the user to revise HTTP 400 prompts but automatically retry HTTP 200 content_filter responses with the identical input

explanation_html:
Microsoft documents different behaviours for filtering the prompt versus filtering generated content. A prompt blocked before inference can return HTTP 400, while generated content can produce an HTTP 200 response whose finish_reason is content_filter. Applications therefore need to inspect both HTTP outcomes and model response metadata instead of treating them as generic infrastructure errors.
Why the other options are incorrect
B. Exponential backoff is appropriate for transient operational conditions such as throttling and some service errors. A content-filter decision indicates that the request or generated material crossed a configured safety boundary rather than that capacity was temporarily unavailable. Resending the identical request does not address the policy reason for the event and violates the scenario’s compliance requirement. This option incorrectly treats safety enforcement as infrastructure instability.
C. An HTTP 200 status means the API request itself was processed successfully, but it does not guarantee that an unrestricted completion was returned. Microsoft explicitly instructs applications to inspect finish_reason, including the content_filter value. Ignoring the field could cause the application to treat incomplete or filtered output as an ordinary successful answer. This option relies on the transport-level status while ignoring the model-level completion state.
D. Asking the user to reformulate a blocked prompt can be an appropriate application response to a prompt-level filter. However, automatically resending an unchanged generation request conflicts with the explicit requirement that policy-filtered content not be resubmitted unchanged. A completion-filter event must still be detected and handled as a safety outcome rather than hidden inside generic retry middleware. This option gets the prompt path partly right but mishandles the generated-content path.
Content Streaming in Azure OpenAI

question_html:
An organization already uses an Azure OpenAI content filter with approved thresholds for hate, sexual, violence, and self-harm categories.
Legal now requires an additional policy that must:
block 40 unreleased internal project codenames
allow exact-match or pattern-based organization-specific terms
leave the existing harm-category thresholds unchanged
be manageable separately from the system prompt
Which solution should you implement?

options.text: A. Enable protected-material detection and add the codenames as copyrighted terms
B. Enable Prompt Shields for indirect attacks and classify the codenames as adversarial instructions
C. Lower all four standard harm-category thresholds and instruct the model not to repeat internal names
D. Create a custom blocklist containing the codenames and attach it to the deployment's content-filter configuration

explanation_html:
Microsoft custom blocklists are designed for use-case-specific terms such as internal project names, competitor names, or other domain-sensitive content. They support custom terms and patterns and are then associated with the applicable content filtering configuration. This lets the organization introduce a separate lexical policy without altering the standard harm thresholds.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Protected-material controls address a different responsible-AI problem involving protected text or code rather than arbitrary company-defined terminology. An internal codename is not necessarily protected material simply because the organization considers it confidential. This approach would also fail to give administrators the explicit organization-controlled list management required in the scenario. It therefore applies a legitimate safety control to the wrong risk category.
B. Prompt Shields are designed to identify adversarial attempts to manipulate model behaviour, including direct and indirect prompt attacks. Merely mentioning a prohibited internal codename does not make the input an adversarial instruction. Treating every codename as prompt injection would conflate application-specific terminology policy with attack detection. The requirement is better represented by deterministic custom blocked terms than by adversarial-prompt classification.
C. Lowering standard harm thresholds would make the existing hate, sexual, violence, and self-harm moderation more restrictive across unrelated content. Those categories do not represent the business-specific requirement to suppress internal project names. A system instruction may discourage the model from repeating a term, but it is not the same control as a configurable filtering list. This option changes unrelated safety behaviour while still providing a weaker mechanism for the actual policy.
Content filtering for Microsoft Foundry Models

question_html:
A team migrates a stateful assistant to the Azure OpenAI Responses API.
The first turn is:
first = client.responses.create(
model=MODEL,
input=”Review this proposed architecture.”
)
For the next turn, the application should send only:
Identify the three highest operational risks.
The service should reconstruct the preceding response context rather than requiring the client to rebuild the entire transcript.
Which configuration should you use on the second request?

options.text: A. Set store=True and omit any reference to the first response
C. Set the response's conversation value to first.id
D. Enable context compaction and pass the first response output as the compaction threshold

explanation_html:
The Responses API supports multi-turn chaining through previous_response_id. Microsoft documents passing the preceding response ID into the next request so the service can continue from the stored conversation state while the caller supplies the new turn.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Stored responses make server-side persistence possible, but persistence alone does not tell a new request which earlier response should supply its context. A second independent request with no predecessor reference starts without that explicit response chain. The caller therefore still needs to identify the preceding response when using this continuation pattern. This option confuses storing state with selecting which state the next turn should continue from.
C. The Responses platform has conversation-related mechanisms, but a response ID and a conversation resource identifier are not interchangeable values. The question specifically starts with a response object and requires direct continuation from that response. Microsoft documents previous_response_id as the field for this exact chaining operation. Passing the response ID as though it were a different resource identifier would therefore use the wrong state-management contract.
D. Context compaction is useful when long-running state needs to be reduced to manage context length. It does not replace the mechanism that establishes which prior response the current request follows. Compaction and response chaining can participate in the same broader conversation design, but they address different problems. This option chooses a context-size optimization when the requirement is predecessor identification.
Foundry Agent Runtime Components
WebSocket Mode for the Responses API

question_html:
A payment agent can call a create_payment function.
Application code will execute the actual payment, but the generated arguments must conform strictly to the function’s JSON Schema before validation begins.
Requirements:
enforce the supplied function schema
prevent simultaneous function calls
process at most one tool call at a time
favour schema correctness over parallel execution
Which configuration should you use?

options.text: C. strict=false, parallel_tool_calls=false, and JSON mode for the assistant response

explanation_html:
Microsoft enables Structured Outputs for function calling through strict: true. Microsoft also states that structured function output isn’t supported with parallel function calls, so parallel_tool_calls should be false when strict function schemas are used.
Why the other options are incorrect
B. strict=true correctly selects schema-constrained function arguments. However, Microsoft explicitly states that Structured Outputs aren’t supported with parallel function calling. Enabling both settings would therefore conflict with the documented constraint even though each feature is valid in other circumstances. This is a deliberately close distractor because it gets the schema requirement right but breaks the execution requirement.
C. Disabling parallel tool calls correctly restricts execution to a serial pattern. However, strict=false gives up the requested strict function-schema guarantee. JSON mode can help ensure syntactically valid JSON in model output, but it is not equivalent to strict adherence to a supplied function schema. The option solves serialization and formatting concerns while missing the central structured-function requirement.
D. tool_choice=”required” can force the model to select a tool rather than answer directly. It does not require the selected function’s arguments to conform to a strict supplied schema. Enabling parallel tool calls also conflicts with the requirement to execute at most one call at a time. This combination therefore strengthens tool usage while weakening both schema enforcement and execution control.
Function calling with Azure OpenAI
Azure OpenAI Responses API

question_html:
A single Foundry prompt agent serves 300 customer tenants.
One Azure AI Search index contains:
tenant_id
document_id
title
content
contentVector
tenant_id is configured as filterable.
Requirements:
use one agent version for every tenant
receive the caller’s tenant ID at runtime
constrain every Azure AI Search query generated by the tool
do not rely only on natural-language instructions for tenant isolation
do not create a separate index for every tenant
Which design should you implement?

options.text: A. Use structured inputs to select a tenant-specific File Search vector store at runtime
B. Insert the tenant ID into the agent instructions and increase the Search tool's top_k
C. Use a structured input inside the Azure AI Search tool's OData filter expression
D. Assign Search Index Data Reader individually to each customer tenant and leave the query unfiltered

explanation_html:
Microsoft Foundry structured inputs can parameterize the Azure AI Search tool’s filter at runtime. Microsoft specifically describes this as a way for one agent definition to serve users who must query different subsets of the same index without creating a separate agent version per filter value.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Structured inputs can indeed change File Search vector-store resources at runtime, so the mechanism itself is real. However, the scenario already has one Azure AI Search index with a filterable tenant_id field and requires continued use of that shared index. Replacing it with tenant-specific File Search stores introduces an entirely different retrieval architecture and additional storage lifecycle to manage. This option applies the right runtime-parameterization concept to the wrong retrieval tool.
B. Runtime instructions can tell the model which tenant it should operate for and can therefore improve behavioural guidance. They do not enforce an OData constraint on the actual documents eligible for the Search tool to retrieve. Increasing top_k changes how many results are considered rather than which tenant’s results are permitted. This option relies on behavioural prompting where the scenario requires retrieval-layer scoping.
D. Azure RBAC can control whether an identity is allowed to query a Search service or index. A broad Search Index Data Reader assignment doesn’t automatically transform a shared index query into a tenant_id-scoped result set. The scenario uses one search index containing multiple tenants and therefore still requires a data-level retrieval filter. This option confuses service authorization with row/document-level search scoping.
Azure AI Search tool for Foundry agents
Filters in Azure AI Search

question_html:
A developer wants a Foundry agent to invoke an existing REST API.
The current API can expose either OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 and can accept either JSON or multipart payloads.
Which specification combination meets the documented Foundry OpenAPI tool requirements?

options.text: A. OpenAPI 3.0, an operationId on every operation, and multipart/form-data request bodies
B. OpenAPI 3.1, an x-ms-operation-id on every operation, and application/json request bodies
C. OpenAPI 3.0, no operation identifiers, and application/json-patch+json request bodies
D. OpenAPI 3.1, an operationId on every operation, and application/json request bodies

explanation_html:
Foundry Agent Service supports OpenAPI 3.0 and 3.1. Microsoft requires each operation exposed through the OpenAPI tool to contain an operationId, and documented supported request body types include application/json and application/json-patch+json.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. OpenAPI 3.0 is supported and supplying operationId is also correct. The failure is the use of multipart/form-data, which is not among the documented body types supported by the Foundry OpenAPI tool. Multipart payloads are common in ordinary REST APIs, making this option technically plausible outside the agent-tool constraint. The API would need to expose a supported JSON body shape for this integration pattern.
B. OpenAPI 3.1 and application/json are both compatible with the Foundry tool. However, the required operation identifier is the standard operationId, not an x-ms-operation-id substitute. Microsoft specifically notes that every function must have an operationId for the tool to work correctly. This option therefore gets the API version and body type right while missing a required operation-level property.
C. application/json-patch+json is a supported request body type and OpenAPI 3.0 is also supported. However, omitting operation identifiers violates the requirement that each exposed function contain an operationId. The tool uses descriptive operation identifiers to expose and select callable actions. This option therefore combines two supported choices with one missing mandatory element.
Foundry Agent Tool Catalog
Foundry Agent Service Overview

question_html:
A Foundry agent connects to a remote MCP server that performs engineering simulations.
Observed behaviour:
the MCP operation usually takes 130–160 seconds
synchronous runs consistently fail near 100 seconds
the selected model supports Responses API background mode
the application doesn’t want to hold an HTTP connection open for the duration
the MCP integration itself must remain unchanged
What should the application do?

options.text: A. Set stream=true and keep the original synchronous request open until the MCP server completes
B. Submit the response with background mode enabled and poll the returned response ID until completion
C. Submit a new request with previous_response_id every 90 seconds to refresh the MCP timeout
D. Enable mandatory MCP tool approval and resume the same synchronous call after approval

explanation_html:
Microsoft documents a roughly 100-second synchronous timeout for MCP calls when the agent isn’t operating through background execution. For supported models, background mode lets long-running work continue asynchronously and allows the client to poll the response until it completes.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Streaming changes how response output is delivered to the client as it becomes available. It does not turn a synchronous MCP execution into the documented asynchronous background pattern for operations exceeding the synchronous timeout. Keeping the connection open also conflicts with the requirement that the application not hold a long-lived request. This option improves delivery behaviour but does not solve the MCP execution-duration constraint.
C. previous_response_id is designed to chain conversation state between completed Responses API turns. It is not a keep-alive mechanism that resets the synchronous timeout of an MCP operation already in progress. Starting repeated turns could also create duplicate work rather than extend one long-running server task. This option misuses conversation continuation as runtime task management.
D. Tool approval can be valuable when a sensitive operation must pause for explicit human authorization. It does not extend the amount of time available for an already approved synchronous MCP operation to finish. The scenario identifies execution duration, not missing approval, as the reason for failure. This option introduces a governance control without correcting the actual asynchronous-processing requirement.
Foundry Agent Tool Catalog

question_html:
A Foundry prompt agent uses the image-generation tool.
The project already contains:
a compatible gpt-5 orchestrator deployment
a gpt-image-1 deployment
an agent definition containing ImageGenTool(model=”gpt-image-1″)
The application invokes the agent directly through the Responses REST endpoint.
Text responses work, but image requests don’t return an image_generation_call.
Which configuration should you use?

options.text: A. Keep gpt-5 as the orchestrator and put "model":"gpt-image-1" in the Responses request body instead of using an image deployment header
B. Change the agent's orchestrator model to gpt-image-1 so that the same model handles reasoning and image generation
C. Keep the two deployments and send x-ms-oai-image-generation-deployment: gpt-image-1 on the Responses request
D. Move gpt-image-1 to a separate Foundry project and reference it through a project connection

explanation_html:
Explanation
Foundry’s image-generation agent tool uses a compatible orchestration model and a separate gpt-image-1 image deployment in the same project. Microsoft documents the x-ms-oai-image-generation-deployment request header when invoking the Responses endpoint for this tool.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. The image deployment is already represented by the agent’s ImageGenTool, so this option appears close to the intended configuration. However, the REST invocation still requires the documented image-generation deployment header for this tool path. Setting a general model value in the Responses body does not replace that header-based image deployment selection. This option confuses the response-orchestration model selector with image-tool deployment routing.
B. gpt-image-1 is the image-generation model rather than the agent’s general orchestration model in the documented pattern. Foundry explicitly describes using two deployments, with a compatible model such as gpt-5 orchestrating the tool call. Replacing the orchestrator with the image model collapses two distinct responsibilities instead of fixing the missing routing configuration. This option identifies the correct image model but assigns it to the wrong role.
D. The documentation requires the compatible orchestrator and gpt-image-1 deployment to be in the same Foundry project for this image-generation tool pattern. Moving the image deployment to another project would therefore make the topology less aligned with the documented prerequisites. Project connections are useful for many external tools and services, but they aren’t the replacement for this image-tool deployment relationship. This option solves a cross-resource integration problem that the scenario does not have.
Azure OpenAI image generation
Foundry Agent Tool Catalog

question_html:
A media company uses Azure AI Video Indexer to prepare footage for automated editing.
The editing application must retrieve:
the exact start and end of each continuous camera shot
representative visual frames belonging to that shot
a unit finer than a semantically grouped scene
Which output should the application consume?

options.text: A. Shot start/end metadata together with the shot's keyframe list
B. Scene start/end metadata together with the scene thumbnail
C. Shot start/end metadata together with only the shot-type classification
D. Scene start/end metadata together with transcript segments occurring during the scene

explanation_html:
Azure AI Video Indexer distinguishes scenes, shots, and keyframes. Microsoft defines a shot as a sequence of frames from the same camera context and documents shot metadata as including start time, end time, and a list of representative keyframes.
Why the other options are incorrect
B. Scene boundaries are useful when an editor needs semantically related groups of consecutive shots rather than individual camera-shot units. A scene can contain multiple underlying shots, so its start and end timestamps are coarser than the requested granularity. A scene thumbnail is also only a representative frame for the broader scene context rather than the complete keyframe list for each shot. This option returns valid Video Indexer insight data but at the wrong hierarchical level.
C. Shot start and end metadata correctly identifies the temporal unit required by the editing system. Shot-type or visual-composition labels can add useful information about how a shot is framed, but they do not provide the representative frame collection requested by the application. The requirement explicitly needs visual frames that can be used to represent the shot. This option gets the temporal object right but substitutes classification metadata for keyframes.
D. Scene timings and transcript segments can be useful for chaptering or finding where spoken topics occur in a video. They do not identify the exact boundaries of each individual camera shot when one scene contains several shots. Transcript information also cannot replace representative visual keyframes when the editing workflow needs image selections. This option is appropriate for semantic spoken-content navigation rather than frame-oriented visual editing.
Azure AI Video Indexer insights overview
Azure AI Video Indexer overview

question_html:
A company has trained and tested a Custom Speech model for specialist engineering terminology.
The implementation has two phases.
Phase 1
process several thousand recorded calls every night
use batch transcription
use the trained Custom Speech model
avoid paying for a hosted custom endpoint if one isn’t required
Phase 2
add real-time recognition to an interactive support application
continue using the same Custom Speech model family
Which implementation should you use?

options.text: A. Deploy a hosted custom endpoint immediately and use the endpoint ID for both batch and real-time workloads
B. Use the custom model URI directly for both batch transcription and future real-time Speech SDK recognition without ever deploying an endpoint
C. Use the base Speech model for Phase 1 and deploy the Custom Speech model only when Phase 2 starts
D. Reference the custom model URI in batch transcription, then deploy a custom endpoint when real-time recognition is introduced

explanation_html:
Microsoft explicitly states that a hosted deployment endpoint is not required to use Custom Speech with batch transcription. Batch jobs can reference the custom model, while non-batch scenarios require deployment of the custom model to an endpoint, making the staged design the most resource-efficient approach.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. Deploying an endpoint would make the custom model available for real-time use and therefore anticipates Phase 2 correctly. However, Microsoft states that batch transcription can use a custom model without a hosted endpoint. Paying for and operating that endpoint throughout Phase 1 therefore violates the explicit resource-conservation requirement. This option works functionally but introduces infrastructure earlier than the workload requires it.
B. The custom model URI is the correct way to identify a custom model for the batch-transcription request. Microsoft distinguishes batch transcription from other Custom Speech use cases and states that other scenarios require a deployed custom endpoint. A real-time Speech SDK workload therefore cannot simply continue treating the model URI as a replacement for deployment. This option correctly handles Phase 1 but incorrectly assumes the same invocation model for Phase 2.
C. Delaying deployment until real-time recognition begins is efficient and therefore satisfies one important requirement. However, Phase 1 explicitly requires the already trained Custom Speech model to improve transcription of specialist engineering terminology. Falling back to the base model during batch processing would give up the custom recognition improvements the organization already prepared. This option optimizes infrastructure cost by violating the Phase 1 model requirement.

Deploy a Custom Speech model
