https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OOAvXtRkR0_VHHsLi486CG0AFxyqZVTDWRz1Kfq2KK0/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy BR4 and C3.
A single technician report can describe a hydraulic leak, an electrical warning, and a procedural breach. The classification output must contain every applicable category. Most training reports are in English, but the same project must process Japanese and French reports.
Which project configuration should you create?
explanation_html:
Custom multi-label text classification permits more than one class to be assigned to the same document. This is required because a single report can describe several unrelated safety issues. A single-label project would force the model to select one category and discard other applicable classifications.
Pinnacle should enable the multilingual option when the project is created and select the language used by most training documents as the project language. Multilingual custom text classification enables one project to process supported languages rather than requiring one project per language. Pinnacle can add representative Japanese and French training examples if evaluation identifies language-specific performance gaps.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Custom named entity recognition extracts labelled text spans such as identifiers, component names, or locations. It does not assign one or more document-level safety categories to an entire report. Pinnacle could use it to identify aircraft registrations or part numbers, but that is not BR4. The required task is document classification.
B. Multilingual custom single-label classification supports one project across languages. However, it returns one classification for each report. Reports containing several issue types would lose valid categories or require artificial combined classes. That design would not satisfy the multi-category requirement.
D. Conversational language understanding predicts intents and extracts entities from conversational utterances. It is useful for routing commands or interpreting user requests. The input in this scenario is a complete technician report that requires multiple document-level labels. CLU is therefore not the correct project type.

question_html:
A technical-support RAG application uses this Azure AI Search hybrid query:

{
  "search": "ZX-419 pressure sensor reset",
  "vectorQueries": [
    {
      "kind": "vector",
      "vector": [0.018, -0.041, 0.027],
      "fields": "contentVector",
      "k": 50
    }
  ],
  "top": 10
}

Evaluation shows:

the BM25 text result list already places the exact ZX-419 manual first
the vector result list provides valuable semantic recall
after RRF fusion, semantically similar manuals frequently outrank the exact product-code manual
k=50 must remain unchanged
the BM25 scoring configuration must remain unchanged
vector retrieval must remain enabled

Which change most directly addresses the problem?

options.text: A. Add a scoring profile that increases the lexical weight of productCode
B. Set the vector query to exhaustive=true while retaining the default weighting
C. Set a vector weight below 1.0 while retaining k=50
D. Increase the vector k above 50 and reduce the final top value

explanation_html:
Azure AI Search supports a weight parameter on vector queries that controls the vector result list’s relative contribution when RRF combines ranking lists. Microsoft documents values below 1.0 as reducing that vector query’s importance while retaining the actual retrieval operation and candidate count.
Why the other options are incorrect
A. A scoring profile can legitimately alter how lexical results are scored and might be useful when the BM25 ranking itself needs improvement. The scenario explicitly states that BM25 already ranks the exact product-code manual correctly and that its scoring configuration must remain unchanged. Changing the lexical ranking would therefore tune a component that has already been verified as working. This option is a plausible relevance technique but targets the wrong ranking stage.
B. exhaustive=true changes the vector nearest-neighbour search behaviour and can be useful when exact vector matching is required rather than approximate HNSW search. It does not reduce the relative RRF contribution assigned to the vector-ranked list after retrieval. The problem occurs during fusion even though vector recall itself is useful. This option changes how vector candidates are found rather than how heavily their ranking contributes to the final hybrid result.
D. Increasing k supplies even more vector candidates to the vector retrieval path. That does not reduce the influence of the vector-ranked list and may increase the amount of vector-derived competition in downstream fusion. Reducing top only changes how many final documents are returned after ranking rather than correcting the ranking imbalance itself. This option changes candidate volume and result count while leaving the underlying weighting issue untouched.
Hybrid Search Scoring with RRF
Hybrid Search Overview

question_html:
An Azure AI Search indexer processes documents through:

document cracking
OCR
Text Split
a custom Web API skill
output field mappings into the search index

The indexer reports Success, but a known test document still produces an empty customerId.

The engineer must:

execute the enrichment pipeline against that specific source document
inspect intermediate nodes in the enriched document tree
inspect the inputs and outputs of individual skills
modify an annotation path or skill mapping experimentally
validate the change before committing it to the production skillset

What should the engineer do first?

options.text: A. Start an Azure AI Search Debug Session against the affected document
B. Set maxFailedItems=0, rerun the production indexer, and inspect its execution history
C. Query the resulting index with debug=all to inspect the missing enrichment contribution
D. Clone the skillset and index, then execute the complete indexer against the full data source

explanation_html:
A Debug Session is a cached indexer and skillset execution scoped to a single document. Microsoft designed it specifically for interactive examination of the enrichment tree, skill inputs and outputs, annotation paths, and experimental skillset changes before those changes are committed back to the production skillset.
Why the other options are incorrect
B. Reducing maxFailedItems can make an indexer run fail more aggressively when document-level errors occur, and execution history is valuable for identifying warnings or failures. However, the indexer is already succeeding and the requirement is to inspect the actual intermediate enrichment state for one known document. Execution history does not provide the same interactive enriched-document tree and editable skill mappings as a Debug Session. This option improves failure visibility but not the detailed single-document skill debugging required here.
C. Query-level debug functionality is useful when engineers need to inspect search relevance, including ranking contributions in retrieval scenarios. The missing customerId was produced during indexing and skillset enrichment rather than query-time ranking. No amount of query score decomposition can reveal an intermediate OCR or custom-skill annotation path that never mapped correctly. This option uses a valid Search debugging capability at the wrong stage of the pipeline.
D. A cloned test environment could eventually be used to validate a revised skillset without touching production resources. However, executing the entire data source is considerably broader than necessary when the failure is already reproducible with one known source document. It also doesn’t inherently provide the interactive visual enriched-tree inspection and node-level editing experience requested by the scenario. This option can support later integration testing but is not the best first diagnostic action.
Skillset Concepts and Enrichment Trees
Reference Enriched Nodes During Skillset Execution

question_html:
A team is operationalizing reflection and critique patterns for a production agent.
Match each requirement to the best implementation choice.
Match the following:
Score answer quality against test data
Explain why an evaluation score was assigned
Re-run checks before deployment
Detect production quality regressions
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Application Insights sampling
Azure Key Vault
Manual prompt editing
Blob lifecycle policy

B.
Azure AI Search
Agent tool approval
Prompt variables
Private endpoint

C.
Foundry evaluators
Evaluator explanations
CI evaluation task
Continuous evaluations

D.
Content Safety filters
Token quota settings
Search indexer schedule
Managed identity

explanation_html:
Foundry evaluators are the correct choice for scoring quality against test datasets because they assess dimensions such as groundedness, relevance, coherence, fluency, and safety. Evaluator explanations help reviewers understand why a score was assigned, which supports controlled reflection without relying on end-user-visible reasoning.
A CI evaluation task is the right way to re-run checks before deployment, while continuous evaluations support production monitoring for quality regressions. Together, these choices form a practical operational loop: evaluate before release, preserve explanatory evidence, and keep monitoring after deployment.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping mostly contains operational support features rather than generative AI evaluation controls. Application Insights sampling can affect telemetry volume, but it does not score answer quality. Key Vault secures secrets, and Blob lifecycle policy manages retention, neither of which implements self-critique. Manual prompt editing alone is not an automated evaluation loop.
  • B. Azure AI Search is useful for retrieval and grounding, but it does not itself score generated response quality. Agent tool approval controls whether an action can proceed, not why an answer received an evaluation score. Prompt variables can support prompt design, but they do not create a CI quality gate. Private endpoints secure network access, not production quality monitoring.
  • D. Content Safety filters are important for moderation and harmful-content controls, but they are not the whole reflection loop. Token quota settings control usage and throughput rather than answer quality. Search indexer schedules refresh content but do not evaluate model output. Managed identity secures access but does not detect quality regressions.

How to run an evaluation in Azure DevOps
Continuously evaluate your AI agents

question_html:
A Foundry agent uses Azure AI Search for grounding. The Search connection uses the project managed identity, but runtime queries fail with a 403 Forbidden error after public network access is disabled. Network connectivity tests from the private environment succeed.
What should you do next?

options.text: A. Assign Search Index Data Reader
B. Enable public network access on Search
C. Add Content Safety moderation filter
D. Recreate the Foundry agent project

explanation_html:
A 403 response after connectivity succeeds usually points to authorization rather than network reachability. For query-only access to an Azure AI Search index, the managed identity used by the agent needs an appropriate data-plane role such as Search Index Data Reader.
This fix keeps the infrastructure aligned with private networking and least privilege. It avoids weakening the network boundary and addresses the actual issue: the identity can reach the service but lacks the required permission to query the index.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Enabling public network access might appear to make the issue disappear in some environments, but it would violate the private infrastructure requirement. The scenario already states that network connectivity tests from the private environment succeed. That means the failure is not primarily about reaching the endpoint. Opening public access would weaken security without addressing the missing identity permission.
  • C. A Content Safety moderation filter helps detect or block unsafe input or output. It does not authorize an agent to query Azure AI Search. The error is a 403 from the Search access path, not a safety policy block. Adding moderation would not grant the managed identity any Search data-plane permissions.
  • D. Recreating the Foundry agent project is excessive and unlikely to resolve the root cause. The project can use the correct managed identity but still fail if that identity lacks Search roles. Recreating infrastructure often adds risk and downtime without fixing RBAC. The better next step is to assign the required role at the correct scope.

Azure AI Search role-based access control
Connect an Azure AI Search index to Foundry agents

A company wants a quality-control assistant for manufacturing images. Users upload photos and ask why an item failed inspection. Answers must be based on visible defects and, when available, retrieved inspection rules.
Problem:
The solution must support question answering grounded in visual evidence and avoid unsupported conclusions.
Proposed solution:
Use a vision-enabled chat model for image-question input, retrieve inspection rules with Azure AI Search, and instruct the model to answer only from visible and retrieved evidence.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
The proposed solution meets the goal because it combines direct visual reasoning with retrieval grounding. The vision-enabled model can inspect the uploaded photo, while Azure AI Search can provide relevant inspection rules that support or constrain the answer.
The instruction to answer only from visible and retrieved evidence is also important because the application must avoid unsupported conclusions. This design supports both visual evidence grounding and document grounding, which is the core requirement of the scenario.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• B. No is incorrect because the proposed solution covers the required evidence sources. The image is handled by a vision-enabled chat model. The inspection rules are handled by Azure AI Search retrieval. The grounding instruction reduces the risk of answers based on unsupported assumptions.

question_html:
A company runs a production RAG assistant in Azure AI Foundry.
The team needs to detect weekly degradation in groundedness and answer quality.
Which capability should they use first?

options.text: A. Azure AI Search indexer diagnostic logs
B. Azure Storage lifecycle management policies
D. Azure Key Vault diagnostic access logs

explanation_html:
Azure AI Foundry evaluations are the best fit because they directly assess generative AI quality signals such as groundedness, relevance, retrieval quality, and response quality. For a RAG assistant, these metrics are more meaningful than generic infrastructure logs because the risk is not just whether the system is running, but whether it is still producing grounded, useful, and safe answers.
This also supports drift-style monitoring because evaluation results can be compared over time against a baseline. A production assistant may still have normal latency and availability while its retrieval quality or groundedness gets worse due to changed source documents, prompts, model behavior, or retrieval configuration.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Search indexer diagnostic logs are useful for troubleshooting indexing failures, document ingestion, and search service behavior. They do not directly evaluate whether generated answers are grounded in retrieved context. They also do not measure model response quality or safety behavior. They are a supporting signal, not the primary monitoring capability for this requirement.
  • B. Azure Storage lifecycle management policies control retention, tiering, and deletion behavior for stored data. They do not evaluate model performance, safety events, or grounding quality. They might affect source data availability if misconfigured, but they are not a monitoring solution for AI behavior. This option focuses on storage cost and data management rather than AI quality.
  • D. Azure Key Vault diagnostic access logs help investigate secret access, authentication, and security operations. They are relevant if the application cannot access keys or secrets. They do not measure groundedness, model drift, response relevance, or safety events. This option confuses security audit logging with AI quality monitoring.

Model monitoring for generative AI applications
Azure AI Foundry evaluation SDK

question_html:
You manage an enterprise support assistant built with Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Search, and Azure AI Foundry. The application is live and handles internal HR and IT questions.
The operations team must monitor:

  • latency and failed requests
  • unsafe prompt and response events
  • groundedness degradation over time
  • retrieval quality changes after content updates

Which monitoring design best satisfies the requirements?

options.text: B. Content Safety Studio moderation workflows
D. Azure Monitor plus Foundry evaluations

explanation_html:
Azure Monitor plus Foundry evaluations is the strongest design because the requirements combine operational telemetry and AI-quality monitoring. Azure Monitor can help capture infrastructure and application signals such as latency, failures, dependency calls, and traces, while Foundry evaluations can assess quality signals such as groundedness, relevance, and retrieval behavior.
The question includes both runtime health and model-behavior monitoring. A complete AI operations approach needs both layers because a generative AI system can be technically healthy while producing low-quality or weakly grounded answers.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure Policy compliance dashboard is useful for governance and resource configuration compliance. It can help enforce rules such as allowed regions, required tags, or approved configurations. It does not evaluate generated answer quality or grounding behavior. It also does not provide model-level performance drift analysis.
  • B. Content Safety Studio moderation workflows are useful for detecting and testing harmful content patterns. They help with safety signals but do not cover latency, failed requests, retrieval quality, or groundedness degradation by themselves. This option covers only one part of the monitoring requirement. It is too narrow for a full production AI monitoring design.
  • C. Azure Search traffic analytics can help analyze search traffic and search service behavior. It may help investigate retrieval-side usage or performance. It does not evaluate final model responses for groundedness or safety. It also does not provide complete application tracing across the model, orchestration, and safety layers.

Application Insights overview

Match the following:
Harm category spikes in generated answers
Unsupported claims in RAG responses
Lower ranking quality after reindexing
Latency growth across agent tool calls
Choices:

A.

Groundedness evaluator

B.

Content Safety event trend

C.

Groundedness evaluator

D.
Document retrieval evaluator

Content Safety event trend
Azure Policy assignment

explanation_html:
Content Safety event trends are the best match for detecting increases in harmful or unsafe content categories. Groundedness evaluation is the best match for unsupported claims because it checks whether the answer is supported by the provided context. Document retrieval evaluation is the right signal for ranking quality after reindexing because it measures retrieval-side quality rather than final answer quality.
Trace telemetry is the best match for latency growth across agent tool calls because tracing shows the sequence and timing of model calls, tool calls, dependencies, and orchestration steps. Together, these mappings separate safety monitoring, grounding quality, retrieval quality, and runtime performance instead of treating them as one generic metric.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. This choice incorrectly maps harm category spikes to groundedness evaluation. Groundedness checks answer support against context, not harm severity. Azure Policy assignment also does not detect unsupported RAG claims. Storage lifecycle policy is unrelated to agent tool-call latency.
  • C. This choice uses generic or configuration-focused signals for AI-quality issues. A metric alert may detect volume or latency thresholds, but it does not classify harm categories by itself. A search index schema does not measure ranking quality after reindexing. Key Vault audit events are security logs, not grounding or retrieval quality signals.
  • D. This choice reverses several important monitoring responsibilities. Document retrieval evaluation measures retrieval quality, not harmful output categories. Trace telemetry can show execution timing, but it does not score unsupported claims. Azure Policy assignment helps enforce governance rules, not diagnose latency growth across agent tool calls.

The proposed solution meets the goal because it combines operational monitoring with AI-quality evaluation. Azure Monitor and tracing help detect latency regressions, dependency failures, and runtime issues, while safety outcomes capture unsafe prompt or response events.
Scheduled Foundry evaluations address the AI-specific part of the requirement by measuring groundedness, relevance, and retrieval quality over time. That makes the design suitable for detecting drift-like degradation even when the application remains available and responsive.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• B. No is incorrect because the proposed solution covers all stated monitoring areas. It includes operational telemetry for latency and dependencies. It includes safety-filter outcomes for unsafe response events. It also includes scheduled evaluations for grounding and retrieval-quality degradation over time.

question_html:
A company deploys a customer-support agent that can search internal policy documents and call refund tools.
The compliance team must reconstruct which tool calls occurred, which source data influenced the response, and which approval step allowed an action.
Which design element best supports this audit requirement?

options.text: B. Search index scoring profile tuning

explanation_html:
Trace spans with metadata are the best fit because they can record the execution path of an agent run, including tool calls, timing, inputs, outputs, and key contextual fields. For auditability, the trace should include metadata such as source document identifiers, retrieved chunk references, workflow IDs, and approval decision IDs.
This approach directly supports responsible AI auditing because it connects what the agent did with why it acted and who approved sensitive actions. Content filters, search scoring, and quota settings can be important controls, but they do not provide the full execution record required for post-incident review.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Content Safety threshold logs help identify moderation decisions and harmful-content filtering outcomes. They are useful for safety governance but do not reconstruct the full agent execution path. They also do not normally show which source document grounded an answer or which human approved a tool action. This makes them too narrow for the stated audit requirement.
  • B. Search index scoring profile tuning affects how search results are ranked. It can improve retrieval relevance, but it is not an audit trail of agent behavior. It does not record approval decisions, tool execution order, or the full chain of runtime actions. It may appear in provenance metadata, but it is not the audit mechanism itself.
  • D. Model deployment quota settings control capacity, throughput, or rate limits for model access. They do not show what happened during a specific agent run. They also do not preserve grounding evidence or approval workflow decisions. This option addresses operational capacity, not responsible AI auditing.

Agent tracing in Microsoft Foundry

question_html:
You need a top-level Azure boundary for building, deploying, securing, and monitoring generative AI apps and agents. The solution must support project-level organization and connected Azure services.
Which component should you create first?
explanation_html:
A Microsoft Foundry resource is the primary Azure resource for building, deploying, and managing generative AI applications, models, and agents. It provides the infrastructure boundary where access, security, networking, billing, and monitoring can be configured.
This is the best starting point because the question asks for an Azure infrastructure foundation, not a single supporting service. Search, storage, and monitoring are commonly connected later, but they are not the top-level Foundry boundary for the AI solution.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Search is important for retrieval and grounding, especially for RAG and agent knowledge. However, it is not the top-level infrastructure boundary for the AI app or agent solution. It stores and queries indexed content, but it does not organize Foundry projects, model deployments, or agent infrastructure. Choosing it first would skip the Foundry resource that governs the broader AI solution.
  • B. Azure Storage account can store source documents, logs, files, or artifacts used by the workload. However, it does not provide the Foundry control plane for models, agents, projects, or deployments. Storage is a supporting resource, not the central infrastructure container for the AI solution. It would not satisfy the requirement to manage the AI app and agent environment.
  • D. Application Insights workspace supports telemetry and observability for application behavior. It is useful after the workload is deployed and instrumented. However, it is not where Foundry models, projects, agents, and connected AI services are managed. Monitoring alone does not establish the required AI infrastructure boundary.

question_html:
You are instrumenting a claims-processing agent. The agent can retrieve policy documents and request approval before issuing a payment adjustment.

Snippet

import os
from opentelemetry import trace
from azure.monitor.opentelemetry import configure_azure_monitor

configure_azure_monitor(
connection_string=os.environ[“APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING”]
)

tracer = trace.get_tracer(“claims-agent”)

def run_claim_review(agent, claim_request, approval):
with tracer.start_as_current_span(“agent.claim_review”) as span:
span.set_attribute(“ai.agent.name”, “claims-review-agent”)
span.set_attribute(“ai.workflow.id”, claim_request.workflow_id)
span.set_attribute(“ai.provenance.source_doc_id”, claim_request.policy_doc_id)
span.set_attribute(“ai.provenance.index_version”, claim_request.index_version)
span.set_attribute(“ai.tool.name”, “payment_adjustment”)
span.set_attribute(“ai.approval.required”, True)

(MISSING CONFIG)

result = agent.run(
input=claim_request.summary,
tool_context={“approval_id”: approval.id}
)

span.set_attribute(“ai.run.status”, “completed”)
return result

Which missing configuration best completes the audit trail?

options.text: C. Replace provenance metadata with embeddings
D. Disable tracing after approvals complete

explanation_html:
Adding an approval decision event is the best completion because the trace already records the agent workflow, provenance fields, and the sensitive tool name. The missing audit element is the actual approval outcome, such as who approved or rejected the action, when the decision occurred, and which approval request it related to.
For responsible AI auditing, approval decisions should be correlated with the same trace that records the agent run and tool execution. This lets reviewers connect the final action to the retrieved evidence, the approval workflow, and the runtime behavior that led to the decision.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Storing a raw prompt archive may create privacy, security, and retention concerns. It also does not directly link the approval outcome to the trace span. A raw prompt can be useful in some debugging scenarios, but it is not the missing workflow approval record. The question needs an auditable event in the existing trace context.
  • C. Replacing provenance metadata with embeddings would weaken auditability. Embeddings help similarity search, but they are not human-readable evidence of the source document or index version. Auditors need clear provenance identifiers, not just vector representations. This option removes useful audit evidence instead of completing it.
  • D. Disabling tracing after approvals complete would reduce visibility into the final action. The system still needs to capture the result of the approved tool call and completion status. Turning off tracing would create a gap between approval and execution. That is the opposite of a responsible audit design.

Trace and observe AI agents in Microsoft Foundry
Using function tools with human in the loop approvals

explanation_html:
Object detection is the best match for locating common objects in still images because it returns object labels with bounding boxes. Dense captions are better for describing separate regions, while people detection is specific to locating people in images.
Azure AI Video Indexer is the best fit for detecting objects across video timelines because it can extract insights from video content rather than requiring a still-image workflow for every frame. This mapping separates image-level analysis, region-level descriptions, people localization, and video insight extraction.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping incorrectly uses image tagging for object localization. Tags can describe image content, but they do not satisfy the same bounding-box requirement as object detection. It also maps object detection to region descriptions, where dense captions are the better fit. Read OCR extracts text, not video object timeline insights.
  • B. This mapping confuses dense captions with object localization. Dense captions describe image regions, but they are not the primary feature for identifying common objects as object records. Smart crop finds a useful crop area, not separate region descriptions. Image tagging is also not the right feature for video timeline object detection.
  • C. This mapping uses OCR for object localization, which is the wrong workload. OCR is for extracting text, not identifying objects or components. It also maps people detection to region descriptions rather than locating people. Smart crop and dense captions are misplaced for people detection and video object timelines.

The field schema gives the downstream system predictable extracted values, while OCR, layout, Markdown table output, and figure description improve the agent’s ability to understand the full claim packet.
The design also keeps responsibilities separated correctly. Content Understanding handles document extraction and structured output, while the downstream agent uses those outputs for reasoning. That is stronger than asking the agent to infer everything from raw PDFs or unstructured OCR text.
Why the other options are incorrect:

It defines structured fields through the analyzer schema and produces Markdown-oriented document content for downstream reasoning. Which configuration should the engineer choose?

options.text: A. Pro mode with reference documents

Standard mode supports multiple content types, including video, and is optimized for efficient schema extraction when complex multi-step document reasoning is not required.
The scenario deliberately includes video input to test a key distinction. Pro mode is currently aimed at advanced document scenarios, not general video pipelines. For independent multimodal content processing where one file is analyzed at a time, a single-file Standard task is the appropriate Content Understanding configuration.

The requirement explicitly says there is no need to compare multiple files or use reference documents. It also adds unnecessary complexity and does not match the video-focused workflow.

question_html:
A production agent passes manual testing but later produces responses that violate the organization’s safety policy. The team can see latency, token usage, and exceptions, but there are no safety scores or evaluator results for production samples.
What should the team implement next?
explanation_html:
The best next step is to enable continuous evaluations so the team can measure quality and safety signals from production samples or representative datasets over time. The issue is not that the system lacks basic telemetry; it already has latency, token usage, and exception data. The missing capability is responsible AI evaluation output that can detect safety regressions.
This is a common AI-103 troubleshooting distinction. Operational monitoring tells you whether the system is running, but evaluator-based instrumentation tells you whether responses remain acceptable against quality and safety criteria. Continuous evaluation helps identify degradation as prompts, data, users, and agent behavior change.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Add a private endpoint improves network isolation and reduces public exposure. It is useful when the problem is secure connectivity to Azure services. However, the reported issue is unsafe generated content and missing safety scores. A private endpoint would not produce evaluator results or detect policy-violating responses.
  • B. Increase model token quota could help if requests were failing because of quota limits or throttling. The scenario does not describe quota errors, rate limits, or insufficient throughput. More quota could even allow more unsafe responses to be produced without better instrumentation. It does not solve the missing safety evaluation gap.
  • C. Rebuild the vector index may help if retrieval quality is poor because documents are stale, badly chunked, or incorrectly embedded. The scenario does not indicate a retrieval failure or index corruption. Even if the vector index were improved, the team would still lack safety scoring for generated responses. This option targets grounding data, not responsible AI instrumentation.

  • B. This choice maps entity extraction to Structured Outputs, which is a schema enforcement mechanism rather than an extraction capability. It also maps topic extraction to summarization, which would produce a condensed description rather than a list of topics or key phrases. Named Entity Recognition is incorrectly assigned to summary generation. Key phrase extraction is then incorrectly used for enforcing JSON shape.
  • C. This choice assigns summarization to entity extraction, which misses the requirement to identify specific named objects. It also maps Structured Outputs to topic identification, even though Structured Outputs does not identify topics by itself. question_html:
You are designing a claims-processing generative AI application in Microsoft Foundry. The application must coordinate multiple steps:

  • Classify the customer request
  • Retrieve policy details
  • Call a claims system
  • Route high-risk cases for human review
  • Continue the workflow after approval

The process must combine agents with business workflow logic and support conditional orchestration.
Which Foundry capability should you use as the primary design approach?
explanation_html:
Foundry workflow is the best fit because the scenario requires business-process orchestration around agents, tools, routing, and approval points. The requirement is not simply to generate a response; it is to coordinate a multistep process with conditional paths and human review.
This is the kind of workload where a workflow design gives structure to the agentic system. The agent can reason and call tools, but the surrounding workflow controls how the overall process moves between steps, systems, and decision points.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Prompt flow is plausible because it has historically been used to prototype and evaluate LLM application flows. However, this scenario is specifically about Foundry agentic orchestration with business-process steps and conditional routing. Prompt flow is not the strongest fit for coordinating agents, approvals, and operational workflow transitions. It would also be less aligned with newer Foundry workflow patterns for agentic automation.
  • C. File search vector store is useful for grounding an agent on documents. It could help retrieve policy details, but it does not orchestrate the full claims process. It cannot manage conditional routing, approval checkpoints, or calls to downstream business systems by itself. Treating retrieval storage as the workflow engine would be an architecture mismatch.
  • D. Code Interpreter lets an agent run Python in a sandbox for analysis and computation. It may be useful for calculations or file analysis, but it is not the orchestration layer for a claims process. It does not provide the business workflow structure required by the scenario. Using it as the primary design approach would overuse a tool meant for computation.

Voice Live API is the best answer because it is designed for low-latency, real-time voice agent experiences. It combines speech recognition, generative AI interaction, and text-to-speech behavior into a voice-first interaction pattern, which is more appropriate than manually stitching together separate speech components for an interactive agent.
The existing Foundry agent already handles retrieval, function-calling, and conversation context. The missing requirement is real-time speech as an agent modality. Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Custom Speech batch pipeline is plausible because custom speech models can improve recognition accuracy for domain-specific audio. However, batch transcription is not the right modality for an interactive voice agent. It is more suitable for offline audio processing or post-call transcription. It also does not directly provide low-latency spoken conversation with the agent.
  • B. Speech SDK manual orchestration is plausible because the Speech SDK can recognize speech and synthesize speech. However, this option requires the developer to manually coordinate speech-to-text, agent calls, and text-to-speech. That can work, but it adds orchestration complexity for a real-time voice-agent scenario. Voice Live is a better fit for the stated low-latency voice modality requirement.
  • D. Azure Translator speech workflow is plausible when the app must translate speech between languages. However, translation is not the core requirement here. The app needs a real-time spoken interface to an agent, not primarily cross-language translation. Translator would not by itself provide the complete voice-agent interaction pattern.

  • C. Enable speaker diarization settings is plausible for meeting transcription or multi-speaker audio. However, diarization identifies who spoke, not whether specialized medical product codes are recognized correctly. The issue is recognition accuracy for domain vocabulary. A custom speech endpoint is the direct control for that requirement.
  • D. Add translation target language is plausible if the app must support cross-language conversations. However, translation does not improve recognition of specialized product codes in the source language. It also introduces a different workflow than the one described. question_html:
A voice-enabled Foundry agent retrieves the correct troubleshooting article when users type their request. When users speak the same request, the transcript often changes serial numbers and product codes before the agent receives the prompt.
What should you do next?

options.text: D. Add Azure AI Search replicas

Deploy custom speech endpoint is the best answer because the failure happens during speech recognition before the agent receives the prompt. A custom speech model can be trained and deployed to improve recognition accuracy for domain-specific terms, product codes, and specialized vocabulary.
The troubleshooting clue is that typed prompts work correctly. That means the agent instructions, retrieval setup, and function-calling logic are likely not the primary issue. The speech transcript is corrupting the user request, so the fix should target recognition accuracy rather than agent temperature, search scaling, or speech synthesis.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Increase Foundry agent temperature changes generation randomness and creativity. It does not improve speech recognition accuracy. In fact, higher temperature may make responses less predictable. The issue occurs before the agent generates a response, so this is the wrong layer to adjust.
  • C. Enable text-to-speech SSML breaks can improve spoken response pacing or pronunciation. However, SSML affects output synthesis, not input transcription. The problem is that spoken product codes are misrecognized before the agent receives them. Output voice formatting does not fix incorrect input text.
  • D. Add Azure AI Search replicas is plausible when retrieval performance or query throughput is the bottleneck. However, retrieval works correctly when the prompt is typed. Scaling the search index does not correct corrupted transcripts. The root problem is speech recognition accuracy, not retrieval capacity.

question_html:
A generative AI app recently added detailed formatting instructions to its system prompt. Since the change, valid responses often stop mid-sentence even though the model selects the correct information and no safety filter is triggered.
What should the engineer adjust first?

options.text: D. Add semantic ranking to retrieval

explanation_html:
Increasing max_tokens is the best first adjustment because the symptom is response truncation after the prompt became longer and more detailed. The model is selecting the correct information, and the issue is not randomness or unsafe content. The response likely needs a larger output budget to complete the required format.
This question tests operational tuning rather than general model quality. Temperature affects randomness, retrieval affects source selection, and content filtering affects safety enforcement. When answers stop mid-sentence, max_tokens is the generation parameter most directly tied to the maximum response length.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Lower temperature can make responses more focused and less random. It does not directly increase the number of tokens the model is allowed to produce. If the response is being cut off because the output budget is too small, lowering temperature will not reliably fix truncation. It may improve consistency, but not completion length.
  • C. Disable content filtering is not justified because the scenario states no safety filter is triggered. Content filters are important controls for production generative AI systems. Disabling them would weaken safety without addressing the observed issue. This option confuses safety enforcement with response length management.
  • D. Add semantic ranking to retrieval may improve relevance when the app retrieves poor or weakly ranked source content. The scenario says the model selects the correct information, so retrieval quality is not the primary issue. Semantic ranking also does not control how many tokens the model can generate. It is plausible in RAG troubleshooting, but not for mid-sentence truncation.

question_html:
A legal knowledge assistant uses Azure AI Search for grounding. The source documents are long PDFs with headings, sections, tables, and embedded figures. Retrieval quality is poor because chunks often split related section content and lose structural context.

  • Improve chunk quality for RAG grounding.
  • Extract content using layout-aware processing.
  • Avoid building a custom parser first.

Which built-in skill should you add to the enrichment pipeline?
explanation_html:
The Document Layout skill is the best fit because it analyzes document structure and can produce layout-aware text or Markdown output. For RAG grounding, preserving headings, sections, and document structure can improve chunk quality and retrieval relevance.
The scenario is not asking only for text translation, keyword extraction, or embedding generation. It specifically describes poor chunk boundaries caused by loss of layout context. The correct enrichment choice is the skill that understands document layout before indexing and retrieval.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Text Translation skill translates text between languages. It is useful when source content must be normalized into a target language before indexing. However, it does not preserve headings, tables, or section structure for better chunking. It solves a language problem, not a layout-aware enrichment problem.
  • B. Key Phrase Extraction skill identifies important phrases in text. It can enrich searchable fields and improve metadata. However, it does not restructure long PDFs or preserve section relationships. It may add useful tags, but it will not fix chunking that loses layout context.
  • D. Azure OpenAI Embedding skill generates vector embeddings for content during indexing. It is important for vector search and semantic similarity. However, embeddings do not by themselves repair poor document chunking or recover layout structure. If chunks are structurally weak, embedding them can still produce weak retrieval results.

question_html:
You are building a support agent in Microsoft Foundry. The agent must answer questions from uploaded product manuals, create tickets in an external ITSM API, and remember the current troubleshooting context across follow-up turns.
Which design best satisfies the requirements?

options.text: A. Fine-tuned model with Blob uploads
B. Code Interpreter with Cosmos cache
C. File Search, function calling, conversation
D. Azure AI Search index with stateless external orchestration

explanation_html:
File Search, function calling, and a conversation are the strongest fit because each requirement maps to a different agent capability. File Search grounds answers in uploaded documents, function calling lets the agent request an external action that your application executes, and a conversation maintains context across turns.
This is not just a retrieval problem or just an API integration problem. The agent needs knowledge grounding, action execution, and stateful interaction. In AI-103 terms, the best design uses the managed agent runtime capabilities rather than pushing all behavior into fine-tuning, storage, or stateless prompt orchestration.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Fine-tuned model with Blob uploads is plausible because the agent must answer product-specific questions. However, uploading files to storage does not automatically make them retrievable by the agent during a conversation. Fine-tuning is also not the right first choice for frequently changing manuals or support content. The scenario requires grounded retrieval, not model retraining.
  • B. Code Interpreter with Cosmos cache is plausible because Code Interpreter can run Python and Cosmos DB can store data. However, Code Interpreter is designed for sandboxed code execution and analysis, not document-grounded support retrieval or external ITSM function execution. A cache is also not the same as conversation state managed by the agent runtime. This option misses both the retrieval tool and the function-calling pattern.
  • D. Azure AI Search index with stateless external orchestration can support a custom RAG architecture. However, the requirement specifically involves building agents by using Foundry, and stateless orchestration does not satisfy conversation memory. It also leaves function-calling behavior outside the agent capability model. This may work as a custom architecture, but it is not the best Foundry agent design for the stated requirements.

Use function calling with Microsoft Foundry agents
Build with agents, conversations, and responses

question_html:
A mortgage-processing app must analyze an application, payslip, and bank statement together. The pipeline must reason across the documents and validate whether the applicant supplied consistent information.
Which Content Understanding mode should you configure?
explanation_html:
Pro mode is the best choice because the requirement involves reasoning across multiple related documents. Content Understanding pro mode is designed for advanced document scenarios that need multi-step reasoning, cross-file analysis, and validation against related information.
A single-file task is better when each file can be processed independently with straightforward schema extraction. In this scenario, the key requirement is not simply extracting fields from one file, but comparing and validating information across multiple inputs.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Search index is useful for search and retrieval workflows. It can store indexed content and support retrieval-augmented generation scenarios. However, it is not the Content Understanding pipeline mode that performs multi-document extraction and reasoning. It would typically be downstream of extracted or structured content rather than the analyzer mode itself.
  • C. Single-file task is plausible because it is a Content Understanding task type. However, it is optimized for processing one file at a time with straightforward extraction. It does not match the requirement to reason across a mortgage application, payslip, and bank statement together. Choosing it would force separate processing and leave cross-document validation to another component.
  • D. Document Intelligence model can extract fields from forms and documents. It is useful for document processing, but this question specifically asks about configuring Content Understanding pipeline modes. Document Intelligence is not the correct choice for Content Understanding pro mode behavior. It also does not directly represent the multi-input reasoning mode described in the scenario.

question_html:

Snippet

        }
      ],

        {
          "name": "keyPhrases",
          "targetName": "keyPhrases"
        }
      ]
    },

        }
      ]

}

Which skill type should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?
explanation_html:
#Microsoft.Skills.Vision.OcrSkill is correct because the pipeline must extract readable text from normalized images. OCR is the built-in skill designed to detect and extract text from image content so it can be added to enriched documents and indexed.
The snippet already includes a text enrichment skill for key phrases. The missing skill is operating on /document/normalized_images/*, which is the expected context for image-based enrichment. Because the target output is text from images, OCR is the most direct fit.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. #Microsoft.Skills.Text.EntityRecognitionSkill extracts named entities from text. It can identify items such as people, locations, organizations, or other entity categories depending on configuration. However, it expects text input rather than extracting text from an image. It could run after OCR, but it is not the missing image-to-text skill.
  • B. #Microsoft.Skills.Util.ShaperSkill reshapes enriched data into complex structures. It is useful when projected output needs a specific structure for indexing or knowledge storage. However, it does not perform OCR or analyze images. It could organize OCR output later, but it cannot create the image text.
  • C. #Microsoft.Skills.Vision.ImageAnalysisSkill analyzes image content and can produce visual features such as tags or captions. It is plausible because the context is normalized images. However, the required output is readable text from scanned images. OCR is the correct built-in skill when the goal is extracting text from images.

question_html:
An Azure AI Search indexer runs successfully, but the OCR skill produces no extracted text from images embedded in PDFs. The skillset uses an OCR skill with the correct image context, and the source documents contain readable scanned pages.
What should you check first?

options.text: B. Rebuild the semantic ranking profile
D. Add Azure Key Vault references

explanation_html:
You should check whether the indexer is configured to generate normalized images. OCR skills that process embedded images need normalized image content produced during document cracking. Without image extraction and normalization, the skill does not receive the image inputs it expects.
This is a common operational issue in enrichment pipelines. A correctly defined OCR skill is not enough if the indexer configuration does not prepare the image data. The enrichment pipeline must expose the images before the OCR skill can extract text from them.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Rebuilding the semantic ranking profile would affect how search results are ranked at query time. It would not cause the OCR skill to receive normalized images during indexing. The problem occurs before ranking because the enriched image text is missing. This option confuses retrieval ranking with enrichment execution.
  • C. Disabling integrated vectorization does not address image extraction for OCR. Integrated vectorization is related to generating embeddings during indexing or query processing. The issue is that OCR receives no usable image content. Turning off vectorization could reduce retrieval capability without fixing the enrichment problem.
  • D. Adding Azure Key Vault references may help secure credentials or secrets used by an application. It does not configure the indexer to extract embedded images from PDFs. The scenario does not describe a secret retrieval error or authentication failure. It describes a missing enrichment input problem.

Indexer overview
Skillset concepts

question_html:
A marketing team needs an Azure solution that creates short video clips from a text prompt and an uploaded product image.
The reference image should guide the generated video.
Which model capability should you use?

options.text: D. Azure AI Search vector index

explanation_html:
Sora 2 video generation is the correct choice because the workload requires generating video from a text prompt and reference media. The requirement is not to analyze an image, extract text, or ground a chat response; it is to create a new video asset.
In Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI, video generation is handled by a video-generation model such as Sora 2. Reference media can be used to influence the generated output, while the text prompt describes the intended motion, scene, style, or transformation.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. GPT-4o multimodal analysis is plausible because it can reason over images and text. However, the requirement is to generate a video, not interpret a reference image. Multimodal analysis can describe or analyze visual content, but it is not the dedicated video-generation capability. Choosing it would confuse visual understanding with video creation.
  • B. Azure AI Vision OCR is used to extract printed or handwritten text from images. It is useful for reading labels, scanned documents, or screenshots. It does not generate video clips from prompts or reference media. It solves a recognition problem, not a generative video problem.
  • D. Azure AI Search vector index is used for retrieval and grounding over indexed content. It can help a generative app retrieve relevant information, but it does not create media. It would be useful in a RAG workflow, not a video-generation workflow. Using it here would fail the main output requirement.

Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry Models

question_html:
A company is building a RAG pipeline over contracts, scanned appendices, and product diagrams. The search index must include extracted text, OCR output, layout-aware chunks, and a custom compliance classification generated by an internal API.
Problem:
The pipeline must implement enrichment by using custom or built-in skills for text, images, and layout.
Proposed solution:
Create an Azure AI Search skillset with built-in text skills, an OCR skill for normalized images, a Document Layout skill for structure-aware extraction, and a Custom Web API skill for compliance classification.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
Yes, the proposed solution meets the goal because it combines the correct enrichment mechanisms in an Azure AI Search skillset. Built-in text skills handle text enrichment, OCR handles text extraction from images, the Document Layout skill handles layout-aware structure, and the Custom Web API skill integrates custom processing hosted externally.
This solution directly supports retrieval and grounding because the enriched outputs can be mapped into searchable and retrievable index fields. It also uses the right boundary between built-in enrichment and custom enrichment: Microsoft-provided skills for common text, image, and layout processing, and a custom skill when the organization needs proprietary classification logic.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• B. No is incorrect because the proposed solution satisfies each stated enrichment requirement. It includes built-in enrichment for text, OCR for image-based text extraction, layout-aware processing, and a custom skill for internal classification logic. Those are the appropriate Azure AI Search enrichment components for this scenario. Rejecting the solution would ignore that skillsets support both built-in and custom skills in the same indexing pipeline.
Document Layout skill

question_html:
A field-service company is building a voice-enabled Foundry agent. Users must speak equipment fault descriptions, hear the agent’s response, and use a custom speech model because equipment codes are frequently misrecognized by the base recognizer.
Problem:
The current app accepts typed prompts and uses a Foundry agent with retrieval, function-calling, and conversation context. It does not yet support speech input or spoken output.
Proposed solution:
Use Voice Live for the real-time voice agent interface, configure recognition to use the deployed custom speech endpoint, and return the agent response as synthesized speech.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
Yes, the proposed solution meets the goal because it addresses each missing speech requirement. Voice Live supports the real-time voice-agent interface, the deployed custom speech endpoint improves recognition for specialized equipment codes, and synthesized speech provides spoken responses back to the user.
The existing Foundry agent already provides retrieval, function-calling, and conversation context. The proposed solution adds the correct speech modality around that agent instead of replacing the agent architecture. It also handles the custom speech requirement at the recognition layer, where the equipment-code problem actually occurs.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• B. No is incorrect because the proposed solution directly satisfies the stated requirements. It adds speech input, spoken output, and custom speech recognition for specialized vocabulary. It does not ignore the existing Foundry agent capabilities. The design keeps retrieval, function-calling, and conversation context while adding the required speech modality.

question_html:
An image review app must support two modes. Brief mode must return one short description for each image. Detailed mode must return a whole-image description and region-level descriptions. The app also supports galleries containing multiple images.
Problem:
The current app uses Tags for every image and formats the tag list as a sentence.
Proposed solution:
Use Caption for brief mode, Dense Captions for detailed mode, and process each gallery image separately.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
The proposed solution meets the goal because Caption is appropriate for a concise whole-image description, and Dense Captions is appropriate when detailed region-level descriptions are required. Processing each gallery image separately also ensures that every image receives the selected captioning behavior.
This solution also corrects the original design flaw. Tags can identify visual concepts, but they are not the same as natural-language captions. Using the captioning features directly produces outputs that better match both brief and detailed app modes.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• B. No is incorrect because the proposed solution maps the required output modes to the correct captioning features. It also handles multiple images by applying the selected analysis to each image. There is no requirement for a single cross-image narrative comparison. The solution satisfies concise captions, detailed captions, and gallery processing.
What is Image Analysis?

question_html:
A support agent must remember a user’s preferred product line when the user starts a new conversation next month.
The team does not want to retrain the model or rebuild a retrieval index.
Which service capability should you use?
explanation_html:
Agent memory is the best fit when an agent needs continuity across sessions, devices, or workflows. It is designed for long-term memory scenarios such as retaining user preferences and personalization signals beyond a single conversation.
File search and knowledge grounding help the agent retrieve external documents, but they are not intended to store durable user preferences. A thread store can preserve conversation history, but it is not the same as a managed memory capability that the agent can use for long-term continuity.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. File search is used to ground an agent on uploaded or connected documents. It is useful for retrieving information from proprietary files, manuals, or reference material. It does not provide a managed long-term memory layer for remembering user preferences across independent sessions. Using it for personalization would confuse knowledge retrieval with memory.
  • C. Code Interpreter lets an agent run Python code in a sandboxed environment. It is useful for calculations, data analysis, and file-based computation. It does not persist user preferences as managed memory. It also does not solve the requirement to remember a user across future conversations.
  • D. Cosmos DB thread store can be involved in storing conversation thread data in some agent setups. That makes it relevant to persistence, but it is not the correct agent-level memory capability. Persisting raw thread messages is different from giving the agent managed long-term memory. It would also add unnecessary implementation responsibility for this requirement.

Build with agents, conversations, and responses

This is a common AI-103 distinction for computer vision workflows. Captioning, dense captioning, OCR, and tagging may all analyze the same image, but they support different app requirements and should not be treated as interchangeable.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This choice reverses the whole-image and regional captioning features. Dense Captions is too detailed for a single concise whole-image sentence. It also maps Tags to screenshot text extraction, which is incorrect because Tags identify visual concepts. Read is the feature that extracts visible text.
  • B. This choice maps Read to whole-image captioning, which is the wrong output type. Read extracts text rather than producing natural-language image descriptions. It also maps Dense Captions to screenshot text extraction, which confuses captioning with OCR. Caption belongs with the whole-image sentence requirement.

question_html:
You are building an Azure AI Search indexing pipeline for a RAG solution. The pipeline must extract entities from text and OCR content from embedded images during indexing.
Which component should you configure?
explanation_html:
An Azure AI Search skillset is the correct component because skillsets define enrichment steps that run during indexing. Built-in skills can extract entities, key phrases, language, OCR text, image information, and layout-aware content depending on the pipeline design.
This is a core retrieval and grounding design concept. Raw storage holds the source files, but the skillset transforms the content into enriched fields that can be indexed and later retrieved for grounding generative AI responses.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure Blob lifecycle policy manages storage tiering and retention for blob data. It can help control storage costs and data lifecycle behavior. However, it does not extract text, images, entities, or layout information. It is related to source data management, not enrichment during indexing.
  • C. Azure SQL full-text indexer can support text search scenarios over relational data. It is not the Azure AI Search enrichment mechanism that applies built-in or custom AI skills. It also does not handle OCR, image enrichment, or layout-aware document processing in an Azure AI Search skillset. This distractor is plausible because it mentions indexing, but it targets a different search capability.
  • D. Azure Monitor diagnostic settings are used to collect logs and metrics from Azure resources. They help with observability and operational troubleshooting. They do not perform content enrichment or add extracted fields to a search index. Monitoring can show whether an indexer failed, but it is not the enrichment component itself.

question_html:
You are creating a custom analyzer for technical documents. The downstream reasoning pipeline performs better when tables are represented in Markdown rather than HTML.

Snippet

  "analyzerId": "technical-manual-reasoning",
  "description": "Extracts sections, equipment references, warnings, and tables from technical manuals.",

  "config": {

    "enableLayout": true,

Which missing configuration should you use?
explanation_html:
“markdown” is the correct value because the requirement is to represent extracted tables in Markdown for downstream reasoning. In Content Understanding analyzer configuration, tableFormat controls how extracted tables are represented, and Markdown is the better choice for simple text-based processing and LLM-friendly reasoning.
This configuration is especially relevant when documents contain tables that must remain understandable after extraction. The analyzer can preserve table structure in a format that downstream prompts, RAG pipelines, or agent reasoning steps can consume more reliably than flattened text.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. “html” is a supported table format, and it can be useful when the output is intended for web rendering or preserving more complex table structure. However, the scenario specifically says the downstream reasoning pipeline performs better with Markdown. HTML may introduce markup that is less convenient for prompt-based reasoning. It does not match the stated output preference.
  • C. “chartjs” is associated with chart extraction output, not table formatting. It can be relevant when extracting data from charts or graphs. The snippet is configuring tableFormat, so chart output is the wrong setting. This distractor confuses table representation with chart representation.
  • D. “plainText” sounds plausible because downstream systems often consume text. However, it is not the correct value for the tableFormat setting shown in the analyzer configuration. This separation is important for AI-103 implementation questions. Content Understanding is not just OCR; it combines analyzer configuration, document structure, field extraction, and classification or routing into a reusable pipeline for downstream automation and reasoning.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping starts by assigning reusable processing behavior to Markdown output, which is incorrect. Markdown is an output representation, not the analyzer definition itself. It also maps structured business fields to content categories, which are for classification and routing. The final mapping treats the analyzer as the routing mechanism instead of the reusable processing unit.
  • B. This mapping incorrectly makes field schema the overall processing definition. A field schema is important, but it defines the extracted fields rather than the full analyzer configuration. It also maps layout-friendly reasoning text to content categories, which does not preserve document structure. The mapping then assigns analyzer and Markdown output to the wrong responsibilities.
  • C. This mapping confuses classification with analyzer definition. Content categories can route or classify documents, but they are not the reusable analyzer itself. question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OOAvXtRkR0_VHHsLi486CG0AFxyqZVTDWRz1Kfq2KK0/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E2, BR1, and TR1.
The security team confirms that attacks can originate from either an engineer’s prompt or hidden instructions contained in a retrieved supplier bulletin. Both input sources must be evaluated before the model generates a response.
Which Azure AI Content Safety capability should you implement?
explanation_html:
Prompt Shields is designed to detect both user prompt attacks and document attacks. User prompt attacks are adversarial instructions supplied directly by a user, while document attacks are instructions embedded in external content that is added to a model’s context. This directly addresses the two attack paths described by BR1 and TR1.
Pinnacle should analyse the engineer’s prompt and the retrieved passages before sending them to the model. If Prompt Shields identifies an attack, the application can reject the affected input, remove the untrusted document, or route the interaction for additional handling. This control is distinct from evaluating whether a completed response is factually supported.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Groundedness detection evaluates whether a generated response is supported by supplied source material. It is applied to model output rather than detecting instructions intended to hijack the model. A response could be grounded in a malicious retrieved instruction and still be unsafe. Groundedness detection therefore does not satisfy TR1.
C. Protected material detection scans generated text or code for content that matches recognised protected material. Typical examples include known articles, song lyrics, recipes, and source code. It addresses intellectual-property risks rather than prompt injection. It would not identify an instruction hidden in a supplier bulletin.
D. A custom blocklist detects explicitly configured terms or phrases. It can support organisation-specific moderation rules, but an attacker can express equivalent instructions without using a listed phrase. A blocklist does not analyse the structure and intent of prompt attacks. It is therefore insufficient as the primary control required by BR1.

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OOAvXtRkR0_VHHsLi486CG0AFxyqZVTDWRz1Kfq2KK0/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E1, BR2, TR2, and C2.
The selected model supports all deployment types shown in the answer options. Pinnacle has sufficient quota in Australia East and plans to purchase a one-year reservation after production load testing.
Which deployment type should you select?
explanation_html:
Regional Provisioned uses the ProvisionedManaged deployment type. It allocates dedicated provisioned throughput and keeps model processing within the deployment’s specific Azure region. This satisfies Pinnacle’s requirement for reserved capacity, predictable latency, and processing restricted to Australia East.
Provisioned deployments can be billed hourly during testing and can later be covered by an Azure Reservation for a sustained production workload. Pinnacle must size the required Provisioned Throughput Units from its expected prompt size, output size, request rate, and model selection. The available PTU quota must exist in the target region before the deployment is created.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Global Standard can dynamically process requests across the global Azure infrastructure that supports the selected model. It provides pay-as-you-go capacity but does not reserve dedicated throughput for Pinnacle. Latency and available throughput can vary with service demand. It also fails C2 because processing is not restricted to Australia East.
B. Data Zone Standard keeps processing within a Microsoft-defined data zone, such as the Asia-Pacific data zone. It does not guarantee that processing remains specifically in Australia East. Standard deployments also use shared pay-as-you-go capacity rather than reserved PTUs. This option therefore fails both TR2 and C2.
C. Global Provisioned provides reserved PTUs and predictable high throughput. However, its processing scope is global rather than restricted to the resource’s deployment region. A reservation changes the capacity and billing model but does not impose single-region processing. It therefore satisfies BR2 but violates C2.

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OOAvXtRkR0_VHHsLi486CG0AFxyqZVTDWRz1Kfq2KK0/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E3, BR3, TR3, and C4.
The application must process each uploaded inspection recording and return native time-coded insight collections named transcript, ocr, scenes, shots, and keyFrames. Engineers must be able to select a search result and navigate to the corresponding moment in the recording.
Which service should process the videos?

options.text: B. Azure AI Vision Image Analysis

explanation_html:
Azure AI Video Indexer analyses both the visual and audio portions of a media file by running multiple AI models. Its insight output includes time-based transcript entries, OCR results, scenes, shots, keyframes, topics, labels, and other media insights. Each insight includes the time range in which it occurs, which supports navigation to an exact moment.
Shot metadata includes start and end times and the keyframes associated with the shot. OCR insights identify visible text in video frames, while the transcript represents spoken content. Using Video Indexer avoids building separate frame extraction, OCR, transcription, scene-detection, and result-correlation pipelines.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. Azure AI Vision Image Analysis processes individual images rather than complete video and audio files. Pinnacle would need to extract frames, select sampling intervals, run image analysis, and correlate results back to video timestamps. It would not generate the required transcript or native scene and shot collections. This conflicts with C4.
C. Azure AI Speech can transcribe the spoken commentary and return timing information. It does not analyse instrument text displayed in frames or identify scenes, shots, and visual keyframes. Additional computer-vision and video-segmentation services would still be required. Speech alone therefore cannot satisfy TR3.
D. Azure Content Understanding can analyse video and produce structured multimodal output, transcripts, segments, and user-defined fields. However, the question requires the native Video Indexer insight collections and its established scene, shot, keyframe, OCR, and transcript schema. Content Understanding uses an analyzer-based output model rather than the specified Video Indexer collections. It is therefore not the service described by TR3.

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/11bs39zbKg115d484zEVCJ9eMwIcefpqMHboIcYOMAIg/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E4, BR4, TR4, and C3.
Operational requests such as “Schedule a tunnel inspection for Friday” must be processed by the existing conversational language understanding project. Questions such as “What controls are required before entering a confined space?” must be processed by the existing custom question answering project.
Which Azure Language project should you create?
explanation_html:
An orchestration workflow project routes an input utterance to the most appropriate connected language project. It can connect conversational language understanding and custom question answering projects and expose them through a unified prediction interface. This allows Redstone to retain its specialised command and knowledge projects while giving the application one routing endpoint.
The orchestration model is trained to distinguish between the high-level categories represented by the connected projects. After selecting a target, the orchestration workflow forwards the request to that project and returns its result. This avoids building a separate rules engine or language-routing service, satisfying TR4 and C3.
Why the other options are incorrect:
B. Custom text classification assigns one or more labels to a text document. It does not natively forward the request to Redstone’s existing CLU or custom question answering projects. Redstone would need application code to interpret the classification and invoke the appropriate downstream endpoint. That would violate the minimal-routing-code requirement.
C. Conversational language understanding can identify intents and entities for operational commands. It does not automatically route safety questions to the existing custom question answering project. Rebuilding all safety answers as CLU intents would also misuse the service and duplicate the established knowledge base. This option satisfies one branch of E4 but not the complete routing requirement.
D. Custom question answering returns answers grounded in an organisation’s configured knowledge sources. It does not execute the intents and entity extraction required for scheduling inspections or performing operational commands. Using it as the single project would leave the CLU functionality disconnected. It therefore cannot satisfy BR4 by itself.
