question_html:
A company analyzes customer chat messages before storing them.
The solution must detect sentiment, harmful content, and personal data.
Which service combination should you use?

options.text: A. Azure AI Search semantic ranking
B. Azure AI Language and Content Safety
D. Azure Monitor diagnostic logs and metric alerts

explanation_html:
Azure AI Language and Azure AI Content Safety are the best fit because the requirements span both text analytics and moderation. Azure AI Language can detect sentiment and personally identifiable information, while Azure AI Content Safety can detect harmful text categories and severity levels.
This is not just a monitoring or search problem. The application needs direct analysis of text content before storage, so the correct design uses language analysis for meaning and sensitive information, plus content safety analysis for unsafe content.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Search semantic ranking improves relevance for search results, but it does not classify sentiment or detect PII by itself. It is useful when retrieving documents, not when analyzing each chat message for risk categories. It also does not provide safety category severity detection. This option confuses retrieval ranking with text analysis.
  • C. Document Intelligence layout extraction is useful for extracting structure and fields from forms and documents. It is not the best choice for sentiment, tone, harmful-content, or sensitive-content detection in chat messages. It may extract text from files, but it does not replace language and safety analysis. This option targets document extraction rather than text moderation and classification.
  • D. Azure Monitor diagnostic logs and metric alerts help observe runtime health and failures. They do not classify message sentiment, tone, PII, or unsafe content. Monitoring can show whether a service call failed, but it does not perform content analysis. This option confuses operational telemetry with AI text analysis.

Azure AI Language PII detection
Azure AI Content Safety overview

question_html:
A company builds a text analysis workflow for customer support messages. The workflow must detect sentiment, classify business-specific tone, detect harmful safety issues, and redact sensitive personal information before long-term storage.
Problem:
The solution must configure separate detection paths for sentiment, tone, safety issues, and sensitive content.
Proposed solution:
Use Azure AI Language sentiment analysis, an LLM classifier for tone labels, Azure AI Content Safety for harmful text, and Azure AI Language PII detection with redaction.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
The proposed solution meets the goal because it assigns each detection requirement to a suitable capability. Sentiment analysis handles polarity, the LLM classifier handles business-specific tone labels, Content Safety detects harmful text categories, and PII detection identifies and redacts sensitive personal information.
This separation is important because these signals are related but not interchangeable. A message can be negative without being unsafe, unsafe without containing PII, or polite while still including sensitive information. The proposed design supports independent routing, moderation, and storage decisions.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• B. No is incorrect because the proposed solution satisfies every stated requirement. It includes sentiment detection, tone classification, safety issue detection, and sensitive content redaction. It also uses service-specific capabilities rather than relying on a single generic classifier for all tasks. The design is maintainable because each signal can be configured and evaluated separately.

question_html:
You are mapping Azure AI Search ingestion components to their roles in a document-grounded RAG pipeline.
Match the following:
Store source PDFs and scanned files
Drive data extraction and skill execution
Extract text from image-based content
Break content into retrieval-sized passages
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Azure AI Search index
Semantic ranker
Text Split skill
OCR skill

B.
Azure Monitor
Azure Blob Storage
Search indexer
Managed identity

C.
OCR skill
Azure Key Vault
Semantic ranker
Content Safety filter

D.
Azure Blob Storage
Search indexer
OCR skill
Text Split skill

explanation_html:
Azure Blob Storage commonly stores the original source documents for an ingestion pipeline. A Search indexer then pulls content from the data source, runs the attached skillset, and writes enriched output into the target Azure AI Search index.
The OCR skill extracts text from image-based content, while the Text Split skill breaks larger text into smaller chunks that are better suited for embeddings and retrieval. This sequence supports a RAG pipeline by turning raw files into searchable, retrievable passages.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping incorrectly uses the search index as the source file store. The index stores searchable documents and fields after ingestion, not the original PDF repository. It also swaps OCR and Text Split responsibilities. Text Split does not extract text from scanned images, and OCR does not perform chunking for retrieval passages.
  • B. This mapping assigns Azure Monitor as the source document store, which is incorrect. Azure Monitor supports observability, not source document storage for ingestion. It also assigns managed identity to chunking, but managed identity is used for authentication and authorization. The mapping mixes security and monitoring components with ingestion transformation roles.
  • C. This mapping places OCR as the source file store, which is not its role. OCR is a processing skill, not a storage location. Azure Key Vault does not drive indexer execution, and semantic ranker does not perform image text extraction. Content Safety filtering is useful for safety controls, but it does not chunk documents for retrieval.

question_html:
A design team reports that an image-editing workflow changes the entire product photo instead of only the intended background area. The prompt is clear, and the model deployment supports image editing. The team expected only the masked area to change.
What should you check first?

options.text: B. Increase Search replicas and partitions
C. Switch to Azure AI Vision OCR
D. Add semantic ranking to retrieval pipeline

explanation_html:
The first thing to check is the mask configuration, especially whether the mask correctly identifies the editable region. In mask based image editing, the mask determines where the model should apply the requested modification, so an incorrect mask can cause edits to apply too broadly or in the wrong area.
The scenario says the prompt is clear and the deployment supports editing, so the likely issue is not model availability or prompt capability. A poorly formed mask, wrong alpha region, incorrect upload, or inverted target area is the most relevant first troubleshooting step.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Increasing Azure AI Search replicas and partitions improves search capacity and availability. It has no effect on how an image-editing model interprets a mask. This is a retrieval scaling control, not an image-generation configuration fix. It would not prevent the model from changing unmasked product pixels.
  • C. Azure AI Vision OCR extracts text from images and documents. It does not troubleshoot mask boundaries or enforce where generative edits occur. OCR could identify label text in a product image, but it would not preserve the product during an edit. The issue is about edit-region targeting, not text recognition.
  • D. Semantic ranking improves the relevance order of search results in Azure AI Search. It is not part of the image edit request and does not affect masks, pixels, or prompt driven modifications. Adding semantic ranking would help a RAG solution, not a product-image inpainting workflow. This option confuses retrieval quality with visual edit control.

Transparency Note for Azure OpenAI
Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry Models REST API

question_html:
A RAG app is grounded on scanned policy PDFs in Blob Storage. The indexer completes successfully, but user queries return only file names and metadata, not policy text from the scanned pages. The skillset includes OCR, but the skill output is empty.
What should you check first?

options.text: B. Add a semantic ranker profile
D. Assign Search Index Data Reader

explanation_html:
You should first check whether the indexer is configured to generate normalized images. OCR needs image inputs from the enrichment pipeline, and scanned PDFs often require normalized image generation before the OCR skill can extract text.
The indexer succeeding does not guarantee that OCR received usable image content. A pipeline can load metadata successfully while failing to enrich scanned page content if image extraction settings are missing or misconfigured.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. A semantic ranker profile can improve query-time ranking when searchable text already exists. It cannot create text from scanned PDF pages. If the index contains only metadata, semantic ranking has no policy body text to rank. This option treats a content extraction failure as a retrieval ranking issue.
  • C. Increasing vector query topK can return more vector matches from an existing vector index. It does not fix missing OCR output or missing text fields. If scanned content was never extracted and embedded, larger retrieval counts will still return incomplete grounding data. This option changes retrieval breadth rather than ingestion correctness.
  • D. Search Index Data Reader is relevant when a caller needs query access to an index. It does not affect whether the indexer can generate normalized images or whether OCR produces text. The symptom is empty skill output, not a 403 authorization failure from an app query. This option confuses runtime access with enrichment pipeline configuration.

Azure Blob indexer
Debug a skillset

question_html:
An insurance company is building a grounded assistant over claim forms, scanned letters, and PDF policy documents. The assistant must answer questions using searchable passages from both text-based PDFs and image-based documents.
Problem:
The ingestion flow must extract document content, use OCR where needed, chunk the extracted text, create embeddings, and populate a searchable vector index.
Proposed solution:
Use Azure Blob Storage as the document source, configure an Azure AI Search indexer with a skillset that includes OCR, split extracted text into chunks, generate embeddings during indexing, and project chunked content into an Azure AI Search index.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
The proposed solution meets the goal because it includes the core ingestion stages needed for document-grounded RAG. Blob Storage holds the files, the indexer drives ingestion, OCR extracts text from image-based content, chunking prepares passages, and embeddings support vector retrieval.
This design also supports both digital and scanned documents. The key is that text extraction and OCR happen before chunking and vectorization, so the final search index contains retrievable passages that can ground generated answers.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• B. No is incorrect because the proposed design directly addresses each stated ingestion requirement. It includes OCR for scanned and image-based content rather than relying on metadata indexing. It also includes chunking and embeddings, which are necessary for a vector-based RAG retrieval pattern. The final Azure AI Search index provides the searchable grounding layer for the assistant.

You need to map each text analysis requirement to the best capability.
Match the following:
Detect positive, neutral, or negative customer attitude
Classify messages as angry, urgent, polite, or confused
Identify personal data such as phone numbers
Detect harmful text categories and severity
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Sentiment analysis
LLM tone classifier
PII detection
Content Safety text analysis

B.
PII detection
Content Safety text analysis
Sentiment analysis
LLM tone classifier

C.
Content Safety text analysis
PII detection
LLM tone classifier
Sentiment analysis

D.
LLM tone classifier
Sentiment analysis
Content Safety text analysis
PII detection

explanation_html:
Sentiment analysis is the best match for detecting positive, neutral, or negative attitude in text. A custom LLM-based tone classifier is appropriate when the business requires tone labels such as angry, urgent, polite, or confused, especially if those labels are part of a custom routing policy.
PII detection is the right capability for identifying sensitive personal data such as phone numbers, email addresses, and other personal identifiers. Content Safety text analysis is the right capability for detecting harmful content categories and severity levels.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. This mapping puts PII detection on customer attitude, which is incorrect because PII detection finds personal data rather than emotional polarity. It also maps Content Safety to tone classification, but safety categories are not the same as business tone labels. Sentiment analysis does not identify phone numbers or other personal identifiers. The final mapping also assigns the tone classifier to harmful content detection, which is not its primary purpose.
  • C. This mapping starts by assigning Content Safety to sentiment detection. Harm categories and severity do not replace sentiment polarity. It then maps PII detection to tone classification, which would not identify whether a user sounds angry or urgent. The remaining mappings also confuse tone classification with sensitive data and sentiment detection with harm analysis.
  • D. This mapping incorrectly uses an LLM tone classifier for basic sentiment polarity. A tone classifier may support custom labels, but sentiment analysis is the purpose-built capability for positive, neutral, and negative sentiment. Content Safety text analysis is also not used to identify phone numbers as sensitive personal data. PII detection is misplaced because it detects sensitive information, not harmful content categories.

Azure AI Language PII detection
Azure AI Content Safety harm categories

question_html:
A regulated finance agent produced a customer-facing recommendation and then called an internal case-escalation tool. During review, the team can see the final response but cannot determine which retrieved policy version was used or which reviewer approved the tool call.
What should you implement as the best fix?

options.text: B. Regenerate embeddings for all indexed chunks
C. Correlate traces and approval records
D. Disable tool-call logging in production

explanation_html:
Correlating traces and approval records is the best fix because the failure is an auditability gap, not a capacity or retrieval-quality issue. The system needs trace IDs, workflow IDs, provenance metadata, and approval decision IDs that can be joined during review.
This design lets auditors reconstruct the agent run from response generation through retrieval and tool execution. It also connects the runtime action to the human approval decision, which is essential when the agent performs high-impact or regulated operations.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Increasing deployment throughput units might help with rate limits or latency under load. It does not solve missing provenance metadata or missing approval correlation. The problem is not that the model could not process requests fast enough. It is that the review team lacks the evidence chain needed for responsible AI auditing.
  • B. Regenerating embeddings can help when retrieval relevance is poor or the index is stale. It does not prove which policy version was actually retrieved during a historical agent run. Embeddings also do not capture who approved a tool call. This option addresses search quality, not traceability and approval evidence.
  • D. Disabling tool-call logging would make the audit problem worse. Tool-call logs are part of the execution evidence needed to reconstruct agent behavior. Removing them would reduce visibility into high-impact actions and make incident review harder. This conflicts directly with the requirement to audit agentic systems.

Monitor your generative AI applications
Using function tools with human in the loop approvals

question_html:
A team is designing speech-enabled AI workflows for different audio scenarios.
Match each requirement to the best Azure capability.
Match the following:
Low-latency spoken interaction
Recorded-file transcription
Speaker-aware transcript attribution
Structured extraction from audio

A.
Batch transcription
Voice Live API
Text to speech
Azure AI Search

B.

Managed identity
Prompt flow tracing

C.
Text to speech
Speaker diarization
Batch transcription
Azure Key Vault

D.
Voice Live API
Batch transcription
Speaker diarization
Content Understanding audio analyzer

explanation_html:
Voice Live API is the best match for low-latency spoken interaction because it supports real-time voice experiences. Batch transcription is better for recorded files, speaker diarization identifies who spoke during the transcript, and Content Understanding audio analyzers can extract structured information from audio content.
This mapping reflects the AI-103 distinction between live speech interaction, file-based transcription, speaker attribution, and higher-level audio understanding. A strong implementation uses the speech or multimodal capability that matches the timing, output, and reasoning requirement.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping reverses live and recorded-audio requirements. Batch transcription is not the best fit for low-latency spoken interaction, and Voice Live API is not primarily a batch file-processing choice. Text to speech synthesizes audio output rather than identifying speakers in a transcript. Azure AI Search can store or retrieve extracted content, but it does not perform structured audio extraction by itself.
  • B. This mapping uses components that do not directly process speech input. Search semantic ranking improves retrieval relevance, but it does not create a live audio interaction. Document Intelligence layout is for document structure, not audio transcription. Managed identity and tracing support security and observability, but neither performs speaker attribution or audio extraction.
  • C. This mapping confuses output synthesis with input understanding. Text to speech produces spoken output, but the requirement is low-latency spoken input interaction. Speaker diarization is useful for speaker attribution, not recorded-file transcription by itself. Key Vault protects secrets, but it does not extract structured fields from audio.

question_html:
A meeting assistant transcribes multi-speaker calls and sends the transcript to a generative model for action-item reasoning. The action items are often assigned to the wrong person because the transcript does not identify speakers.
What should you enable first?
explanation_html:
Speaker diarization is the best first step because the failure is caused by missing speaker attribution. If the transcript does not identify who said each utterance, the generative model has weak input for reasoning about ownership, responsibility, and action-item assignment.
The issue is not that the model lacks creativity or that the transcript needs to be replaced by vectors. The reasoning quality depends on the structure and accuracy of the audio-derived input, so speaker-aware transcription is the right speech-layer fix.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Increasing model temperature generally increases variation in generated responses. It does not add missing speaker labels to the transcript. The problem is not that the model is too deterministic; it is that the input lacks attribution. Higher temperature could make action-item assignment less stable.
  • C. Replacing the transcript with embeddings would remove the readable conversational evidence the model needs. Embeddings can support semantic retrieval, but they are not a substitute for speaker-attributed transcript text. The model still needs clear utterances and speaker context to reason about ownership. This option solves a search representation problem, not the audio-understanding issue.
  • D. Disabling detailed recognition output would likely reduce useful speech metadata. Detailed output can include richer recognition information that supports downstream processing. Removing detail would not add speaker attribution or improve assignment accuracy. It would make troubleshooting harder rather than fixing the core issue.

Speech to text overview
Speech to text quickstart

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/11bs39zbKg115d484zEVCJ9eMwIcefpqMHboIcYOMAIg/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E1, E2, BR1, and TR1.
The developers already have Reader access at the Foundry resource scope. You must grant the additional permissions required for their assigned development project.
Which role should you assign at the project scope?
explanation_html:
The Foundry User role at the project scope is the least-privilege role for team members who need to build agents and work with existing resources inside a project. Combined with Reader at the Foundry resource scope, it allows developers to use predeployed models and existing connections while working within their assigned project. This is Microsoft’s documented enterprise mapping for project developers.
The role does not grant the elevated resource-level responsibilities reserved for project managers and account owners. Redstone can therefore separate platform administration from project development: administrators continue to create projects, deploy models, and manage shared connections, while developers build and test the solution. This satisfies BR1 without violating TR1.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. Foundry Agent Consumer is intended for users or service principals that interact with published agent endpoints. It does not provide the project-development permissions required to build agents, run development activities, or inspect project assets. The role is suitable for application users rather than the engineering team. Assigning it would leave BR1 unsatisfied.
B. Foundry Project Manager can create projects and perform project-management activities at the Foundry resource scope. Those capabilities exceed the developers’ responsibilities and conflict with TR1. Redstone has already assigned project creation and management to administrators. Granting this role would weaken the intended separation of duties.
C. Foundry Account Owner is an elevated management role for administering the Foundry resource, deploying models, auditing resources, and creating shared connections. These are specifically the operations that developers must not perform. The role would provide substantially more control than BR1 requires. It is therefore not a least-privilege assignment.

question_html:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/11bs39zbKg115d484zEVCJ9eMwIcefpqMHboIcYOMAIg/edit?usp=sharing
You need to satisfy E3, BR2, TR2, and C3.
The permit workflow already performs all required approval, Teams, and SharePoint operations. It uses a request trigger and is hosted in the same Azure subscription and resource group as the Foundry project.
Which agent action should you configure?
explanation_html:
The Azure Logic Apps action allows a Foundry agent to run an eligible Consumption logic app workflow. Redstone can register the existing workflow as an agent action, allowing the model to select the action and provide the inputs required by its request-trigger schema. The workflow then performs its existing approval, Teams, and SharePoint operations.
This design reuses the automation in E3 and avoids creating another API or tool-execution service. Logic Apps also provides workflow run history that Redstone can use to investigate connector, action, or approval failures independently of the agent conversation. The solution therefore meets BR2, TR2, and C3 with minimal additional code.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. A function tool would allow the agent to request execution of an application-defined function. Redstone would remain responsible for hosting code that receives the function request and then invokes or reproduces the approval process. That adds a custom execution layer even though the complete workflow already exists. It therefore conflicts with TR2 and C3.
C. Code Interpreter runs Python in a sandbox for tasks such as calculations, data processing, and file analysis. It is not intended to trigger an enterprise approval workflow or execute Teams and SharePoint connectors. Giving the model Python execution does not make the existing logic app callable. This option addresses a different agent capability.
D. An OpenAPI tool is appropriate when an existing REST API is described by an OpenAPI specification. The case study provides a request-triggered logic app rather than an API contract that Redstone wants the agent to consume directly. Redstone could build and maintain an API wrapper, but TR2 explicitly requires avoiding that additional component. The native Logic Apps action is more direct.

Redstone must extract the following fields from every supplier certificate:

Certificate number
Supplier name
Delivery date
Concrete batch identifier
Test result
Approved quantity

The relative positions, table structures, labels, and number of pages vary significantly between suppliers. The team can label representative examples by identifying the value of each required field.

Which model should you train?
explanation_html:
A custom neural model is designed to extract labelled fields from mixed-type documents with varying layouts. Redstone defines the required schema, assigns appropriate field types, and labels representative values in the training documents. Document Intelligence can then return normalised values such as dates, numbers, and strings, satisfying BR5 and TR5.
Unlike a template model, the custom neural model does not depend on every document having the same basic visual structure or relative field positions. This makes it suitable for certificates from multiple suppliers that express the same business information through different layouts. Microsoft recommends beginning with a custom neural model when it meets the functional requirements.
Why the other options are incorrect:
A. The prebuilt invoice model uses a Microsoft-defined schema for common invoice fields. Supplier delivery certificates are not invoices, and several required fields—such as concrete batch identifier and test result—do not map reliably to that schema. Redstone cannot redefine the prebuilt model’s field set for its certificate process. This option would produce incomplete and inconsistent extraction.
B. A custom template model extracts labelled fields by learning a consistent visual structure and the relative positioning of elements. It is effective when documents have substantially uniform layouts. E5 and C5 explicitly state that supplier layouts and field positions vary significantly. The model would likely require separate training and routing for each stable layout family.
C. A custom classifier identifies the class or type of an input document. It can determine that a file is a supplier certificate or identify which supplier layout it resembles. It does not extract and normalise the required business fields. Redstone would still need one or more extraction models after classification.

question_html:
A production chat application receives intermittent 429 responses during business hours. Logs show the same model deployment is being used successfully outside peak periods. The workload has predictable high-volume traffic and must reduce throttling without relying on unlimited pay-as-you-go bursts.
What should the team do first?

options.text: A. Add Azure AI Search replicas

explanation_html:
Provisioned throughput is the best first action because the symptoms point to model deployment capacity and rate limiting under predictable peak load. Provisioned throughput units provide reserved model processing capacity that can be sized to expected prompt and completion token usage.
Scaling the application tier alone does not increase the model deployment’s available TPM or provisioned model capacity. The team should estimate input and output tokens per minute, compare that with assigned deployment capacity and regional quota, and then select a throughput configuration that supports peak demand.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Adding Azure AI Search replicas can improve search query throughput and availability, but it does not increase the model deployment’s token processing capacity. The issue appears during model calls, not during retrieval or indexing. Search capacity is important in a RAG workload, but it is a different bottleneck. This option confuses retrieval service scaling with model inference throughput.
  • B. Increasing application instance count may help if the app server is CPU-bound or connection-bound, but it can worsen throttling if more app instances send more requests to the same constrained deployment. The logs show successful calls outside peak periods, which points to capacity pressure rather than broken application code. App scaling does not automatically increase TPM or PTU quota. The model deployment capacity must be addressed directly.
  • D. Enabling semantic ranking improves search relevance in Azure AI Search, not model request capacity. It can improve grounding quality for retrieval scenarios, but it will not resolve 429 throttling from model inference. It may also add search-side processing overhead. The scenario is about rate limits, throughput, and predictable traffic volume.

question_html:
A team is building a chatbot that must answer from internal policy documents without fine-tuning the model. The application must retrieve relevant grounding content at query time and pass it to the model.
Steps
Retrieve relevant chunks from the search index
Chunk and enrich source documents
Send grounded context with the user prompt to the model
Generate embeddings and populate the search index
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
The correct order is 2, 4, 1, 3. You first prepare the content by chunking and enriching source documents because retrieval quality depends on clean, searchable units of content. You then generate embeddings and populate the search index so the application has a retrieval layer to query. At runtime, the app retrieves relevant chunks and sends that grounded context with the user prompt to the model.
2 is first because documents must be prepared before they can be indexed effectively. 4 is second because embeddings and index population create the searchable retrieval layer. 1 is third because retrieval happens at query time after the index exists. 3 is last because the model should receive the user prompt together with the retrieved grounding context.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This sequence starts by retrieving chunks before the source documents are chunked and indexed. That is not operationally possible because there is no prepared search index to query yet. It then performs chunking after retrieval, which reverses the data preparation flow. The final generation step is in the right general position, but the pipeline leading to it is invalid.
  • C. This sequence generates embeddings and populates the index before chunking and enrichment. Embeddings should normally be generated from the prepared chunks, not from unprocessed source material. It also retrieves before the content preparation step appears, which makes the retrieval layer inconsistent. The order does not represent a reliable RAG ingestion and query pipeline.
  • D. This sequence starts correctly with chunking, but then retrieves from the index before embeddings and index population occur. Retrieval requires an existing populated index. It also sends grounded context to the model before the index is built. The final indexing step comes too late because indexing must happen before runtime retrieval.

Vector search in Azure AI Search
Hybrid search in Azure AI Search

Hybrid search and vector search solve different parts of the grounding problem. Vector search improves conceptual matching, keyword search preserves exact term matching, and semantic ranking improves the final relevance ordering using language understanding. This combination is common for grounded generation when the application needs high-quality retrieved context.

  • B. top controls how many results are returned, not whether semantic ranking is used. Increasing or setting top can change the number of returned documents, but it does not convert the query into a semantic query. The snippet already includes top: 5. This option confuses result count with ranking configuration.
  • C. scoringProfile can influence scoring for keyword-oriented search scenarios, but it is not the semantic ranking switch. It does not replace the need to specify semantic query behavior with a semantic configuration. A scoring profile is useful for custom boosting, not for enabling semantic reranking over hybrid candidates. The requirement is semantic search configuration, not custom field weighting.

question_html:
An engineering team is building a RAG solution over policy manuals, HR procedures, and product guides. The source files are long, contain headings and tables, and must support both exact keyword matches and conceptual matches.
The solution must:

  • split large documents into useful retrieval units
  • generate embeddings during ingestion
  • search both text and vectors
  • rerank the strongest candidates by semantic meaning
  • tune relevance without retraining the language model

Which design should you implement?

options.text: B. Blob Storage with prompt concatenation
C. Cosmos DB vector container with manual summaries
D. SQL full-text index with model fine-tuning

explanation_html:
Hybrid semantic vector search is the best fit because Azure AI Search can support chunked content, vector fields, hybrid keyword-plus-vector retrieval, semantic ranking, and relevance tuning in one retrieval layer. This directly supports RAG because the model receives grounded chunks selected through search rather than unstructured full documents pasted into a prompt.
The key distinction is that chunking, embeddings, indexing, ranking, and tuning belong in the retrieval pipeline, not in model fine-tuning. Fine-tuning can change model behavior, but it does not replace a searchable grounding system that retrieves current enterprise content at query time.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Blob Storage is useful for storing documents, but it does not provide ranking, semantic reranking, vector search, or retrieval scoring by itself. Prompt concatenation also fails when documents are too large for the model context window. It would increase token cost and reduce precision because the model receives too much irrelevant content.
  • C. Cosmos DB can store application data and can support vector-related scenarios, but this option does not provide the full Azure AI Search retrieval pipeline described in the requirement. Manual summaries would also create freshness and governance problems because they can drift from the source documents. The scenario specifically requires chunking, indexing, semantic ranking, and relevance tuning, which points to Azure AI Search.
  • D. SQL full-text search can help with structured relational data and keyword-based retrieval, but it is not the strongest fit for hybrid vector retrieval and semantic ranking in RAG. Model fine-tuning is also the wrong response to a grounding problem. The requirement is to retrieve relevant content from enterprise documents, not to bake document knowledge into the model.

explanation_html:
Speech to text is used to convert spoken audio into transcripts. Text to speech generates spoken audio from text. Speech translation handles real-time speech-to-text or speech-to-speech translation across languages. Custom Speech is used when recognition quality must be improved for domain-specific vocabulary, accents, product names, or internal terminology.
Voice Live-style interactions are appropriate for low-latency spoken agents because they combine real-time speech input, generative AI interaction, and spoken output in a conversational experience. Audio-capable multimodal models are the right fit when the application needs the model to reason over audio input as part of the prompt context rather than treating the audio only as a transcription source.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping reverses speech to text and text to speech for the first two requirements. It also assigns Custom Speech to live translation, which is incorrect because Custom Speech improves recognition accuracy rather than translating between languages. The mapping assigns speech translation to custom vocabulary improvement, which is the wrong responsibility. It also swaps the low-latency voice-agent and audio-reasoning capabilities.
  • B. This mapping assigns speech translation to call transcription, but translation is not required when the goal is searchable transcripts in the same language. It maps Custom Speech to spoken response generation, which confuses model customization with speech synthesis. It also assigns Voice Live API to acronym recognition improvement, which should be handled through Custom Speech. Several items are close speech capabilities, but they are applied to the wrong workload needs.
  • C. This mapping assigns Custom Speech to general transcription rather than the specific need to improve recognition accuracy for domain terms. It assigns a multimodal model to text-to-speech output generation, but speech synthesis is the direct capability for spoken responses. It also maps speech to text to translation, which misses the cross-language requirement. The mapping places Voice Live API on audio reasoning instead of low-latency spoken agent interaction.

A media team needs an internal workflow for editing marketing images. Designers must upload an original image, mark the region to change, and describe the edit in natural language. The application must avoid modifying unselected areas and must apply built-in safety checks.
Problem:
The team needs targeted prompt driven editing, not general image analysis or OCR.

Deploy a supported GPT-image model, send the original image with a mask and edit prompt to the image edit workflow, validate the mask before submission, and keep Azure OpenAI content filtering enabled.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?
explanation_html:
Correct

Option A. Yes

The proposed solution meets the goal because GPT-image models support prompt-driven image editing using an original image, a mask, and a natural-language editing instruction.

  • Original image: Designers upload the image they want to modify.

  • Mask: Identifies the region targeted for editing, helping preserve unselected areas.

  • Natural-language prompt: Describes the required changes within the selected region.

  • Mask validation: Helps ensure the mask is correctly formatted before submitting the edit request.

  • Content filtering: Keeps Azure OpenAI safety checks enabled to help prevent unsafe image-editing requests or outputs.

This approach supports targeted image editing rather than general image analysis or OCR.

Option B. No

question_html:
You are designing a text analysis pipeline for a support platform. Customer messages arrive from web chat, email, and mobile app feedback.
The pipeline must:

  • classify sentiment for reporting
  • identify tone for escalation routing
  • detect harmful safety issues
  • find sensitive personal data before storage
  • keep the design service-specific and maintainable

Which design best satisfies the requirements?

options.text: A. Translator, language detection, Blob lifecycle policies
B. Azure AI Search, semantic ranker, index projections
C. Sentiment analysis, LLM tone classifier, PII, Content Safety
D. Key Vault logging, Azure Policy, Monitor alerts

explanation_html:
Correct

Option C. Sentiment analysis, LLM tone classifier, PII, Content Safety.

This design uses specialized services and models to address each text analysis requirement.

  • Sentiment analysis: Uses Azure AI Language to classify customer messages as positive, negative, or neutral for reporting.

  • LLM tone classifier: Uses an LLM to identify communication tone, such as frustration, urgency, or dissatisfaction, helping route messages for escalation.

  • PII detection: Uses Azure AI Language Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection to identify sensitive personal information before storing messages.

  • Content Safety: Uses Azure AI Content Safety to detect harmful content and safety risks.

This approach keeps each analysis task separate, making the pipeline easier to maintain and update.

Option A. Translator, language detection, Blob lifecycle policies.

  • Translator converts text between languages.

  • Language detection identifies the language of incoming messages.

  • Blob lifecycle policies manage storage retention and deletion.

  • These services do not provide the required sentiment classification, tone identification, harmful-content detection, or PII detection.

Option B. Azure AI Search, semantic ranker, index projections.

  • Azure AI Search supports indexing, searching, and retrieving relevant information.

  • Semantic ranker improves search result relevance.

  • Index projections help organize indexed content.

  • These capabilities are designed for search and retrieval, not the required sentiment, tone, safety, and sensitive-data analysis.

Option D. Key Vault logging, Azure Policy, Monitor alerts.

  • Azure Key Vault manages secrets, keys, and certificates.

  • Azure Policy enforces resource configuration and compliance requirements.

  • Azure Monitor provides monitoring and alerting.

  • These services support infrastructure governance and monitoring but do not perform the required text analysis tasks.

Which evaluation approach should you use?
explanation_html:
Groundedness and relevance evaluators are the best fit because the app must be assessed for fabrications and response usefulness. Groundedness checks whether generated responses are supported by the provided context, while relevance checks whether the response addresses the user’s query.
This is an evaluation task, not only a runtime blocking or infrastructure monitoring task. Foundry evaluations let you run a test dataset against the model or app and measure quality-related outputs before release.

They also do not measure whether the answer is relevant to the user’s query. This option handles safety control, not full quality evaluation for fabrications and relevance.
  • C. Azure Monitor metrics alerts can help track operational signals such as failures, latency, and resource behavior. Those signals are important in production, but they do not judge whether an answer is fabricated or relevant. A healthy endpoint can still produce poor or ungrounded responses. Monitoring metrics alone would miss the content-quality requirement.
  • D. Prompt token usage dashboard can help analyze cost and token consumption. It does not evaluate whether the generated answer is faithful to source material. It also does not determine whether the response directly answers the user’s question. Token analytics are useful operational data, but they are not the correct evaluation method here.

The key issue is not whether the model can produce fluent text, but whether the answer can be verified from the retrieved material. Mapping both response and context gives the evaluator the generated answer and the source content needed to detect fabrications.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. The query can help some evaluators, but this mapping omits the response and context pairing required to verify grounding. A model name does not provide the evidence used to judge whether the answer was fabricated. This option would not let the evaluator compare claims to source material. It focuses on metadata rather than the actual evaluation inputs.
  • B. The response is included, but the risk category is not the grounding source. Risk categories are more relevant to safety classification than factual support against retrieved documents. Without context, the evaluator cannot determine whether the response is supported by source material. This option confuses safety assessment inputs with groundedness inputs.
  • D. Deployment and index values identify infrastructure elements, not the content being evaluated. They do not contain the generated answer or the retrieved context. The evaluator needs data-row fields that represent the response and supporting material. This mapping would not test fabrication against source evidence.

The solution must meet these requirements:

  • Use private connectivity where possible

  • Support future projects for other departments
  • Minimize custom hosting infrastructure

Which architecture should you recommend?

options.text: A. Public Foundry project with API keys
B. Foundry project with private endpoints
C. App Service with embedded search keys
D. Blob storage with static agent files

explanation_html:
A Foundry project with private endpoints is the strongest fit because it keeps the solution aligned to Foundry infrastructure while supporting network isolation. Foundry organizes workloads through resources and projects, and private endpoints help secure communication to Foundry and connected services.
For an agent-based solution that retrieves from Azure AI Search, private networking and managed identity are important design choices. This approach avoids public exposure and avoids embedding keys in application code while still using the managed Foundry Agent Service platform.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. A public Foundry project with API keys might be faster to configure for a development prototype. However, it does not meet the requirement to avoid public exposure of the management plane, agent endpoint, or connected services. API keys also create secret-management risk and are not the preferred approach for a private, identity-based enterprise design. This option fails both the networking and authentication requirements.
  • C. App Service can host an application front end or orchestration layer, but embedding search keys is a poor infrastructure design for this requirement. It increases secret exposure risk and does not use project managed identity for Search access. It also shifts the design away from a managed Foundry Agent Service pattern. The requirement asks to minimize custom hosting infrastructure, not expand it.
  • D. Blob storage is suitable for holding source documents, but it does not provide agent runtime, tool orchestration, model deployment, or secure retrieval. Static files alone cannot replace Azure AI Search indexing or Foundry Agent Service. This option confuses raw document storage with searchable, grounded agent infrastructure. It is useful when the agent must retrieve documents, chunks, or enterprise knowledge from a search index. It does not directly expose arbitrary REST operations from an existing business system. Using it here would confuse search-based grounding with API action execution.

It can support workflows that need document field extraction or media analysis. It is not the correct tool for calling a secured REST API. The scenario already has an API contract, not unstructured content to analyze.
  • C. Foundry file search tool helps an agent search uploaded files through a vector store. It is appropriate for user-provided documents or proprietary files that need retrieval. You are building a Foundry agent for an insurance operations team. The agent must support several workflows:

  • answer policy questions from an indexed enterprise knowledge base
  • extract claim numbers and repair costs from uploaded PDFs
  • call a claims status API with managed authentication
  • run custom validation logic before submitting a settlement

Which tool combination best satisfies the requirements?

options.text: A. File search, Blob Storage, Azure Key Vault, Prompt flow
B. Content Understanding, Azure AI Search, OpenAPI, Azure Functions
C. Azure AI Language, Cosmos DB, Service Bus, Content Safety
D. Document Intelligence, Azure SQL, API Management, Azure Monitor

explanation_html:
Content Understanding is the best fit for extracting structured information from uploaded PDFs, while Azure AI Search is the right fit for grounding answers in an indexed enterprise knowledge base. OpenAPI supports calling the claims status API through a defined API schema, and Azure Functions can host custom validation logic that the agent invokes as a tool.
This combination separates retrieval, extraction, API action, and custom business logic into the correct Foundry-aligned components. That is important in AI-103 scenarios because the best answer is usually not one generic tool, but the correct set of tools mapped to specific workload responsibilities.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. File search can help with uploaded files, but it does not fully cover structured extraction from claim PDFs. Blob Storage can store documents but does not provide agent retrieval or field extraction by itself. Azure Key Vault secures secrets, but it is not an agent action tool. Prompt flow can orchestrate evaluation or flows, but this option misses the best API and custom-function integration choices.
  • C. Azure AI Language can analyze text for language tasks, but it is not the best service for structured claim extraction from PDFs. Cosmos DB can store application data, but it is not a grounding tool by itself. Service Bus supports messaging, not direct agent API schema invocation. Content Safety is useful for moderation, but the scenario does not ask for harmful-content detection.
  • D. Document Intelligence is plausible for document extraction, but this option does not map the remaining requirements cleanly. Azure SQL is a database, not a search-grounding tool for indexed knowledge retrieval. API Management can front APIs, but the agent still needs a tool integration pattern to call them. Azure Monitor provides observability, not custom validation logic for settlement submission.

options.text: B. Azure AI Search vector index

explanation_html:
Azure AI Video Indexer is the best next step because the workload is video insight extraction, not isolated still-image processing. It is designed to analyze video and extract insights such as objects, people, scenes, and timing information that reviewers can use.
Sending every frame to Image Analysis can work in limited custom scenarios, but it often creates unnecessary cost and operational complexity. For an AI-103 design decision, the key is choosing a video-aware service when the requirement includes object detection over a video timeline.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Azure AI Search vector indexes are useful for retrieval, semantic search, and similarity search scenarios. They do not directly analyze video files and produce object timestamps. A vector index could store extracted metadata after processing, but it is not the video-analysis component itself. This option solves a retrieval problem, not a video understanding problem.
  • C. Document Intelligence layout models are designed to extract structure from documents, forms, and document-like files. They are not intended for detecting objects across moving video content. Layout extraction would not provide reviewer-friendly object timelines. This distractor is plausible only if the input were scanned documents rather than videos.
  • D. Image Analysis smart crop identifies a useful crop region for an image. It does not analyze long videos or generate object appearances over time. It also would not solve the workflow’s cost and timestamp problems. Smart crop is a presentation feature, not a video insight pipeline.

options.text: A. Azure AI Search indexer schedule

Microsoft Foundry evaluators are the best fit because they are designed to assess the quality, safety, and reliability of generative AI responses. They can evaluate dimensions such as groundedness, relevance, coherence, fluency, and safety, which directly supports model reflection and self-critique before release.
This is operationally stronger than relying on manual review alone because evaluations can be run repeatedly against test datasets and integrated into release workflows. The key exam distinction is that search, secrets management, and telemetry settings support the application, but evaluators measure whether the model output meets expected quality and safety criteria.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Search indexer schedules control when content is crawled and refreshed into a search index. That can improve retrieval freshness for RAG workloads, but it does not evaluate generated answers. It also does not implement a self-critique loop or score answer quality. It is a supporting data-ingestion feature, not an evaluation component.
  • C. Azure Key Vault access policies help control access to secrets, keys, and certificates. This is important for secure operations, but it does not assess model output quality. It cannot determine whether an answer is grounded, relevant, or safe. It solves a security-management problem rather than a generative AI evaluation problem.
  • D. Application Insights sampling settings affect how much telemetry is collected. They can reduce monitoring volume and cost, but they do not provide reflection-style scoring of model outputs. Sampling may help observability scale, but it is not the mechanism that evaluates response quality. It would not satisfy the requirement to review generated answers before prompt promotion.

question_html:
A team added a self-critique prompt that asks the model to review its own answer before returning it. After release, users still receive confident but unsupported responses from a RAG assistant. Evaluation results show low groundedness but acceptable fluency.
What should the team do next?

options.text: A. Gate release on groundedness evaluation
B. Increase model temperature for critique
C. Replace retrieval with token counting
D. Disable context in evaluation data

explanation_html:
The best next step is to gate release on groundedness evaluation because the observed issue is unsupported responses, not poor wording or fluency. A self-critique prompt can help, but it is not a reliable operational control unless measured against grounding metrics and used as a release criterion.
Groundedness evaluation checks whether generated answers are supported by the provided context. For a RAG assistant, this is a more relevant quality signal than fluency because a polished answer can still be wrong or unsupported.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Increasing temperature generally increases variability and creativity. That can make unsupported responses worse in a grounded RAG scenario. It does not address the evaluation finding that answers are not sufficiently supported by source context. The issue requires a grounding control, not more generative randomness.
  • C. Token counting can help monitor cost, context length, and prompt size. It does not verify whether the answer is supported by retrieved evidence. Replacing retrieval with token counting would remove the grounding mechanism entirely. This would make the system less capable of producing source-backed answers.
  • D. Disabling context in evaluation data would prevent groundedness evaluation from working correctly. Groundedness requires comparing the response to the source context. Removing the context would make the metric less meaningful or unusable. This would hide the problem rather than fix it.

Approval workflows are the correct control when a risky or high-impact action must pause until a human or business process approves it. Together, these three controls create a practical audit chain: what happened, what evidence was used, and who approved sensitive execution.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This choice incorrectly maps tool-call timing to an approval workflow. Approval workflows can record decisions, but they do not replace runtime trace logging. It also maps retrieved document IDs to trace logging instead of provenance metadata. The result would blur execution telemetry and source lineage, which weakens audit review.
  • B. This choice treats provenance metadata as if it captures tool execution. Provenance metadata explains source lineage, not the sequence and timing of agent actions. It also maps risky-action review to trace logging, which records activity but does not enforce a pause for approval. The mappings confuse evidence capture with workflow control.
  • C. This choice correctly maps trace logging and approval workflow in two places, but it uses Azure Key Vault for retrieved document IDs. question_html:
You are building a RAG pipeline for product manuals stored as PDFs and scanned image files. The app must retrieve text from both digital documents and image-based pages before chunking and embedding.
Which component should you include in the ingestion flow?

options.text: A. Azure AI Search semantic ranker
D. Azure Key Vault secret rotation

explanation_html:
A skillset with an OCR skill is the correct choice because the ingestion flow must extract text from image-based content before it can be indexed and retrieved. OCR converts text inside images or scanned pages into searchable text that can later be chunked, embedded, and stored in an Azure AI Search index.
For RAG, the ingestion pipeline must prepare source content before retrieval can work well. If scanned content is not converted into text, the model may receive incomplete grounding context even if the files were successfully indexed as blobs.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Search semantic ranker improves ranking of already indexed searchable text. It does not extract text from scanned pages or image files. If OCR is missing, semantic ranking has little useful text to rank for those documents. This option is plausible in a RAG retrieval design, but it does not solve the ingestion requirement.
  • C. Azure Monitor metrics alerts help detect operational issues such as failures, latency, and resource behavior. They do not transform document content or extract text from images. Monitoring can help operate the pipeline, but it cannot create searchable text from scanned files. This option addresses observability rather than ingestion enrichment.
  • D. Azure Key Vault secret rotation helps manage secrets securely. It is important for production security, especially when keys or connection strings are involved. However, it does not perform OCR, chunking, vectorization, or indexing. This option confuses secure operations with content extraction.

AI enrichment in Azure AI Search

question_html:
A retail design app must replace the background behind a product while preserving the product itself. The user uploads the original image, identifies the editable area, and provides a text instruction.
Which workflow should you configure?

options.text: D. Azure AI Search semantic ranker

explanation_html:
The Image edit API is the correct workflow because the requirement is to modify an existing image by using the original image, a target area, and a text instruction. This aligns with image-editing workflows such as inpainting and mask based edits, where the model changes a selected region while preserving surrounding content.
OCR, video indexing, and search ranking do not perform targeted visual edits. They can analyze text, video, or retrieval relevance, but they do not generate revised pixels in a specified image region.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Vision OCR is useful for extracting printed or handwritten text from images. It does not perform prompt driven visual modifications or replace selected image regions. OCR could help analyze an image before editing, but it is not the editing workflow itself. The scenario requires generating new visual content inside a target area.
  • B. Azure AI Video Indexer is designed for video analysis, indexing, transcripts, insights, and search across video content. It does not provide the image inpainting workflow needed to modify a still product image. Even if the source media were video, indexing would analyze content rather than generate edited pixels. This option confuses media analysis with generative editing.
  • D. Azure AI Search semantic ranker improves the ordering of search results based on semantic relevance. It does not edit images, apply masks, or interpret visual prompt modifications. Search could support metadata retrieval in a larger app, but it cannot replace the background in a product image. The required capability is generative image editing, not retrieval ranking.

question_html:

explanation_html:
A vision-enabled chat model is required because the application must answer a question based on visible image content. The model needs to accept both the image and the user’s question so it can reason over visual evidence instead of relying on text-only context.
Text embeddings can help with retrieval, but they do not directly inspect pixels, screenshots, charts, or visual layouts. For visual question answering, the solution needs multimodal input handling, usually combining the image, prompt instructions, and any retrieved supporting context.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Text embeddings are useful for semantic retrieval over text or text representations of content. They can support a RAG pipeline, but they do not directly answer questions from image pixels. If the screenshot has not been converted into useful text or visual features, embeddings alone miss the visual evidence. This option confuses retrieval representation with multimodal reasoning.
  • C. Speech recognition model is used to convert spoken audio into text. It is relevant for audio transcription scenarios, not visual evidence grounding. The scenario involves an uploaded screenshot rather than spoken input. This option targets the wrong modality.
  • D. Document translation model is used to translate text between languages. It does not analyze screenshots for visible alerts or explain image evidence. Translation could be useful after OCR if the image contains foreign-language text, but it would not provide visual question answering by itself. This option solves a language problem, not a multimodal understanding problem.

question_html:
You are designing a support assistant for field engineers. Users upload photos of equipment panels and ask troubleshooting questions.
The solution must:

  • answer questions from visible labels, indicators, and layouts
  • retrieve related maintenance procedures
  • cite supporting source documents when available

D. Image captions with Key Vault rotation

A vision model with Azure AI Search grounding best satisfies the requirements because the system must reason over the uploaded image and retrieve supporting maintenance content. Azure AI Search can support RAG patterns that ground generated answers in indexed enterprise content, while the vision-capable model handles the visual question-answering part.
This design also supports a safer answer policy: the assistant can use image evidence and retrieved procedures as grounding sources, then avoid unsupported responses when evidence is missing. Multimodal search and RAG are especially relevant when visual content such as charts, screenshots, forms, and diagrams must be connected to answer generation.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. OCR results can be useful when images contain readable text, but Blob lifecycle rules only manage storage tiering and retention. They do not provide visual reasoning, retrieval grounding, or answer generation. OCR alone may also miss non-textual visual evidence such as indicator positions or equipment layout. This option combines a partial extraction step with an unrelated storage-management feature.
  • C. Translator can help with language conversion, and Azure SQL query logging can support operational audit scenarios. Neither component provides visual question answering from uploaded photos. SQL logging also does not create a grounding layer for maintenance procedures. This option focuses on language and logging rather than multimodal evidence grounding.
  • D. Image captions can summarize visual content, and Key Vault rotation can improve secret hygiene. However, this combination does not retrieve maintenance procedures or support grounded question answering with cited sources. Captions alone may oversimplify the visual evidence and lose details needed for troubleshooting. Key Vault rotation is a security practice, not a multimodal QA architecture.

Image-to-image

Text-to-image
Inpainting

explanation_html:
Text-to-image is used when the input is a written prompt and the expected output is a new generated image. Inpainting is the correct match for replacing a selected area because it uses a mask to focus the edit on part of an existing image.
Image-to-image is the broader prompt driven modification pattern where an uploaded image and text instruction guide the generated output. Content filtering is the correct control for blocking harmful or policy-violating image-generation requests before returning output.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. This mapping incorrectly assigns inpainting to new image generation from text. Inpainting requires an existing image and a target region, not just a written description. It also assigns content filtering to image modification, which confuses safety control with editing behavior. The mapping mixes generation, editing, and safety responsibilities.
  • C. This mapping uses analysis and retrieval capabilities rather than generative editing workflows. OCR extracts text, Video Indexer analyzes video content, semantic ranking improves search relevance, and vector search retrieves similar items. None of these mappings describe targeted inpainting or prompt driven image modification. This option would be plausible only for a search or media-analysis solution.
  • D. This mapping assigns image-to-image to pure text-to-image generation, which is not the cleanest match. It also assigns content filtering to targeted area replacement, but content filtering does not perform pixel edits. Text-to-image is placed against uploaded-image modification, which reverses the input pattern. Inpainting is incorrectly used for blocking harmful requests rather than mask based editing.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Batch transcription is useful for processing recorded audio files asynchronously. It is a strong option for archives, call recordings, or media files that do not require immediate response.   • C. Document Intelligence layout extracts structure from documents such as forms, invoices, and pages. It is not intended to process live speech or reason over audio input. It may be relevant if the app processed scanned documents, but no document layout requirement exists here. This option targets the wrong modality.
  • D. Search semantic ranking improves the ordering of search results in retrieval scenarios. It can support grounding after text is available, but it does not capture or process live audio input. It also does not create a voice conversation loop by itself. This option is a retrieval enhancement, not a speech solution.

question_html:
You are preparing a procurement assistant for a controlled pilot. The assistant answers questions from contract PDFs, summarizes supplier terms, and recommends next actions.
The release board requires evidence that the app has been tested for:

  • answers unsupported by source documents
  • poor response quality
  • unsafe generated content
  • repeatable scoring against a fixed test dataset
  • comparison between two model deployments

Which approach should you recommend?

options.text: B. Azure AI Search semantic ranker
C. Manual review of random chats
D. Foundry evaluation with built-in evaluators

explanation_html:
Foundry evaluation with built-in evaluators is the strongest choice because it supports repeatable testing against datasets and can measure quality, RAG behavior, and safety. It can be used to compare model or application outputs before release rather than relying on subjective sampling.
The requirements include multiple evaluation dimensions: fabrication detection, quality, safety, and comparison between deployments. Built-in evaluators in Foundry are designed for this kind of structured pre-production assessment.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Application Insights availability tests can confirm that an endpoint responds and meets basic availability expectations. They do not determine whether the assistant fabricated a supplier clause or summarized a contract incorrectly. They also do not provide built-in model-quality or safety scoring. This option addresses operational uptime, not generative AI evaluation quality.
  • B. Azure AI Search semantic ranker can improve the ranking of retrieved search results. It is valuable in a RAG pipeline, especially when retrieval quality affects grounding. However, it is not an evaluation framework for measuring generated output quality or safety. It also does not compare model deployments against a fixed test dataset by itself.
  • C. Manual review of random chats can provide useful human feedback, but it is not the best answer for the stated requirements. Random review is hard to reproduce and does not provide consistent evaluator scoring across model deployments. It can miss edge cases and safety risks if the sampled conversations are too narrow. Manual review may supplement evaluation, but it should not replace structured Foundry evaluation.

Object detection is the best fit because it identifies physical objects in an image and returns bounding box coordinates. The bounding boxes let the application locate where each detected object appears, not just describe the overall image.
This distinction matters on AI-103 because image tagging can identify concepts in an image, but it does not provide the same localized object-coordinate output. Smart crop finds a useful crop region, and OCR extracts text, but neither satisfies the requirement to locate individual shelf items.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Smart crop is useful when you need a representative area of an image for thumbnail generation. It can return a crop region, but it is not designed to label and locate multiple objects. It would not identify each shelf item as a separate detected object. This makes it too limited for inventory-style object localization.
  • B. Image tagging can return descriptive tags for image content, such as objects, scenery, or actions. However, tags are not the same as localized object detections with bounding boxes. A tag may tell you an object appears somewhere in the image, but not where it appears. The scenario specifically needs labels with pixel coordinates.
  • D. Read OCR extracts printed or handwritten text from an image. It is useful for signs, labels, documents, and visible text, but it does not locate general objects. Even if shelf labels contain text, OCR would not identify the actual products as objects. The requirement is object localization, not text extraction.

question_html:
You are building a RAG ingestion flow for scanned operating manuals. The manuals contain images, headings, tables, and handwritten notes.
Steps

Extract OCR text and document layout.
Split normalized content into chunks.
Index text, metadata, and vectors.
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
2 is first because the pipeline must extract readable text and layout from scanned documents before it can create meaningful retrieval units. OCR and layout extraction make the content usable for downstream chunking.
3 is second because the normalized text and structure should be split into chunks that fit retrieval and embedding limits. 1 is third because embeddings are generated for those chunks. 4 is last because the search index should store the final text, metadata, and vector fields for retrieval.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This sequence chunks before OCR and layout extraction. That fails for scanned manuals because the raw pages may not yet contain usable text. It also creates embeddings before the content has been properly normalized.
  • C. This sequence generates embeddings before extraction and chunking. Embeddings should represent final retrieval chunks, not raw or incomplete source files. Indexing before the content pipeline runs would produce weak or missing grounding data.
  • D. This sequence indexes before extraction, chunking, and embedding. An index should receive processed content and vectors, not unprocessed files. It also leaves embedding generation until after indexing, which prevents the vector fields from being available during retrieval.
