This option confuses visual enrichment with structured business-field extraction.
  • D. Fixed-size Markdown chunking can be useful for RAG ingestion and text segmentation. It does not by itself guarantee structured JSON fields for automation. Chunked Markdown may help retrieval, but it is weaker for deterministic validation and routing. The requirement emphasizes clean structured output rather than chunk size.

Content Understanding best practices
Content Understanding analyzer reference

question_html: In Microsoft Foundry, a _____ is the organizing workspace that groups agents, evaluations, files, deployments, indexes, tracing, and datasets for an AI application lifecycle.
explanation_html:
A project is the Foundry workspace used to organize the assets involved in building and operating AI applications. This includes agents, evaluations, files, deployments, indexes, traces, and datasets associated with a development effort.
A resource group or storage container can hold Azure resources or data, but those are Azure infrastructure constructs rather than the Foundry project-level workspace. The exam-relevant distinction is that Foundry projects organize AI development artifacts and lifecycle assets inside the Foundry experience.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. The model catalog helps users discover and select models. It does not organize the full lifecycle of agents, evaluations, indexes, files, datasets, and tracing. A model catalog is model-selection focused. The question asks for the workspace construct that groups many project assets.
  • C. A resource group organizes Azure resources for management, billing, deployment, and access control. It is not the Foundry project workspace that directly organizes agents, evaluations, files, deployments, indexes, tracing, and datasets. A Foundry project may depend on Azure resources in a resource group. That does not make the resource group the Foundry-level organizing unit.
  • D. A storage container stores blobs such as files or data artifacts. It cannot organize agents, evaluations, model deployments, indexes, and tracing as a Foundry project does. It may support data storage behind a solution. It is too narrow for the lifecycle organization described in the stem.

Azure AI Projects client library for Python
Azure AI Projects client library for .NET

question_html:
A field-service app lets technicians upload photos of damaged equipment and ask natural-language questions about visible issues. The answer must use both the image and the technician’s text prompt.
Which model capability should the solution use?
explanation_html:
A vision-enabled chat model is the best fit because the solution must combine image input with a natural-language question. The requirement is not merely to generate a caption or create embeddings; it is to reason over visual content in the context of a user’s prompt.
Multimodal models can accept image and text inputs together and return text responses grounded in the visual evidence. This supports interactive troubleshooting scenarios where the same image may need different answers depending on the technician’s question.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. A text embedding model converts text into vector representations for search, clustering, or similarity. It does not analyze image pixels directly. It could support retrieval over text descriptions, but it would not answer questions grounded in the uploaded photo. This option confuses retrieval infrastructure with multimodal reasoning.
  • B. A speech recognition model converts spoken audio into text. It is useful if the technician records a voice note, but it does not analyze visual equipment damage. The scenario requires image understanding plus text prompting. Speech recognition addresses a different modality.
  • C. An image captioning model can describe the overall image content. However, captioning is not the same as answering arbitrary user questions about visual evidence. The technician may ask targeted questions about damage, safety, or visible parts. A vision-enabled chat model is more appropriate for prompt-driven visual reasoning.

Get started with multimodal chat apps
Foundry Models overview

question_html:
A publishing platform needs automatically generated descriptions for uploaded product images. The descriptions must support screen-reader accessibility and include enough detail for users who cannot see the image.
Which Azure AI capability should be configured?

options.text: A. Image captions and dense captions

explanation_html:
Image captions and dense captions are the strongest fit because the goal is to produce human-readable descriptions of image content. Dense captions can add localized detail about regions within an image, which is useful when accessibility descriptions need more than a single generic sentence.
Accessibility-aligned image descriptions should communicate meaningful visual context, not just detect objects or extract text. Captioning capabilities are therefore closer to the required output than raw bounding boxes, OCR, or identity-oriented face features.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. Face verification and identification are identity-focused capabilities. They do not produce accessibility descriptions of product images. They may also introduce privacy and responsible AI concerns if used unnecessarily. The requirement is descriptive accessibility, not recognizing people.
  • C. OCR with language detection extracts readable text from images and identifies language. That can help if the product image includes labels or packaging text. It does not provide a complete visual description of objects, layout, appearance, and context. It is a supporting feature, not the main captioning capability.
  • D. Object detection bounding boxes identify and locate objects. This can be useful for machine processing or region-level metadata. However, bounding boxes are not the same as natural-language alt text. The platform needs user-facing descriptions rather than coordinates and object labels.

Image Analysis quickstart
Language support for Azure Vision

question_html:
A finance analyst uploads CSV files and asks an assistant to calculate trends, generate charts, and iteratively inspect intermediate results. The assistant must run Python in a controlled execution environment rather than relying only on text generation.
Which capability should be included?
explanation_html:
The Code Interpreter tool is the best fit because the requirement is to execute Python over uploaded data and generate analytical outputs such as calculations and charts. A model can reason about the user’s request, but the tool provides the execution environment needed to perform the data analysis reliably.
This is a common AI-103 distinction: not every task is solved by choosing a larger model. Foundry Tools extend an agent or application with specific capabilities such as code execution, retrieval, or external tool use. For this workload, the correct design is model plus tool, not a different model category alone.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. A large language model deployment can reason about the request and produce explanations, but it does not by itself execute Python against uploaded CSV files. It may generate code, but generated code is not the same as executing code in a managed sandbox. The requirement specifically asks for iterative calculations and charts from data. That makes a tool capability necessary.
  • B. A multimodal model deployment is useful when inputs include images, audio, video, or other non-text modalities. The scenario is about CSV analysis and Python execution, not visual or multimodal understanding. A multimodal model would add capability that is not required for the workload. It still would not replace the need for a code execution environment.
  • C. A small language model deployment can be useful for narrow, low-latency, or lower-cost text tasks. It is not the best choice for interactive data analysis that requires running Python. Even if it can classify or summarize text efficiently, it does not provide sandboxed execution. The key requirement is computational tool use, not smaller model size.

Agent tools overview for Foundry Agent Service
Microsoft Foundry Models overview

question_html:
A team is adding safety checks to a generative AI application that accepts text, images, retrieved documents, and user prompts.
Match each requirement to the most appropriate Azure AI Content Safety capability.
Detect harmful text and image content
Detect jailbreak and prompt-injection attempts
Check whether generated answers are supported by sources
Detect protected text or code material
Check whether responses follow the assigned task
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Text and image moderation
Prompt Shields
Groundedness detection
Protected material detection
Task adherence checks

B.
Prompt Shields
Groundedness detection
Protected material detection
Task adherence checks
Text and image moderation

C.
Groundedness detection
Text and image moderation
Prompt Shields
Task adherence checks
Protected material detection

D.
Protected material detection
Task adherence checks
Text and image moderation
Prompt Shields
Groundedness detection

explanation_html:
Choice A correctly maps each responsible AI requirement to the Content Safety capability that addresses it. Text and image moderation detects harmful content, Prompt Shields help detect adversarial prompt attacks, groundedness detection checks support from grounding sources, protected material detection identifies protected content, and task adherence checks whether the response stays aligned to the assigned task.
The key exam distinction is that these controls are safety and quality gates, not retrieval, identity, or indexing controls. They can be used together in a production AI application, but each one targets a different risk surface.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. This option incorrectly treats Prompt Shields as general harmful-content moderation. Prompt Shields focus on jailbreak and prompt-injection style attacks, not general text and image harm categories. It also maps groundedness to prompt-attack detection, which confuses factual support with adversarial input protection.
  • C. This option starts by mapping groundedness detection to harmful content detection, which is the wrong control. Groundedness checks whether generated output is supported by grounding data, not whether the text or image is harmful. The option also assigns Prompt Shields to source support, which misses their role in detecting prompt attacks.
  • D. This option misplaces almost every safety capability. Protected material detection does not replace moderation for harmful text and images. Task adherence does not detect jailbreak attacks, and groundedness detection does not check whether an answer follows the assigned task.

Prompt Shields in Azure AI Content Safety

question_html:
A team is choosing Foundry model types for four workloads before creating deployments and consuming them from application code.
Match the following:
Contract summarization with multi-step reasoning
High-volume intent classification with tight cost controls
Python code migration and refactoring assistance
Product inspection from images and text prompts
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Small language model
Multimodal model
Large language model
Code model

B.
Code model
Large language model
Multimodal model
Small language model

C.
Large language model
Small language model
Code model
Multimodal model

D.
Multimodal model
Code model
Small language model
Large language model

explanation_html:
A large language model is the strongest fit for contract summarization that requires reasoning across complex text. A small language model is better for high-volume classification where the task is narrow, latency-sensitive, and cost-sensitive. A code model is designed for code generation, refactoring, explanation, or migration tasks. A multimodal model is the appropriate choice when the input includes both images and text.
In Microsoft Foundry, the model catalog is used to select models with different capabilities, deployment options, and regional availability. After choosing the correct model category, you deploy the selected model and consume it from the application by using the deployment endpoint and the deployment-specific configuration. The exam focus is not just recognizing model names, but matching model capabilities to workload shape.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping assigns a small language model to contract summarization, which is likely insufficient for multi-step reasoning over complex legal text. It also assigns a multimodal model to high-volume intent classification, which adds unnecessary capability and cost for a text-only classification task. The code model is incorrectly mapped to product inspection from images and text, which requires multimodal input handling. The mapping confuses model capability with general AI usefulness.
  • B. This mapping assigns a code model to contract summarization, but code models are specialized for programming-related tasks rather than legal reasoning over natural language documents. It also assigns a large language model to a narrow high-volume classification workload, which may work but is not the best cost and latency fit. The multimodal model is incorrectly mapped to code migration, where image understanding is irrelevant. The small language model is incorrectly used for image-and-text inspection.
  • D. This mapping assigns a multimodal model to contract summarization even though the task is text-only and reasoning-heavy. It assigns a code model to high-volume classification, which is the wrong specialization. It also assigns a small language model to code migration, where code-specific capabilities are more relevant. The large language model is mapped to product inspection, but multimodal understanding is the key requirement there.

Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models
Work with Azure OpenAI models in Microsoft Foundry

question_html:
A claims-processing app receives photos of vehicle damage. Adjusters ask questions such as “Is the rear bumper cracked?” and “Which visible panel appears most damaged?” The solution must answer only from visible image evidence and avoid inventing unseen details.
Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: A. OCR extraction followed by keyword matching
B. Image captioning stored in Blob Storage
C. Vision-enabled chat with grounding instruction
D. Text embeddings over adjuster questions

explanation_html:
Vision-enabled chat with a grounding instruction is the best design because the application must answer natural-language questions using image evidence. The model needs to inspect the uploaded image and respond to the specific question while being instructed not to infer details that are not visible.
This is a visual question answering pattern rather than a general captioning or document extraction problem. Strong system instructions should constrain the answer to visible evidence, require uncertainty when evidence is insufficient, and reduce unsupported claims.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. OCR extraction followed by keyword matching can extract visible text, such as license plates or labels, where appropriate. It cannot reliably assess bumper cracks, panels, or vehicle damage from visual features. Keyword matching also lacks the visual reasoning needed for adjuster questions. This option is plausible only if the image evidence is mostly text.
  • B. Image captioning stored in Blob Storage creates a general image description. It does not allow the adjuster to ask targeted follow-up questions grounded in the same image. A caption might omit the exact detail needed for the claim decision. Storage is also not an answering mechanism.
  • D. Text embeddings over adjuster questions can support semantic similarity or retrieval. They do not analyze the vehicle photo itself. This option might help route common question types, but it cannot determine whether the rear bumper is visibly cracked. It confuses text retrieval with visual evidence analysis.

Prompt engineering techniques
Responsible AI for Azure workloads

question_html:
A RAG application begins returning outdated and weakly relevant policy answers after a document refresh. The Azure AI Search indexer reports partial failures, and vector queries return fewer high-scoring matches than expected.
What should the team investigate first?
explanation_html:
Indexer execution history is the best first place to investigate because the symptoms began after a document refresh and the search indexer reports partial failures. Ingestion quality, document cracking, enrichment, chunking, embedding generation, and index population all affect the quality of retrieved grounding content.
Weak relevance in a RAG system is often caused by stale or incomplete indexing, poor chunking, missing fields, failed enrichment, or vector field population issues. The team should verify which documents failed, which enrichment steps failed, and whether the expected searchable and vector fields were populated correctly.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Model temperature can affect response variability, but it does not explain indexer partial failures or fewer high-scoring vector matches. Lowering temperature might make answers more deterministic, but it would not repair missing or stale grounding content. The problem started after a document refresh, which points to ingestion and indexing. This option focuses on generation behavior rather than retrieval health.
  • C. Content Safety threshold settings can block or filter harmful content, but they do not explain stale policy answers or vector retrieval degradation. Safety controls are important for responsible AI, but the scenario provides evidence of search indexer issues. Adjusting moderation thresholds could mask symptoms without fixing the retrieval problem. The relevant issue is ingestion quality and search index health.
  • D. Application Insights sampling affects how much telemetry is collected or retained, not whether the search index has current content. Sampling might make troubleshooting harder if too much telemetry is dropped. However, it would not cause vector queries to return weaker matches. The indexer failure signal is more directly tied to the observed relevance problem.

Vector relevance and ranking in Azure AI Search
Performance tips for Azure AI Search

question_html:
A marketing app uses Azure OpenAI image generation models. Users can create new product-background images, but requests to replace only a selected region of an existing image are returning full-image generations instead of localized edits.
What should the developer configure?
explanation_html:
A mask-based image edit request is the best fix because the issue involves modifying only a selected region of an existing image. Inpainting and localized image editing depend on providing the source image, edit instructions, and a mask that identifies the area to modify.
The current behavior suggests the app is using generation rather than edit semantics. Prompt-driven generation can create an entirely new image, but mask-based editing is the appropriate pattern when the unchanged regions must remain intact.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. A text embedding deployment supports vector search and semantic similarity. It does not edit images or preserve selected image regions. It could help retrieve prompts or assets, but it cannot perform inpainting. The issue is image modification, not text retrieval.
  • C. Image Analysis dense captions describe regions within an image. They do not modify image pixels or apply localized edits. Dense captions might help understand what is present in a region before editing. They are not the correct mechanism for replacing a selected region.
  • D. A Content Understanding video analyzer processes video content into structured outputs. It does not perform image inpainting or prompt-driven visual edits. It is useful for video extraction and media understanding workflows. The scenario is specifically about localized image editing.

Azure OpenAI REST API reference
Microsoft Foundry Playgrounds

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ENASvCHfdLcmLCbNaDDClGWnxkItxJw2OQHw6EpbP9M/edit?usp=sharing
Contoso needs generated responses to use approved policy documents and product guides as grounding data. Customer service agents must receive responses with relevant source references, and the retrieval layer must support keyword and semantic matching across policy wording variations.
Which component should Contoso include in the design?
explanation_html:
Azure AI Search is the best fit because Contoso needs a retrieval layer that can index enterprise documents and support grounded generative AI responses. It can support full-text, vector, and hybrid retrieval patterns, which are important when users ask questions that do not exactly match the wording in policy documents.
Blob Storage is still useful as the document source, but it is not the retrieval engine for grounded question answering. The case study specifically requires approved enterprise documents, hybrid retrieval, vector search, and source references, which aligns directly with Azure AI Search.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure Blob index tags are useful for basic object metadata and lifecycle organization, but they do not provide semantic retrieval for grounded AI answers. They cannot perform hybrid search across document chunks. They also do not provide ranking, vector similarity, or retrieval features needed for RAG-style responses. This option confuses storage metadata with a searchable grounding layer.
  • B. Azure SQL full-text search can search structured or relational content, but it is not the best fit for indexing mixed policy documents, PDFs, and product guides from Blob Storage for generative AI grounding. It does not provide the same native AI search capabilities for vector and hybrid retrieval. It would also add unnecessary data movement and schema design overhead for document-heavy content. This option is plausible only if the data were primarily relational.
  • D. Azure Container Apps ingress controls how traffic reaches containerized workloads. It does not index documents or retrieve grounding passages for a model. It might host the backend API, but it is not responsible for document ranking, semantic matching, or source retrieval. This option confuses application hosting with search and retrieval.

Hybrid search in Azure AI Search
Vector search in Azure AI Search

Which configuration should replace the missing configuration?
explanation_html:

The application must still be granted the appropriate Azure role permissions for Azure AI Search. The code change alone does not grant access, but it enables the application to request Microsoft Entra tokens using the managed identity instead of a static secret.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. AzureKeyCredential from app settings uses an API key stored in configuration. That directly violates the case study constraint that production workloads must not store secrets or API keys. It might technically authenticate to Azure AI Search, but it does not satisfy Contoso’s security requirement. This option is a common shortcut that fails the identity design constraint.
  • C. ClientSecretCredential from environment variables uses an application registration and client secret. That still requires storing a secret somewhere in the runtime environment. It also creates secret rotation and operational management overhead that managed identity avoids. This option is plausible for some service-to-service authentication scenarios, but not for this case study.
  • D. InteractiveBrowserCredential with user prompt is not appropriate for a production backend service. It expects interactive user authentication and is mainly useful in development or local tooling scenarios. A Container Apps backend should authenticate non-interactively. question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ENASvCHfdLcmLCbNaDDClGWnxkItxJw2OQHw6EpbP9M/edit?usp=sharing
Contoso needs to extract loan applicant details, income fields, document identifiers, and supporting evidence values from scanned and digital application documents. The extraction process must be validated before it is used by the production review workflow.
Steps
Review extraction accuracy and improve labels.
Label representative loan documents.
Train a custom extraction model.
Analyze production documents from the backend API.
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
2 is first because Contoso must provide representative loan documents and label the fields that the model needs to extract. A custom extraction model depends on labeled examples so the service can learn the target schema and field locations.
3 is second because the labeled examples are used to train the custom extraction model. 1 is third because Contoso must evaluate the model’s extraction quality and refine labels or examples before production use. 4 is last because the backend API should call the validated model only after the model has been trained and reviewed.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This sequence trains the model before the documents are labeled. That does not match the custom extraction workflow because the model needs labeled examples first. Training before labeling would not provide the service with the target fields to learn. The later validation and production analysis steps are reasonable, but the first two steps are reversed.
  • B. This sequence reviews extraction accuracy before the model is trained. There is no trained extraction model to evaluate at that point. Reviewing labels before training can be part of quality control, but that is not the same as validating model output. The sequence delays training until after a review step that depends on training results.
  • C. This sequence runs production document analysis before reviewing extraction accuracy. That creates operational risk because incorrect field extraction could enter the loan review workflow. The business goal is to reduce manual review time, but not by skipping validation. Production use should follow model evaluation and refinement.

Contoso is preparing the production deployment for customer-facing grounded question answering. Compliance has not approved any exception for customer data processing outside Australian Azure regions.
Problem:
The solution must keep customer data in Australian Azure regions.
Proposed solution:
Deploy the generative model by using a Global Standard deployment in Microsoft Foundry. Keep Azure Blob Storage and Azure AI Search in Australia East.
Does the proposed solution meet the goal?

For this case study, Contoso must choose a deployment approach and region alignment that satisfies Australian data residency requirements or obtain a compliance exception. The proposed solution optimizes capacity and availability, but it does not fully satisfy the stated non-negotiable residency constraint.
Why the other options are incorrect:
• A. Yes is incorrect because it ignores the model processing location. The requirement applies to customer data in the solution, not just the storage and search index. A grounded AI workflow sends user prompts and retrieved content to the model endpoint, so the deployment type matters. This proposed design leaves a compliance gap.

question_html:
Refer to:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ENASvCHfdLcmLCbNaDDClGWnxkItxJw2OQHw6EpbP9M/edit?usp=sharing
After Contoso disables public network access on Azure AI Search, the Container Apps backend can no longer query the search index. Network tests show that the search service hostname still resolves to a public IP address from the integrated virtual network.
What should Contoso configure next?

options.text: C. Azure Front Door WAF policy

explanation_html:
A private endpoint gives the service a private IP address inside the virtual network, but clients must resolve the service hostname to that private address. If the hostname still resolves publicly, the backend will not reach the private endpoint path correctly.
Configuring the appropriate private DNS zone and linking it to the virtual network is the best next step. This aligns name resolution with the private endpoint so the backend can connect privately while public access remains disabled.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. An Application Insights sampling rule affects telemetry collection volume. It does not change network routing or DNS resolution. It might help reduce monitoring costs, but it cannot make a private endpoint reachable. This option confuses observability configuration with private connectivity.
  • C. Azure Front Door WAF policy protects public web endpoints from web threats. It does not resolve private endpoint DNS issues inside a virtual network. It also does not provide private name resolution for Azure AI Search. This option is plausible for public application protection, but not for private backend access.
  • D. A search semantic ranking profile affects result ranking quality. It does not control whether the backend can connect to the search service. It cannot fix hostname resolution to a private endpoint. This option confuses search relevance configuration with networking configuration.

Match the following:
Requirements:

Translate customer text interactions

Azure AI Translator supports text translation for multilingual customer interactions. Azure Monitor is the correct destination for reviewing operational telemetry such as latency, token usage, traces, and related runtime signals when integrated with the application and AI workload.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This mapping incorrectly uses Azure Blob Storage as the grounding component. Blob Storage can store the source documents, but it does not provide the retrieval and ranking layer needed for grounded answers. It also maps translation and search responsibilities to the wrong requirements. Azure Key Vault stores secrets and keys, but it is not used to review token usage or latency.
  • B. This mapping incorrectly assigns Document Intelligence to grounded policy answering. Document Intelligence extracts fields and structure from documents, but it is not the retrieval layer for live grounded responses. It also assigns Azure Monitor to harmful content detection, which confuses monitoring with safety filtering. The translation and content safety entries are present, but they are mapped to the wrong requirements.
  • C. This mapping reverses several responsibilities. Azure AI Translator does not ground answers against approved enterprise documents. question_html:
A media company wants to build a grounded assistant over contracts, product images, recorded interviews, and training videos. The assistant must answer questions using extracted content from all modalities and retrieve relevant passages or segments at query time.
The solution must:

  • process documents, images, audio, and video
  • transform extracted content into searchable grounding data
  • support retrieval from indexed content
  • avoid placing raw media directly into every prompt

Which design should you implement?

options.text: A. Blob Storage with manual prompt attachments
B. Azure SQL with full-text search
C. Vision OCR with speech captions
D. Content Understanding with Azure AI Search

explanation_html:
Content Understanding with Azure AI Search is the best design because Content Understanding can extract structured and semantic information from multimodal content, while Azure AI Search can index the extracted content for retrieval. This separates media processing from query-time grounding.
The key RAG design principle is to convert raw content into searchable grounding assets before the user asks a question. Raw documents, images, audio, and video should not be repeatedly pasted into prompts because that is expensive, unreliable, and difficult to rank.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Blob Storage is appropriate for storing source media, but it is not a retrieval and enrichment pipeline by itself. Manual prompt attachments do not scale and do not provide consistent ranking across many files. The requirement is to ingest and index content for grounding, not to attach raw files at runtime.
  • B. Azure SQL with full-text search can support some structured and text-based search scenarios. It is not the strongest fit for extracting and indexing multimodal content such as images, audio, and video. It also does not provide the same built-in RAG-oriented search capabilities as Azure AI Search.
  • C. Vision OCR and speech captions can extract some content from images and audio. This option is incomplete because it does not address video, document structure, multimodal field extraction, or indexing for retrieval. It also lacks a retrieval layer that can rank and return grounding content at query time.

Azure AI Search indexing overview
Retrieval Augmented Generation in Azure AI Search

question_html:
You need to build a support agent that answers from policy files, checks live ticket status through a function, and preserves follow-up context for each user.
Steps
Submit requested function-call outputs to continue.
Create the agent with retrieval and function tools.
Create or reuse a conversation for the user.
Add the user message and start response processing.
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
2 is first because the agent must be configured with the retrieval and function tools before it can decide whether to search files or call live systems. Without the agent definition and tool definitions, the runtime has no valid tool inventory to use.
3 is second because the conversation provides the stateful context for the user’s ongoing interaction. 4 is third because the user message starts the response process within that conversation. 1 is last because function-call outputs are submitted only after the model requests a function call during response processing.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This sequence creates or reuses the conversation before creating the tool-enabled agent. That can preserve user context, but it does not prepare the agent to perform retrieval or function calling. The agent should be configured before the user message is processed.
  • C. This sequence starts response processing before establishing the user conversation. That weakens conversation memory because follow-up context is not anchored correctly before the message is processed. It also submits function outputs before the ordered conversation flow is established.
  • D. This sequence starts with the user message before the agent and conversation are prepared. That reverses the normal runtime setup and makes tool use ambiguous. Function outputs cannot be submitted before the model has requested a specific function call.

File search tool for agents
Use function calling with Microsoft Foundry agents

question_html:
An agent must use different tools depending on the task. Match each requirement to the most appropriate tool or capability.

question_html:
A developer uploads 200 product PDFs for an agent that uses file search. Immediately after upload, the agent answers from its base model and does not cite the uploaded files. The vector store status still shows ingestion is in progress.
What should the developer do next?

options.text: A. Increase prompt token limit for every request
B. Replace files with prompt examples
C. Wait for vector store readiness
D. Disable hybrid search and reranking

explanation_html:
The best next step is to wait until the vector store is ready. File search depends on ingestion steps such as chunking, embedding generation, indexing, and retrieval preparation before uploaded files can reliably ground responses.
Changing model temperature, prompt size, or retrieval behavior does not fix an incomplete ingestion pipeline. The issue is not that the model is unable to reason; it is that the file search tool does not yet have a fully prepared vector store to retrieve from.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Increasing the prompt token limit does not make unprocessed files searchable. Token limits affect how much context can be sent to the model, not whether uploaded files have been chunked, embedded, and indexed. This may increase cost without addressing the root cause.
  • B. Prompt examples can guide response style, but they do not replace the file search ingestion process. The requirement is grounded retrieval from uploaded PDFs, not few-shot prompting. Replacing files with examples would reduce factual grounding and make the solution less maintainable.
  • D. Disabling hybrid search and reranking would likely reduce retrieval quality rather than fix ingestion. Hybrid search and reranking help file search identify useful content once the vector store is prepared. The failure occurs before retrieval quality can be evaluated because ingestion is still in progress.

question_html:
A legal operations team needs a workflow where an intake agent gathers the request, specialist agents analyze privacy and contract risk, and a coordinator agent prepares the final recommendation. Human approval is required before the workflow creates any downstream legal task.
Steps
Add a human approval step before side-effecting actions.
Define specialized agents with tools and handoff boundaries.
Create a workflow pattern for agent coordination.
Pass outputs between agents using routing logic.
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
2 is first because the workflow needs clearly defined agents before collaboration can be orchestrated. Each specialist agent should have its own role, instructions, tools, and boundaries so that handoff behavior is predictable.
3 is second because the workflow pattern defines how agents coordinate. 4 is third because routing logic passes outputs between agents after the orchestration structure exists. 1 is last because approval should gate the final side-effecting action after the agents have produced and routed their analysis.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. This sequence creates the workflow before defining the participating agents. That makes the orchestration design premature because the workflow cannot correctly route tasks without knowing each agent’s role and boundary. It also places approval before output routing, which prevents the approver from reviewing the combined specialist analysis.
  • C. This sequence defines the agents first, but it routes outputs before creating the workflow pattern. Routing logic needs an orchestration structure, such as a sequential, branching, or group pattern. It also puts approval before workflow creation, which disconnects the approval gate from the actual automated process.
  • D. This sequence starts with human approval before the agents have analyzed anything. Approval should be based on the proposed final action and supporting context, not performed before the workflow produces a recommendation. It also delays agent definition until after workflow creation, which weakens the handoff design.

A static prompt chain can support simple linear workflows, but this scenario needs dynamic tool selection and conditional reasoning. The requirement to preserve the tool-call path also makes an agentic design more appropriate than a single model invocation or a search-only pattern.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. A single Azure OpenAI chat deployment can generate responses, but it does not by itself orchestrate multiple tools, API calls, and escalation decisions. It would require custom orchestration around it to meet the workflow requirements. It also does not inherently provide the agent-style tool execution pattern needed for this scenario. That makes a tool-augmented agent pattern a better fit.
  • D. Azure AI Search vector index and embeddings can support retrieval and grounding, but they do not orchestrate the full reasoning workflow. Search can supply relevant policy content, but it will not call the order API or manage human escalation. It is a useful supporting component, not the main workflow design. A financial services app must classify customer requests using deterministic business rules first. Ambiguous requests must be routed to an LLM, and high-risk responses must pass through a safety check before being returned.

Prompt flow with conditional nodes is the best orchestration choice because the scenario requires routing between deterministic rules, model calls, and safety checks. The key requirement is not simply to call an LLM, but to coordinate multiple decision paths in a controlled workflow.
A hybrid LLM-plus-rules system needs an orchestration layer that can sequence and branch logic. Conditional flow design allows rules to run before model inference and safety checks to run after generated output, which directly matches the required pipeline.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure Blob Storage lifecycle policy manages retention and tiering for stored data. It does not orchestrate runtime decision logic across models, rules, and safety checks. It could store artifacts or logs, but it is not a workflow controller. This distractor is plausible only if the learner confuses storage management with application orchestration.
  • B. Azure AI Search semantic ranking profile improves retrieval ranking for search results. It does not route requests through business rules, LLM calls, and safety checks. Search may be part of a grounded workflow, but the scenario is about orchestration. Selecting it would address retrieval quality rather than multistep control flow.
  • C. Azure OpenAI model deployment provides model inference capacity, but it is not the orchestration layer. It can process ambiguous requests after routing, but it does not implement deterministic pre-checks or post-generation safety branching by itself. The deployment is a component inside the architecture. It is not sufficient as the coordinator for a hybrid rules-and-LLM system.

Measures whether the answer addresses the user query
Measures harmful or unsafe content risk
Measures invented unsupported claims

explanation_html:
Groundedness evaluates whether an answer is supported by the supplied or retrieved context, which is critical for RAG and grounded assistants. Relevance checks whether the response actually addresses the user query, while safety checks for harmful categories and fabrication targets unsupported invented content.
This mapping tests the difference between quality, safety, relevance, and grounding signals. These metrics are related, but they are not interchangeable; a response can be fluent and still ungrounded, or relevant and still unsafe.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. This mapping incorrectly places relevance where groundedness belongs. Coherence and fluency are quality dimensions, but they do not directly prove that retrieved context supports the answer. Groundedness is also misplaced under harmful content risk. The option sounds plausible because all labels are evaluation-related, but the mappings do not match the evaluation goals.
  • C. Safety is not the metric for checking support from retrieved context. Fabrication is also not the same as query relevance, even though fabricated answers can appear responsive. Relevance and groundedness are reversed in effect across the mapping. This option confuses risk categories with retrieval-support and answer-fit metrics.
  • D. Coherence and fluency assess readability and logical flow, not context support or unsafe content risk. Similarity may be useful in some evaluation scenarios, but it is not the direct metric for detecting fabricated unsupported claims. The mapping fails the core grounded-assistant requirements. It emphasizes surface quality rather than the requested evaluation dimensions.

A custom evaluator is the best fit because the company needs to measure a domain-specific requirement that is not fully represented by general built-in quality or safety evaluators. Internal legal wording is a business-specific criterion, so a custom evaluator can encode the required scoring logic.
Built-in evaluators are useful for common dimensions such as groundedness, relevance, coherence, fluency, and safety. When the evaluation criterion depends on company-specific policy language or legal phrasing, custom evaluation is the more precise choice.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. A safety evaluator checks harm-related risks, not whether return-label language follows internal legal wording. It is valuable for responsible AI controls, but it does not encode the company’s specific text requirement. The option is plausible because legal wording can sound like a risk issue. In this case, the requirement is compliance with internal phrasing, not harmful-content detection.
  • B. Groundedness verifies whether generated content is supported by retrieved context. It does not necessarily score whether the exact legal wording standard is followed. Even a grounded answer can fail internal wording requirements. This option would help if the problem were unsupported claims, but that is not the stated evaluation gap.
  • D. Token analytics can reveal length, usage, and cost patterns, but it does not evaluate legal wording quality. It may help operational monitoring after deployment. It cannot replace an evaluator that scores domain-specific response content. This option confuses observability metrics with semantic evaluation.

Application Insights tracing integration is the best next step because the team needs execution-path visibility, including tool calls and step-level behavior. Aggregate request counts are insufficient for diagnosing where latency occurs or why a safety block happened in a multistep agent workflow.
Tracing supports deeper observability than high-level metrics alone. For agents and generative AI systems, useful investigation often requires correlating model calls, tool calls, latency, tokens, errors, and safety signals across a single run.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Blob lifecycle rules can manage storage retention, but they do not produce traces or step-level telemetry. They might help control the cost of retained artifacts after observability data exists. They do not solve the immediate visibility gap. This option confuses data retention management with diagnostic instrumentation.
  • B. Azure AI Search scoring profiles affect search ranking behavior. They may improve retrieval quality, but they will not reconstruct agent tool calls or isolate latency across workflow steps. The issue is observability, not relevance tuning. Search configuration would be premature without trace evidence showing retrieval as the bottleneck.
  • C. Higher max tokens may increase output length and potentially latency. It does not provide diagnostic visibility into where the agent is spending time. It could make the production symptom worse if responses become longer. The problem is missing telemetry, not insufficient generation length.

question_html:
A bank is designing an agent-based loan-assistance app. The app must access Foundry model deployments, a private search index, customer documents, and Key Vault secrets. Security requires least privilege, no embedded secrets in code, and private access paths for platform resources.
Which infrastructure design best satisfies the requirements?

options.text: A. API keys stored in app configuration
B. Managed identities with private endpoints
C. Public endpoints with IP allowlists

explanation_html:
Managed identities with private endpoints best satisfy the security requirements. Managed identity supports secretless access with Azure RBAC, while private endpoints reduce public network exposure for supported Azure resources.
The scenario requires both identity hardening and network isolation. API keys or shared credentials may allow access, but they do not provide the same least-privilege and secretless operational model as managed identities combined with private connectivity.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. API keys stored in app configuration introduce secret-management risk and do not meet the no-embedded-secrets requirement. App configuration may centralize settings, but it does not remove the need to protect and rotate secrets. API keys are also typically broader and less identity-aware than RBAC assignments. This design is weaker for least privilege.
  • C. Public endpoints with IP allowlists can reduce exposure, but they still rely on public network paths. IP allowlists do not solve secretless authentication by themselves. They also become operationally brittle when clients, agents, or hosted services change outbound addresses. This option addresses part of networking but misses the identity requirement.
  • D. A shared service principal credential can authenticate workloads, but it creates credential distribution and rotation overhead. Sharing one credential also weakens workload-level accountability and least privilege. It does not inherently provide private network access. This option is plausible for automation, but it is not the best design for secure agent-based infrastructure.

]
)

Which configuration should replace (MISSING CONFIG)?

options.text: A. Environment variable containing a static API key
B. Storage account shared access signature
D. Entra token provider for Cognitive Services

explanation_html:
An Entra token provider for Cognitive Services is the correct configuration because the application is using keyless authentication with DefaultAzureCredential. The token provider obtains Microsoft Entra tokens for the correct resource scope, allowing the SDK client to authenticate with the managed identity.
This approach aligns with keyless credentials and RBAC because access is granted to the workload identity rather than to a shared secret. The security boundary becomes the managed identity and its assigned roles on the Foundry or Azure OpenAI resource. That enables least privilege, auditing, and easier credential rotation management.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. A static API key violates the requirement to avoid stored API keys. It may work technically for some requests, but it does not provide identity-based access control or per-workload traceability. It also increases secret rotation and leakage risk. The scenario explicitly says the managed identity already has the required RBAC role.
  • B. A storage account shared access signature is used to delegate scoped access to Azure Storage resources. It is not the credential mechanism for calling a Foundry model deployment through this SDK client. It would not obtain a token for the Cognitive Services resource scope. This option confuses storage data access with model endpoint authentication.
  • C. An anonymous bearer token callback is not a secure or valid enterprise authentication design. The client needs a real Microsoft Entra token provider that can acquire tokens using the managed identity chain. Anonymous access would not satisfy RBAC and would fail against protected endpoints. This option removes authentication rather than implementing keyless authentication.

question_html:
A regulated enterprise is deploying a Foundry-based assistant that uses model deployments, Azure AI Search, and storage-backed grounding content. Security requires no public network exposure, identity-based access to dependencies, and guardrails to prevent future resources from being deployed with public access enabled.
Which design best satisfies the requirements?

options.text: A. Private endpoints, managed identity, and Azure Policy
B. API keys, firewall allowlists, and diagnostic settings
C. Service endpoints, shared secrets, and content filters
D. Public endpoints, customer-managed keys, and RBAC

explanation_html:
Private endpoints, managed identity, and Azure Policy best satisfy the combined network, access, and governance requirements. Private endpoints remove public exposure for supported resources, managed identity provides identity-based access to dependencies, and Azure Policy can audit or deny noncompliant resource configurations.
The key is that the scenario requires multiple controls working together. Private networking restricts the path, RBAC and managed identity control who can access resources, and policy controls prevent drift from enterprise standards. No single security feature replaces all three responsibilities.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • B. API keys are shared secrets and do not provide the same identity-based governance as managed identity. Firewall allowlists can restrict access, but they do not provide private connectivity in the same way as private endpoints. Diagnostic settings help with logging but do not prevent public exposure. This option mixes useful controls but misses the strongest required network and identity pattern.
  • C. Service endpoints can be useful in some Azure networking designs, but they are not the strongest answer when the requirement says no public network exposure. Shared secrets also conflict with the requirement for identity-based dependency access. Content filters are responsible AI controls, not network isolation controls. This option does not cover the governance requirement to prevent future public deployments.
  • D. Public endpoints directly violate the no-public-exposure requirement. Customer-managed keys protect encryption key control, but they do not provide network isolation or identity-based runtime access by themselves. RBAC is important, but it cannot replace private networking. This option includes some enterprise controls while failing the core network requirement.

question_html:
A platform team wants to make Foundry project and agent releases repeatable. The team must avoid untracked portal changes, promote tested versions, and make recovery possible through automated redeployment.
Steps
Run evaluations and release quality gates
Define Foundry resources and dependencies as IaC
Deploy versioned agents or applications through the pipeline
Store agent definitions and tool bindings in source control
What is the correct order?
explanation_html:
The correct order is 2, 4, 1, 3. The team should first define the Foundry resource, projects, identities, and dependencies as infrastructure as code so environments can be reproduced. Then agent definitions, prompts, versions, and tool bindings should be stored in source control. Evaluations and quality gates should run before the release is promoted. Finally, the tested version is deployed through the pipeline.
2 is first because repeatable infrastructure is the base for lifecycle management and recovery. 4 is second because the agent configuration must be version-controlled before automation can reliably deploy it. 1 is third because release gates should validate the candidate before deployment. 3 is last because deployment should promote the tested and approved version.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This order starts with source-controlled agent definitions, but it delays infrastructure as code until the end. That makes the environment less repeatable and weakens recovery. It also deploys before evaluations and quality gates, which increases production release risk. The sequence does not establish a reliable promotion path.
  • B. This order starts with evaluations before the infrastructure and versioned artifacts are defined. Quality gates need a candidate artifact and target environment assumptions to be meaningful. It then deploys after source control, which is partly reasonable, but the early evaluation step is misplaced. The pipeline should validate a versioned candidate before release, not before the candidate is established.
  • D. This order begins by deploying before infrastructure, source-controlled definitions, or quality gates are established. That encourages manual or untracked changes and undermines repeatability. It then runs evaluations after deployment, which is too late for a release gate. The ordering conflicts with controlled lifecycle management.

question_html:
A support chatbot must answer complex follow-up questions over indexed enterprise content. The solution should decompose conversational queries, use configured search sources, and expose a retrieval operation that agents can call.
Match the following:
Knowledge source
Knowledge base
Agentic retrieval
Retrieve action
Choices:

options.text:
A.
Stores chat transcripts
Generates embeddings directly
Hosts OpenAPI tools
Deletes stale index chunks

B.
Defines source data to query
Stores all conversation memory
Applies model fine-tuning
Creates uploaded file stores

C.
Defines source data to query
Coordinates knowledge-source retrieval defaults
Plans subqueries with chat context
Calls the knowledge base pipeline

D.
Creates an agent role
Stores function schemas
Executes approval workflows
Publishes an agent endpoint

explanation_html:
Choice C correctly maps the Azure AI Search agentic retrieval components. A knowledge source identifies the content source to retrieve from, while a knowledge base coordinates the retrieval pipeline across one or more configured knowledge sources.
Agentic retrieval is the query-planning behavior that breaks complex conversational questions into better retrieval subqueries. The retrieve action is the API operation that invokes the knowledge base pipeline so an agent or application can use the retrieval result.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. This option confuses search retrieval components with unrelated storage and management tasks. Knowledge sources are not chat transcript stores, and knowledge bases are not embedding generators by themselves. The retrieve action invokes the retrieval pipeline; it is not a delete operation for stale chunks.
  • B. This option starts correctly for the knowledge source but then drifts into incorrect responsibilities. A knowledge base is not the same thing as conversation memory, and agentic retrieval is not model fine-tuning. Uploaded file stores can support file search scenarios, but they are not the same as the retrieve action on an Azure AI Search knowledge base.
  • D. This option describes agent application and workflow concepts rather than Azure AI Search retrieval concepts. Agent roles and function schemas are important for agent design, but they do not define knowledge sources or knowledge bases. Publishing an agent endpoint is also separate from invoking the Azure AI Search retrieval pipeline.

question_html:
A company is releasing a public-facing assistant. The assistant must detect harmful user-generated and model-generated content, reduce prompt injection risk, and apply runtime moderation before responses reach users.
Which service or capability should be included?

options.text: A. Azure AI Language PII detection
C. Azure AI Search semantic ranker

explanation_html:
Azure AI Content Safety is the best fit because it provides APIs and capabilities for detecting harmful user-generated and AI-generated content. It also includes safety features such as prompt injection risk detection through Prompt Shields, which is directly relevant to public-facing assistant guardrails.
The scenario is about runtime safety controls, moderation, and risk detection. These controls complement identity, networking, monitoring, and grounding, but they are not replaced by those capabilities. For AI-103, the important distinction is choosing the safety and moderation service rather than a monitoring, search, or language extraction feature.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Azure AI Language PII detection can identify and redact personally identifiable information in text. That is useful for privacy and compliance, but it does not provide the full harmful-content moderation and prompt injection protection described in the scenario. PII detection is a narrower language capability. The requirement is broader safety filtering and risk detection for assistant interactions.
  • C. Azure AI Search semantic ranker improves search result relevance by reranking candidates with language understanding. It can improve grounding quality in RAG systems, but it does not moderate harmful content or detect prompt injection attacks. It belongs in the retrieval layer, not the safety layer. This option confuses relevance improvement with responsible AI filtering.
  • D. Azure Monitor metric alerts can notify teams about operational thresholds such as latency, failures, or resource usage. Alerts are valuable for reliability monitoring, but they do not classify harmful content or block unsafe responses. They can observe events after instrumentation exists, but they are not the content moderation engine. The scenario needs runtime safety enforcement.

question_html:
A regulated claims-processing agent summarizes retrieved policy evidence and can recommend claim approval. Auditors must review how each answer was produced and who approved high-impact actions.
Which design element should you include?

options.text: A. Token metrics and model temperature
B. Content filters and private endpoints

explanation_html:
Traces, provenance metadata, citations, and approvals directly support auditability. Trace logging shows execution flow, provenance metadata and citations connect outputs to source material, and approval workflows document human authorization before high-impact actions.
The important distinction is that auditability is about reconstructing what happened and why. Monitoring, filtering, networking, and evaluation can all be valuable, but they do not by themselves provide the evidence chain required for review.
Why the other options are incorrect:

  • A. Token metrics and model temperature can help analyze cost, latency, and generation behavior. They do not show the full decision path, cited evidence, or approval history. Auditors would still lack a reliable record of which sources supported the answer and who approved the action.
  • B. Content filters and private endpoints improve safety and network security. They do not provide provenance, citations, or workflow approval records. A secure system can still be unauditable if it does not capture trace and decision evidence.
  • D. Fine-tuning and batch evaluation can improve or assess model behavior. They do not create per-request traceability for production decisions. Batch evaluation also happens outside the live approval path and cannot prove that a specific claim recommendation used the correct cited evidence.
